INVESTMENT BANKING — TECHNICAL QUESTIONS AND ANSWERS
Prepared: 15 October 2026

2,053 entries covering 2,188 original finance-question IDs.
135 repeated variants consolidated; 71 personal/recruiting or unusable fragments listed in the scope appendix.

HOW TO USE THIS FILE
The original question-only list is unchanged. Original F-number IDs are preserved; merged IDs appear under "Also covers". Firm labels show where a question was reported. They do not mean the firm supplied or approved the answer.
Answers are identified as guide answers, prepared model answers, concepts/methods, or frameworks. Date-dependent questions need fresh, dated research. Incomplete source cases receive formulas and assumptions rather than invented inputs. Stock pitches and personal deal discussions require a real example; sample reasoning is not a claim about your own experience.
For later website import, the companion JSON includes questions, answers, source labels, source references, answer status, and original/merged IDs.

COMMON NOTATION
EV = operating enterprise value; E = market value of common equity; D = debt; NI = net income; t = tax rate; r = required return; g = growth rate; D&A = depreciation and amortization; NWC = operating net working capital; FCFF/UFCF = unlevered free cash flow; FCFE = free cash flow to equity; WACC = weighted average cost of capital; MOIC = multiple of invested capital; IRR = internal rate of return.
Three-statement tax shields assume current usability only where stated. Book expenses and tax deductions may differ. Dollar amounts use the units in each question. A formula without a supplied rate or amount is intentionally symbolic.

[F0001] What is your outlook on the economy and financial markets?
Asked by / question source: Adams Street; Bank of America Credit; Bank of America NY; BlackRock SF; Citi LA; D.E. Shaw Research; Evercore (compiled interview notes); Evercore ECM; Evercore SF; Goldman Sachs Wealth Management; Guggenheim Partners; J.P. Morgan Asset Management; J.P. Morgan Finance and Business Management; J.P. Morgan Fixed Income; J.P. Morgan Research; J.P. Morgan SF; Nomura Global Markets; Nomura NY; Perella Weinberg Partners CHI; PIMCO Product & Strategy; PNC Capital Markets; RBC Capital Markets NY; Stephens; TD Securities NY
Answer status: Framework — dated research required
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
A useful macro answer links growth, inflation, employment and policy to earnings, discount rates, credit and investor positioning. Higher rates generally reduce fixed-rate bond values and increase funding costs; equity effects also depend on why rates rose and on earnings expectations. The Fed’s U.S. goals are maximum employment and stable prices; its inflation objective is measured using PCE, with core PCE often watched for underlying pressure. Fiscal policy changes government spending/taxes, while monetary policy changes financial conditions. An inverted curve can signal expected easing or weak growth but is not a certain recession forecast. Give a base case, a contrary case and indicators that would change your view rather than presenting a forecast as fact.

Asked by / question source: Adams Street
Answer status: Open-ended answer framework
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:

Reconcile reported earnings with cash generation and balance-sheet funding. In diligence, verify key claims against filings/contracts, cohort or customer data and independent industry evidence; stress downside assumptions. Recommend an action only after comparing its incremental cash return and risk with alternatives. If the business is unspecified, this is an analysis framework rather than a factual claim about a particular firm.

[F0006] Suppose that I put $10 into some investment vehicle and that 4 years from now, it's worth $50. Without using pen, paper, or calculator, determine the average yearly growth rate of said investment.
Asked by / question source: Advent International
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
The investment grows fivefold. CAGR = (50/10)^(1/4)-1 = 49.53% per year. A useful mental check is 1.5^4 = 5.0625, so the answer is just under 50%, not the 100% annual simple average.

[F0007] Walk me through a leveraged buyout (LBO) model.
Asked by / question source: Advent International; Ardian Private Equity; Bank of America NY; Barclays SF; BMO Capital Markets; BNP Paribas Leveraged Finance; Cain Brothers; Canaccord Genuity Boston; Citi Technology SF; Citizens Bank; DC Advisory NY; Deloitte Corporate Finance; Evercore (compiled interview notes); Evercore Healthcare MP; Financial Technology Partners SF; Goldman Sachs TMT SF; Greenhill NY; Guggenheim Partners NY; Houlihan Lokey Healthcare; Houlihan Lokey NY; Intrepid LA; J.P. Morgan (compiled interview notes); Jefferies; Jefferies NY; Lazard LA; Leerink Partners; LionTree; M&I 400 Questions Guide (2025), p. 120; M&I 400 Questions Guide (2025), p. 121; M&I 400 Questions Guide (2025), p. 124; M&I 400 Questions Guide (2025), p. 125; M&I 400 Questions Guide (2025), p. 31; Morgan Stanley NY; Morgan Stanley Singapore; Nomura NY; Piper Sandler NY; PJT Partners M&A; Raymond James NY; Shea & Co; Stephens; The Sage Group; UBS NY; Vista Equity Partners; William Blair SF
Also covers: F0436, F0849, F1014
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Start with the purchase price and an enterprise-to-equity bridge. Build sources and uses: purchase of equity, debt refinancing and fees are funded by new debt, sponsor equity and any permitted target cash. Forecast revenue, EBITDA, taxes, CapEx and working capital to derive cash available for debt service. Build debt schedules for interest, mandatory amortization, revolver draws and optional cash sweeps, checking minimum cash and covenants. At exit, multiply a defensible EBITDA by an exit multiple, subtract net debt and other claims, and allocate equity proceeds after management incentives. Calculate sponsor MOIC and dated IRR, including interim distributions. Sensitize entry/exit multiples, growth, margins and leverage; show a downside case with liquidity and covenant headroom.

[F0008] What are the most important drivers for value growth in a industrial roofing company?
Asked by / question source: Advent International
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Build revenue from operating units rather than assuming a growth rate: customers/volume * frequency/utilization * net price, plus ancillary streams. Separate variable costs from fixed costs to model contribution margin, operating leverage and break-even volume. For a pharmacy use prescription volumes, reimbursement/mix, dispensing margin and payer terms; roofing uses crew capacity, projects, ticket size and repair/replacement mix; software/telecom uses subscribers, ARPU, churn and network/service costs; a food outlet uses footfall, conversion, ticket and opening days. Forecast working capital, maintenance/growth CapEx and taxes. Value sustainable after-tax cash flow and cross-check peers; local concentration, regulation and reinvestment can explain different multiples despite similar current profits.

[F0009] What drives revenue and EBITDA growth for a pharmacy?
Asked by / question source: Advent International
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Pharmacy revenue depends on prescription volume, reimbursement per prescription, drug mix, customer retention, payer/network access and front-of-store sales. EBITDA depends on the spread between reimbursement and drug acquisition cost, dispensing/labor productivity, occupancy and overhead, generic/specialty mix and reimbursement pressure. Revenue can grow while EBITDA falls if mix or payer rates deteriorate. Distinguish independent retail, specialty and pharmacy-benefit-management economics.

[F0012] What is private equity?
Asked by / question source: Advent International; Moelis & Co. PFA NY; Vista Equity Partners
Also covers: F1614
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
A PE fund raises commitments from limited partners, calls capital for investments, supports portfolio companies and distributes exit proceeds. The manager earns management fees and, subject to the agreement/hurdle, carried interest on gains. A fund of funds invests in underlying funds, offering diversification and access with an additional fee layer. Secondaries transfer existing fund interests or assets; GP-led continuation deals may offer investors liquidity or a rollover choice. Buyers assess NAV quality, unfunded commitments, concentration, remaining duration and price discounts/premiums. Secondaries can reduce blind-pool risk and duration, but do not automatically deliver higher IRR or MOIC; timing, pricing, leverage and asset performance determine returns.

[F0013] What is a leveraged buyout (LBO)?
Asked by / question source: Advent International; Deutsche Bank SF; Evercore (compiled interview notes); Moelis & Co. PFA NY; Shea & Co
Also covers: F1186
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
An LBO buys a company using sponsor equity and debt serviced by the target’s cash flows. Set entry EV and equity purchase price, build sources and uses including fees/refinancing, forecast operations and cash generation, model debt interest/amortization and the cash sweep, then estimate exit EV and subtract exit net debt and other claims. Sponsor MOIC = proceeds/invested equity; with one entry and exit, IRR = MOIC^(1/years)-1. Returns come from operating growth, deleveraging, entry/exit valuation and distributions. More leverage increases both upside and default risk. Favor resilient cash conversion, manageable CapEx, credible improvements and a defensible purchase price. Strategic buyers may pay more for synergies; sponsors may offer certainty, speed, rollover equity or management continuity.

[F0015] Why might software companies have a large negative working capital balance?
Asked by / question source: Aeris Partners
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Negative operating working capital can be healthy when customers pay before delivery and suppliers are paid later; subscriptions and some retailers fund operations this way. It can also reflect overdue suppliers or distress. Examine cash conversion, deferred revenue, aging schedules and liquidity. For a growing business with sustainably negative operating working capital, growth can release cash; a slowdown can reverse that benefit. Distinguish operating NWC from the broad current-assets-minus-current-liabilities definition.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

[F0016] Why is EBITDA an important metric?
Asked by / question source: Aeris Partners; BlackRock SF; William Blair SF
Also covers: F0267
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
EBITDA = revenue - cash operating expenses before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization; EBIT = EBITDA - D&A. Net income also includes interest, taxes and non-operating items. EBITDA helps compare operating performance across financing and depreciation conventions, but is not cash flow: it ignores CapEx, working capital and cash taxes. A business can have positive EBITDA yet run out of cash because of reinvestment, interest, maturities, working-capital needs or one-time payments. EBIT can be more meaningful for asset-heavy businesses because depreciation captures part of asset consumption. Evaluate adjusted EBITDA add-backs critically and avoid adding recurring costs back simply because management labels them exceptional.

[F0017] Walk me through a typical sell-side M&A process.
Asked by / question source: Aeris Partners; Citizens Bank; Evercore (compiled interview notes); Houlihan Lokey Healthcare; Jefferies NY; M&I 400 Questions Guide (2025), p. 29; Piper Sandler NY; Société Générale NY; Stephens
Also covers: F0847
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Clarify shareholder objectives and transaction perimeter; perform diligence and valuation; prepare the teaser, confidential information memorandum and buyer list; contact approved buyers and execute NDAs; distribute materials and receive indications of interest; run management presentations and data-room diligence; obtain final bids; negotiate terms, financing and the definitive agreement; then satisfy conditions and close. Maintain confidentiality, competition and process discipline. Strategic fit, certainty, terms and timing can matter as much as headline price.

[F0018] Name an industry where beta is negative.
Asked by / question source: Aeris Partners
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
CAPM estimates cost of equity as risk-free rate + levered beta * equity risk premium, with justified additional risk adjustments where appropriate. Estimate beta using a regression of stock excess returns on market excess returns, or bottom-up comparable-company betas. Beta reflects systematic risk; leverage, cyclicality and operating fixed costs can raise it. It is not a measure of all uncertainty or an invariant property of an industry. Historical estimates depend on window, frequency and benchmark, and CAPM’s single-factor assumptions are simplifications. Compare operating risk first, then financing; a higher-growth firm does not mechanically have a higher beta.

[F0019] Walk through a recent M&A transaction you have followed.
Asked by / question source: Aeris Partners; Union Square Advisors
Answer status: Framework — dated research required
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Assess a transaction through strategic fit, price versus standalone and synergy value, financing, execution and integration risk. Explain buyer/target businesses, consideration, purchase multiple, expected cash benefits and why a deal is preferable to organic investment. Test downside cases, regulatory constraints and ability to finance/close. More EPS or more revenue alone does not prove value creation; incremental risk-adjusted returns should exceed the cost of capital. For a named historical transaction, use the announcement, filings and investor presentations to establish terms, and distinguish the rationale known at signing from later outcomes. No unspecified deal supports a factual purchase multiple or recommendation.

[F0023] How does a decrease in deferred revenue flow through the financial statements? Assume a 20% tax rate.
Asked by / question source: Aeris Partners
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Cash arrives before the service is delivered, so it sits as a liability until earned. Take $100 collected upfront for a service delivered evenly over a year, no delivery costs, 20% tax rate.

• At collection: no income-statement effect. Cash +$100 and Deferred Revenue +$100, so the balance sheet balances with no change in equity.

• Income Statement, as delivered: Revenue +$100, so Pre-Tax Income is up $100 and Net Income is up $80.

• Cash Flow Statement: Net Income +$80, and the $100 decrease in Deferred Revenue is a negative, so cash falls $20.

• Balance Sheet: Cash −$20 and Deferred Revenue −$100, so assets fall $20 while liabilities fall $100 and Retained Earnings rises $80; both sides fall $20 and balance.

• Intuition: the company already holds the cash, so recognition only moves the obligation into earnings and triggers the $20 of tax.

Straight-line delivery over N months recognises contract value / N each month. Bookings, billings, revenue and cash collection are four different things, and tax recognition can differ from book.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

[F0024] What happens to the three statements if you change deferred revenue by 10 dollars? Assume a 20% tax rate.
Asked by / question source: Aeris Partners
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Clarify which direction is meant, because the two cases differ. Take $10 and a 20% tax rate.

• A $10 prepayment: Cash +$10 and Deferred Revenue +$10, no income-statement effect and no change in equity.

• Recognising $10 of previously deferred revenue, with no delivery cost: Pre-Tax Income +$10 and Net Income +$8.

• Cash Flow Statement: Net Income +$8 less the $10 reduction in Deferred Revenue, so cash falls $2.

• Balance Sheet: Deferred Revenue −$10 and Cash −$2, against Retained Earnings +$8, so both sides fall $2 and balance.

• Intuition: the cash came in earlier; recognition only triggers the $2 of tax.

[F0025] What happens to CFs when NWC goes up?
Asked by / question source: Aeris Partners
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
An increase in operating net working capital uses cash, so it reduces CFO and FCFF dollar-for-dollar, holding earnings and other items constant. More inventory/receivables tie up funds; higher operating payables/deferred revenue release funds. Broad working capital including cash or debt is not the same as operating NWC used in a DCF.

[F0026] How should a seller select a financial sponsor when there are multiple potential buyers?
Asked by / question source: Aeris Partners
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Compare sponsor bids on net proceeds, financing certainty, conditions, timing, diligence progress, management treatment, governance and rollover terms, operating plan and execution record. A higher headline price can be worse if it includes an uncertain earn-out or weak funding. Assess conflicts and negotiate comparable terms so the seller can compare risk-adjusted value.

[F0027] Walk through a multi-year inventory purchase financed with debt, including depreciation and interest payments. Assume a 20% tax rate. [Amounts and timing not recorded.]
Asked by / question source: Aeris Partners
Answer status: Method / conditional answer — source details needed
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
The source omits the amounts and timing, so work the depreciation step from a clean example: $10 of incremental depreciation at a 20% tax rate.

• Income Statement: EBIT and Pre-Tax Income fall $10 and Net Income falls $8.

• Cash Flow Statement: Net Income −$8 plus the $10 non-cash add-back, so cash rises $2.

• Balance Sheet: Cash +$2 and Net PP&E −$10, so assets and Retained Earnings both fall $8 and the balance sheet balances.

• Intuition: the only cash effect is the $2 tax saving.

Depreciation allocates an asset's cost over its useful life rather than measuring its market value. Buying the asset is a separate, capitalised step with no income-statement effect.

[F0028] For a market-sizing estimate, what databases would you consult to replace your assumptions with more accurate information, and why?
Asked by / question source: Alpine Investors
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Use both top-down and bottom-up estimates. Define geography, period and units, estimate addressable customers * penetration * usage frequency * spend, and cross-check against capacity * utilization * price or supplier volumes. State assumptions, avoid double counting, and show a range and sensitivity to the largest driver. Market share times total market volume gives company volume; revenue share need not equal unit share when prices differ. If the input population, price or demand is absent, a unique numerical total cannot be calculated.

[F0029] You have 2 companies: A & B. A has 20m revenue, 5m EBITDA, 40% customer concentration, and is 80% recurring revenue. B has 20m revenue, 4m EBITDA, 10% customer concentration, and is 100% recurring revenue. Which would you invest in and why?
Asked by / question source: Alpine Investors
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
A has a 25% EBITDA margin; B has 20%. B offers lower customer concentration and more recurring revenue, which can justify a higher multiple and lower downside risk. I would provisionally prefer B for resilience, but cannot choose conclusively without price, growth, retention, cash conversion and debt. A could be the better investment if materially cheaper or its concentrated customer relationships are durable.

[F0033] How much would you pay for 2x your money on a 12% PIK, no compounding security?
Asked by / question source: Apollo Global Management Private Equity
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
The prompt is ambiguous about purchase price, face value and maturity. With simple non-compounding 12% PIK, principal doubles in 1/0.12 = 8.33 years if bought at par and fully repaid. Its annualized return over that period is 2^(1/8.33)-1, about 8.67%, not 12%. For a target required annual return r and payoff of 2*face at year T, maximum price is 2*face/(1+r)^T.

[F0034] Estimate IRR of your deals?
Asked by / question source: Apollo Global Management Private Equity
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
MOIC = total cash proceeds/total invested capital and does not account for timing. With a single entry and exit, annualized return or IRR = (exit proceeds/entry investment)^(1/years)-1. With interim cash flows, solve 0 = sum[CF_t/(1+r)^t]; use dated cash flows for XIRR. Earlier distributions generally increase IRR at the same MOIC. MOIC can favor a larger long-held gain while IRR favors rapid capital return; assess both alongside risk and absolute profit. ROE is accounting net income/average book equity and is not the same as an investment IRR.

[F0037] Walk me through a discounted cash flow (DCF) valuation.
Asked by / question source: Apollo Global Management Private Equity; Apollo Global Management Real Estate Credit; Ardian Secondaries; Bain Capital Credit; Bank of America CHI; Bank of America NY; Barclays SF; BlackRock; BlackRock SF; Blackstone Group; BMO Capital Markets; BMO Capital Markets SF; BNP Paribas NY; Cain Brothers; Canaccord Genuity Boston; Centerview Partners NY; Citi Healthcare; Citi LA; DC Advisory NY; Deloitte Corporate Finance; Deutsche Bank SF; Ducera Partners NY; Eastdil Secured SF; Ernst & Young M&A; Evercore (compiled interview notes); Evercore Healthcare MP; Financial Technology Partners SF; Goldman Sachs HK; Goldman Sachs LA; Goldman Sachs NY Financing; Goldman Sachs Wealth Management; Greenhill NY; Guggenheim Partners NY; Intrepid LA; J.P. Morgan (compiled interview notes); J.P. Morgan CHI; J.P. Morgan LA; J.P. Morgan SF; Jefferies; Jefferies NY; KeyBanc NY; KKR; Lazard Healthcare SF; Lazard LA; Leerink Partners; LionTree; M&I 400 Questions Guide (2025), p. 100; M&I 400 Questions Guide (2025), p. 86; M&I 400 Questions Guide (2025), p. 94; M&I 400 Questions Guide (2025), p. 95; Macquarie Group LA; Miller Buckfire; Moelis & Co. PFA NY; Morgan Stanley NY; Morgan Stanley SF; MUFG; MUFG LA; Nomura NY; Perella Weinberg Partners; Perella Weinberg Partners Healthcare SF; Perella Weinberg Partners NY; Perella Weinberg Partners SF; Piper Sandler NY; PJT Partners M&A; PJT Partners RSSG NY; Raine Group; Raymond James FIG; Raymond James NY; Rothschild & Co. LA; Shea & Co; Société Générale NY; Stephens; TD Securities NY; TD Securities SF; The Sage Group; UBS NY; Union Square Advisors; Wells Fargo NY; William Blair CHI; William Blair SF
Also covers: F0425
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Forecast operating cash flow for a period long enough to reach a sustainable state. Calculate unlevered free cash flow as EBIT*(1-tax rate) + D&A - CapEx - increase in operating working capital. Discount it at WACC, and add the present value of terminal value, estimated using FCF in the first terminal year/(WACC-g) or a defensible exit multiple. This gives operating enterprise value. Add excess cash and non-operating assets, subtract debt, preferred stock and noncontrolling interests as applicable, and divide by diluted shares for price per share. Match currency, cash-flow timing and lease treatment; sensitize WACC, terminal assumptions and operating performance.
Supporting reference: https://pages.stern.nyu.edu/~adamodar/New_Home_Page/lectures/val.html

[F0038] How does a $10 increase in depreciation affect the three financial statements? Assume a 20% tax rate.
Asked by / question source: Apollo Global Management Real Estate Credit; Bank of America Credit; BMO Capital Markets; Canaccord Genuity Boston; Citi LA; Deloitte Corporate Finance; Evercore Healthcare MP; GCM Grosvenor; Goldman Sachs NY Financing; Jefferies NY; Leerink Partners; LionTree; Perella Weinberg Partners CHI; Perella Weinberg Partners NY; Raymond James FIG; Stephens; William Blair SF
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
A $10 increase in depreciation, with the deduction usable now and a 20% tax rate.

• Income Statement: depreciation is an operating expense, so EBIT and Pre-Tax Income fall $10 and Net Income falls $8.

• Cash Flow Statement: Net Income is down $8, but you add back the $10 of non-cash depreciation, so cash rises $2.

• Balance Sheet: Cash +$2 and Net PP&E −$10, so assets fall $8; Retained Earnings falls $8, so both sides fall $8 and balance.

• Intuition: the only cash effect is the $2 tax saving, because the asset was paid for earlier.

Reverse every sign for a decrease. If the depreciation is not currently deductible there is no cash benefit and the difference goes to deferred taxes.

[F0039] Value an office building in New York. Explain the relevant multiples, forecast its profit and loss, assess growth opportunities and risks, and evaluate debt leverage. [Property inputs not recorded.]
Asked by / question source: Apollo Global Management Real Estate Credit
Answer status: Method / conditional answer — source details needed
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
The source omits inputs needed for a unique conclusion. Choose companies with similar business model, geography, growth, margins, risk and capital intensity. Calculate consistent enterprise/equity values and calendarized historical or forecast metrics, normalize unusual items, and apply a justified peer range to the target metric. EV/Revenue divided by EV/EBITDA equals EBITDA margin when periods and EV are consistent. P/E uses equity value/net income; EV/EBITDA uses operating value/pre-interest earnings, so taxes and financing can produce different rankings. Higher multiples can reflect growth, stronger returns, recurring revenue or lower risk, not automatically overvaluation. Negative EBITDA makes its multiple unhelpful; revenue multiples require a credible path to margins. Share price alone is not comparable across firms because share counts differ.

[F0042] Explain liquidity ratios.
Asked by / question source: Bank of America Credit
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Current ratio = current assets/current liabilities. Quick ratio generally excludes inventory and prepayments from current assets; cash ratio uses cash and cash equivalents (and sometimes liquid securities). Examine operating cash flow, revolver availability, receivable quality, working-capital seasonality and near-term maturities alongside the ratios. A high ratio can reflect slow inventory or uncollectible receivables rather than strong liquidity.

[F0043] Walk me through the three financial statements.
Asked by / question source: Ares Management Direct Lending; Bank of America Credit; Bank of America PA; Blackstone Group; BMO Capital Markets; BMO Capital Markets SF; Canaccord Genuity Boston; Canaccord Genuity NY Technology; Centerview Partners NY; Deloitte Corporate Finance; Dodge & Cox; Ducera Partners NY; Evercore Restructuring; Evercore SF; Financial Technology Partners SF; Greenhill NY; Intrepid LA; J.P. Morgan (compiled interview notes); Jefferies NY; Lazard LA; M&I 400 Questions Guide (2025), p. 50; Morgan Stanley SF; MUFG; PJT Partners Park Hill; PNC Capital Markets; Shea & Co; Société Générale NY; Stephens; TD Securities SF; William Blair SF
Also covers: F0472, F1765
Answer status: Guide answer
Answer origin: Supplied M&I 2025 400 IB Questions guide

ANSWER:
The three main financial statements are the Income Statement, Balance Sheet, and Cash Flow Statement. The Income Statement shows the company’s revenue, expenses, and taxes over a period and ends with Net Income, which represents the company’s after-tax profits. The Balance Sheet shows the company’s Assets – its resources – and how it paid for those resources – its Liabilities and Equity – at a specific point in time. Assets must equal Liabilities plus Equity. The Cash Flow Statement begins with Net Income, adjusts for non-cash items and changes in operating assets and liabilities (working capital), and shows the company’s Cash Flow from Investing and Financing activities; the last lines show the net change in cash and the company’s ending cash balance. You need the financial statements because there’s always a difference between the company’s Net Income and the cash flow it generates, and the statements let you estimate and forecast the cash flow more accurately.
Supporting reference: https://www.sec.gov/about/reports-publications/beginners-guide-financial-statements

[F0044] How does issuing $100 of debt affect the three statements?
Asked by / question source: Bank of America Credit
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Assuming the proceeds remain as cash and ignoring fees, cash and debt increase by the same stated amount, financing cash flow rises by that amount, and there is no immediate net-income effect. Operating enterprise value is unchanged because increased debt and cash offset. Later interest and use of proceeds require separate assumptions.

[F0046] How would you loan money to a company?
Asked by / question source: Bank of America Credit
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Credit underwriting asks whether cash flow can pay obligations in downside scenarios and what lenders recover if it cannot. Assess business resilience, leverage, interest coverage, fixed-charge coverage, free cash flow, liquidity and maturity/refinancing risk. Review collateral, guarantees and covenant headroom. Expected credit loss is approximately PD * LGD * exposure, though valuation also includes timing and risk premiums. The “3 Cs” are commonly character, capacity and capital, with collateral and conditions added in a five-C framework. Maintenance covenants are tested periodically; incurrence covenants when specified actions occur. Do not set leverage from EBITDA alone: cyclicality, cash conversion, CapEx and rates can make equal leverage ratios very different risks.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

[F0047] Explain to me how we would use different types of financial statements when analyzing different types of companies.
Asked by / question source: Bank of America Credit
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Start with revenue, subtract COGS for gross profit, operating expenses and D&A for operating income/EBIT, then interest and non-operating items for pre-tax income, and taxes for net income. Add back D&A to EBIT for EBITDA. Examine growth, gross and operating margin, recurring versus unusual items and conversion into cash. Statements must be analyzed together: balance sheets show financing and working-capital requirements, and cash-flow statements test whether earnings produce liquidity. A financial-statement exercise without the transaction amounts or schedules cannot yield unique numbers.

[F0049] What factors would you consider when analyzing the creditworthiness of a pharmaceutical company?

[F0050] What are the two different kinds of leverage?
Asked by / question source: Bank of America Credit
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Operating leverage comes from fixed operating costs: a change in sales creates a larger proportional change in EBIT. Financial leverage comes from debt/fixed financing obligations: changes in operating profit create amplified changes in equity returns. Both magnify downside as well as upside. At a given output level, degree of operating leverage is contribution margin/EBIT and degree of financial leverage is EBIT/(EBIT-interest), under simplifying assumptions.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

[F0051] What is the difference between a revolver and a term loan facility?
Asked by / question source: Bank of America Credit
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
A revolver is a committed facility that can be drawn, repaid and redrawn, subject to conditions, generally for seasonal working capital or liquidity. Interest applies to drawn amounts and commitment fees may apply to undrawn capacity. A term loan is funded at inception or under a defined draw schedule and repaid through amortization and/or a maturity balloon; repaid principal normally cannot be redrawn. Compare maturity, collateral, covenant package, pricing, amortization and prepayment flexibility. Seasonal retailers, manufacturers and commodity businesses often use revolvers.

[F0052] What are the 3 C's of credit?
Asked by / question source: Bank of America Credit
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
The three Cs are commonly Character, Capacity and Collateral: willingness/governance and payment history; ability to service debt from sustainable cash flow; and assets supporting recovery. Some institutions use alternative mnemonics, so explain the underlying analysis. A five-C framework adds Capital and Conditions. Collateral does not substitute for a viable repayment source.

[F0054] Explain the business model of one of this firm's portfolio companies.
Asked by / question source: Ardian Private Equity
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Prepare this per firm rather than answering generically: read the firm's portfolio page, choose two or three companies you can speak about from their own materials, and structure each as a business model rather than a description. Naming the revenue model precisely and one verified figure from the company's own disclosure is worth more than a long general description.

[F0055] Is MOIC or IRR greater for primary or secondary funds?
Asked by / question source: Ardian Private Equity
Also covers: F0062
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Neither metric is automatically higher for either strategy. Secondary buyers often invest closer to realizations and at a negotiated NAV discount, potentially producing a faster return of cash and higher IRR, but sometimes less remaining growth and a lower MOIC. Primary commitments usually have a longer investment ramp and a more pronounced J-curve. Compare fund vintage, purchase price, remaining commitments, cash-flow dates, fees and asset quality. IRR is an annual rate and MOIC is a multiple, so they are not directly comparable numerical units.

[F0056] Describe how a PE firm operates?
Asked by / question source: Ardian Private Equity
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
An asset manager invests client capital within mandates and earns fees, often based on assets under management and sometimes performance. Analyze investment process, team stability, risk controls, capacity, alignment, track record versus an appropriate benchmark, fees and operational infrastructure. For PE managers, management fees support recurring fee-related earnings and carried interest depends on realizations and fund terms. Value a manager through forecast fee earnings and risk-adjusted performance fees, not by treating all client AUM as the manager’s assets. Claims about a named manager’s current funds or hit rate require its own disclosures; do not invent them.

[F0058] Let's say Apple is buying $100 worth of new iPod factories with debt. What is on the 3 financial statement. Now let's go out 1 year, to the start of Year 2. Assume the debt is high-yield so no principal is paid off, and assume an interest rate of 10%. Also assume the factories depreciate at a rate of 10% per year assuming the tax rate is 20% What happens? At the start of Year 3, the factories all break down and the value of the equipment is written down to $0. The loan must also be paid back now. Walk me through the 3 statements.
Asked by / question source: Ardian Private Equity
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Depreciation is 10% of $100, so $10 a year, and interest is 10% of $100, so $10 a year, at the stated 20% tax rate with no principal repaid.

• At purchase: PP&E +$100 and Debt +$100 — a $100 financing inflow against a $100 investing outflow, so cash does not move and nothing hits the income statement.

• Year 1 Income Statement: $10 of depreciation and $10 of interest, so Pre-Tax Income falls $20 and Net Income falls $16.

• Year 1 Cash Flow Statement: Net Income −$16 plus the $10 depreciation add-back, so cash falls $6.

• Year 1 Balance Sheet: Cash −$6 and Net PP&E $90, so assets fall $16; Debt stays at $100 and Retained Earnings falls $16, so both sides balance. Year 2 repeats, leaving PP&E at $80.

• Start of year 3, writing the factories down to zero and repaying the loan: an $80 non-cash loss, so Net Income falls $64; adding the $80 back gives operating cash flow of +$16, and the $100 repayment is a financing outflow, so cash falls $84 in that step. PP&E −$80 and Debt −$100 against Retained Earnings −$64 leaves both sides down $164.

• Intuition: the debt funded the asset, so the only annual cash cost is the $10 coupon less $4 of tax relief. The write-off itself moves just $16 of tax; repaying the loan is what drains the cash.

[F0059] What is the difference between primary, early secondary, and late secondary private equity investments?
Asked by / question source: Ardian Private Equity
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
A primary investor commits to a new fund before most assets are known and funds capital calls as investments are made. A secondary investor buys an existing fund interest or portfolio/continuation-vehicle stake, often with more visibility into assets and a shorter remaining life. Early secondaries retain more deployment risk; late secondaries are closer to realizations. Pricing versus NAV, unfunded commitments, asset quality, fees and conflicts are central. Secondaries can shorten the J-curve but are not automatically cheaper or higher-returning.

[F0064] What are the three levers of value creation in an LBO?
Asked by / question source: Ardian Private Equity; Evercore (compiled interview notes); J.P. Morgan (compiled interview notes); J.P. Morgan CHI; LionTree; Stephens; The Sage Group
Also covers: F0929, F1547, F1747
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
An LBO buys a company using sponsor equity and debt serviced by the target’s cash flows. Set entry EV and equity purchase price, build sources and uses including fees/refinancing, forecast operations and cash generation, model debt interest/amortization and the cash sweep, then estimate exit EV and subtract exit net debt and other claims. Sponsor MOIC = proceeds/invested equity; with one entry and exit, IRR = MOIC^(1/years)-1. Returns come from operating growth, deleveraging, entry/exit valuation and distributions. More leverage increases both upside and default risk. Favor resilient cash conversion, manageable CapEx, credible improvements and a defensible purchase price. Strategic buyers may pay more for synergies; sponsors may offer certainty, speed, rollover equity or management continuity.

[F0066] If you had a million dollars what would you invest it in?
Asked by / question source: Ardian Secondaries

Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

[F0067] How would you set up a sensitivity analysis in a DCF, and which variables would you test?
Asked by / question source: Ardian Secondaries; William Blair SF
Also covers: F1670
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
DCF value rises with higher sustainable cash flow and falls with higher discount rates. Faster growth creates value only if incremental returns exceed the cost of capital; growth that requires excessive reinvestment can destroy value. Test WACC against terminal growth or exit multiple, then separately stress revenue growth, margins, CapEx and working capital. Keep taxes and cash-flow timing consistent. No universal ranking exists for the impact of a one-percentage-point change in different assumptions: compare changes using the actual base values, forecast duration and proportion of value in the terminal period.

[F0068] What is the private equity secondaries market?
Asked by / question source: Ardian Secondaries; Blackstone Group; Blackstone Strategic Partners
Also covers: F0319
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
A PE fund raises commitments from limited partners, calls capital for investments, supports portfolio companies and distributes exit proceeds. The manager earns management fees and, subject to the agreement/hurdle, carried interest on gains. A fund of funds invests in underlying funds, offering diversification and access with an additional fee layer. Secondaries transfer existing fund interests or assets; GP-led continuation deals may offer investors liquidity or a rollover choice. Buyers assess NAV quality, unfunded commitments, concentration, remaining duration and price discounts/premiums. Secondaries can reduce blind-pool risk and duration, but do not automatically deliver higher IRR or MOIC; timing, pricing, leverage and asset performance determine returns.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

[F0069] Would you prefer a higher IRR over a shorter holding period or a lower IRR over a longer period? [Numerical examples not recorded.]
Asked by / question source: Ares Management Direct Lending
Answer status: Method / conditional answer — source details needed
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
The source omits inputs needed for a unique conclusion. MOIC = total cash proceeds/total invested capital and does not account for timing. With a single entry and exit, annualized return or IRR = (exit proceeds/entry investment)^(1/years)-1. With interim cash flows, solve 0 = sum[CF_t/(1+r)^t]; use dated cash flows for XIRR. Earlier distributions generally increase IRR at the same MOIC. MOIC can favor a larger long-held gain while IRR favors rapid capital return; assess both alongside risk and absolute profit. ROE is accounting net income/average book equity and is not the same as an investment IRR.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

[F0070] A company is acquired for $600 and sold for $1,200. What proportion of the purchase price must be equity to produce a 3x equity return? [Debt-repayment assumptions not recorded.]
Asked by / question source: Ares Management Direct Lending
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Assume entry debt stays constant and there are no distributions or fees. Let E be entry equity, so debt = 600-E. Exit equity = 1200-(600-E)=600+E. Set (600+E)/E=3: E=300, or 50% equity. If debt is repaid during the hold, the result changes; with debt repayment P, E=(600+P)/2.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

[F0071] What should a debt investor research to assess default risk?
Asked by / question source: Ares Management Direct Lending
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Credit underwriting asks whether cash flow can pay obligations in downside scenarios and what lenders recover if it cannot. Assess business resilience, leverage, interest coverage, fixed-charge coverage, free cash flow, liquidity and maturity/refinancing risk. Review collateral, guarantees and covenant headroom. Expected credit loss is approximately PD * LGD * exposure, though valuation also includes timing and risk premiums. The “3 Cs” are commonly character, capacity and capital, with collateral and conditions added in a five-C framework. Maintenance covenants are tested periodically; incurrence covenants when specified actions occur. Do not set leverage from EBITDA alone: cyclicality, cash conversion, CapEx and rates can make equal leverage ratios very different risks.

[F0074] Give a purchase price of the company given that the acquisition will save an additional million in EBITDA.
Asked by / question source: Audax Group
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
The acquisition price is not determined by $1 million of additional EBITDA alone. If the synergy is sustainable, estimate its after-tax cash benefit less implementation cost, incremental CapEx and working capital, then discount it. A multiple shortcut is $1 million times a justified synergy EBITDA multiple, but it can overstate value if costs and taxes are ignored. Maximum price equals standalone target value plus the portion of synergy value the buyer can afford to transfer while retaining an acceptable return.

[F0075] Estimate the pizza market in a local town using two different methods.
Asked by / question source: Audax Group
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Build two independent estimates and reconcile them. Top-down: start from the town's population and work to spending. For 50,000 people, if 60% buy restaurant or takeaway pizza roughly 12 times a year at about $12 a visit, that is 50,000 * 0.6 * 12 * $12, or about $4.3 million a year. Bottom-up: count the supply side instead. If the town has about 10 pizza outlets each taking roughly 60 orders a day at a $20 average ticket over 360 trading days, that is also about $4.3 million. Define the geography, the period and whether you are estimating revenue or volume; decide explicitly whether grocery and frozen pizza count or only prepared pizza, and do not let delivery and dine-in spend be counted twice. Then name the assumption that moves the answer most, usually frequency or average ticket, and sanity-check the result against something known, such as plausible household food spending in a town that size. Two methods landing within the same order of magnitude is the point of the exercise; without local data no exact figure is available, so state the assumptions and show the range.

[F0080] What is a bond?
Asked by / question source: BlackRock SF; J.P. Morgan Asset Management
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
A bond is a debt security with contractual interest and repayment terms. Coupon rate determines interest based on face value; current yield is annual coupon divided by market price; yield to maturity is the discount rate equating price with promised coupons and principal. A below-par bond normally has YTM above its coupon rate, assuming conventional cash flows. Realized return can differ because of default, reinvestment, sale price or early redemption.
Supporting reference: https://www.investor.gov/introduction-investing/investing-basics/investment-products/bonds-or-fixed-income-products

[F0087] How does issuing a corporate bond affect the three financial statements?
Asked by / question source: J.P. Morgan Asset Management
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Debt avoids immediate ownership dilution and can provide a usable tax shield, but imposes interest, maturity and covenant obligations. Equity has no mandatory repayment and absorbs downside but dilutes owners and normally demands a higher return. Choose a sustainable mix using downside cash generation, collateral, funding horizon, liquidity and market access. Issuing debt and retaining cash raises both equally without initial earnings effects. Issuing primary equity raises cash and paid-in equity; neither immediately creates operating profit. Distressed or pre-revenue businesses may need equity even when debt looks nominally cheaper.

[F0088] If you had $100 to invest for one year, where would you invest it to maximize returns, and why?
Asked by / question source: J.P. Morgan Asset Management
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
There is no guaranteed maximum-return investment over one year. A short horizon argues for preserving principal in cash-like/high-quality short-duration assets if the money is needed; seeking the highest possible upside can imply a material chance of losing the entire $100. I would clarify whether the objective is expected return, maximum possible payoff or capital preservation and state the trade-off explicitly.

[F0090] Discuss how interest rates, inflation and Federal Reserve policy affect markets.
Asked by / question source: J.P. Morgan Asset Management
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
A useful macro answer links growth, inflation, employment and policy to earnings, discount rates, credit and investor positioning. Higher rates generally reduce fixed-rate bond values and increase funding costs; equity effects also depend on why rates rose and on earnings expectations. The Fed’s U.S. goals are maximum employment and stable prices; its inflation objective is measured using PCE, with core PCE often watched for underlying pressure. Fiscal policy changes government spending/taxes, while monetary policy changes financial conditions. An inverted curve can signal expected easing or weak growth but is not a certain recession forecast. Give a base case, a contrary case and indicators that would change your view rather than presenting a forecast as fact.

[F0091] What are the main ways to value a company?
Asked by / question source: Ardian Private Equity; Bank of America CHI; Barclays NY; BlackRock; BMO Capital Markets SF; Canaccord Genuity Boston; Citi LA; Citi Technology SF; DC Advisory NY; Deloitte Corporate Finance; Financial Technology Partners SF; Goldman Sachs LA; Goldman Sachs NY; Goldman Sachs NY Financing; Goldman Sachs TMT SF; Guggenheim Partners NY; Houlihan Lokey Restructuring LA; J.P. Morgan Asset Management; J.P. Morgan CHI; J.P. Morgan SF; Lazard LA; Lazard Technology SF; LionTree; M&I 400 Questions Guide (2025), p. 194; Miller Buckfire; Morgan Stanley Investment Management; Morgan Stanley MP; Morgan Stanley NY; Morgan Stanley SF; Nomura NY; Oak Hill; Perella Weinberg Partners; Perella Weinberg Partners Healthcare SF; Perella Weinberg Partners NY; Perella Weinberg Partners SF; PJT Partners M&A; PJT Partners Park Hill; Raymond James FIG; Raymond James NY; Shea & Co; Société Générale NY; Stephens; The Sage Group; UBS NY; Union Square Advisors; Wells Fargo NY; William Blair SF
Also covers: F0063, F1132
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
The main corporate valuation approaches are discounted cash flow, public trading comparables and precedent transactions. DCF estimates intrinsic value from future cash flows; trading comps infer value from similar listed businesses; precedents use prices paid in comparable acquisitions. LBO analysis tests a sponsor’s feasible purchase price, and asset/liquidation or sum-of-the-parts analysis can be useful for particular businesses. Use multiple appropriate methods and reconcile differences; real-estate cap rates and replacement cost are sector-specific tools, not the only ways to value a company.

[F0096] How would $10 at a coffee shop flow through the 3 statements?
Asked by / question source: BMO Capital Markets
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Clarify whose books and whether $10 is price or cost. For the coffee shop collecting $10 for a delivered item with cost c: revenue +10, expense +c, NI +(10-c)(1-t). Cash rises by receipts less costs actually paid and cash tax; inventory decreases by the consumed cost if previously purchased. For a business buying $10 of refreshments for immediate use, expense rises 10 and cash falls 10 before any tax benefit. There is no single answer without perspective and cost assumptions.

[F0100] How do you estimate beta for a company?
Asked by / question source: BMO Capital Markets; Wells Fargo NY
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
CAPM estimates cost of equity as risk-free rate + levered beta * equity risk premium, with justified additional risk adjustments where appropriate. Estimate beta using a regression of stock excess returns on market excess returns, or bottom-up comparable-company betas. Beta reflects systematic risk; leverage, cyclicality and operating fixed costs can raise it. It is not a measure of all uncertainty or an invariant property of an industry. Historical estimates depend on window, frequency and benchmark, and CAPM’s single-factor assumptions are simplifications. Compare operating risk first, then financing; a higher-growth firm does not mechanically have a higher beta.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

[F0101] How changing from straight line depreciation method to double discount depreciation method influence DCF?
Asked by / question source: BMO Capital Markets
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
In an unlevered DCF, FCFF = EBIT(1-t) + D&A - CapEx - change in operating NWC. Additional tax-deductible depreciation d reduces EBIT but is added back, increasing cash flow by d*t, provided the tax shield is currently usable. Earlier tax depreciation therefore generally increases present value by bringing tax savings forward. Changing book depreciation alone while cash taxes stay unchanged does not create cash value: deferred taxes offset the accounting change. Also distinguish a depreciation-method change from new CapEx, which has its own cash cost.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

[F0102] How does a $10 asset write-down affect the three statements at a 40% tax rate?
Asked by / question source: BMO Capital Markets
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Assuming an immediately deductible $10 impairment: net income falls $6, add back the $10 non-cash loss in CFO, so cash rises $4. The written-down asset falls $10 and retained earnings falls $6. If the impairment is only a book write-down, cash does not rise immediately; deferred-tax treatment must be considered.

[F0103] Which valuation method generally produces the highest value, and why?
Asked by / question source: Bank of America NY; Blackstone Group; BMO Capital Markets; BMO Capital Markets SF; BNP Paribas NY; Canaccord Genuity Boston; Deloitte Corporate Finance; Goldman Sachs LA; Greenhill NY; J.P. Morgan (compiled interview notes); J.P. Morgan CHI; Shea & Co; TD Securities SF; Union Square Advisors; William Blair SF
Also covers: F0330, F0708
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Core methods are public trading comparables, precedent transactions and DCF. An LBO is a sponsor’s return-constrained price analysis; asset-based/liquidation value and sum-of-the-parts are additional approaches. Trading comps reflect current minority market prices; precedents reflect historical deal conditions, control and possible synergies; DCF reflects forecast cash generation and risk. Precedents often exceed trading comps, and LBO prices can be lower than strategic values, but there is no guaranteed ranking or universal valuation floor. Select methods suited to the business, compare their assumptions and present a range rather than averaging incompatible outputs.

[F0105] What characteristics would you look for when evaluating an M&A deal?
Asked by / question source: BMO Capital Markets
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Assess a transaction through strategic fit, price versus standalone and synergy value, financing, execution and integration risk. Explain buyer/target businesses, consideration, purchase multiple, expected cash benefits and why a deal is preferable to organic investment. Test downside cases, regulatory constraints and ability to finance/close. More EPS or more revenue alone does not prove value creation; incremental risk-adjusted returns should exceed the cost of capital. For a named historical transaction, use the announcement, filings and investor presentations to establish terms, and distinguish the rationale known at signing from later outcomes. No unspecified deal supports a factual purchase multiple or recommendation.

[F0107] What happens to my earnings per share immediately after the buyback?
Asked by / question source: BMO Capital Markets
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
A repurchase reduces shares outstanding, which increases EPS if net income is unchanged. Cash funding sacrifices after-tax interest income; debt funding adds after-tax interest expense. Pro forma EPS = (old net income - lost after-tax interest or new after-tax interest expense)/(old shares - repurchase amount/share price). EPS rises when the repurchase earnings yield exceeds the relevant after-tax funding cost. EPS accretion alone does not establish value creation; repurchasing overpriced shares can destroy value.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

[F0108] Why is tax adjusted for in WACC calculation?
Asked by / question source: BMO Capital Markets
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
WACC = E/(D+E)*Ke + D/(D+E)*Kd*(1-t), extending the weights for preferred capital if present. Use market-value, sustainable capital weights. Ke is often estimated with CAPM; Kd is the current marginal borrowing yield for comparable risk and maturity, not necessarily an old coupon. The debt tax adjustment reflects usable interest deductibility. Match currency, inflation and risk to the cash flows. Moderate leverage can lower WACC through tax shields, but greater default risk raises required debt and equity returns; the relationship is not universally decreasing. For a private company, estimate operating risk from public peers and use a defensible target capital structure.

ANSWER:

Avoid presenting a single stock or private investment as the universal answer. Set rebalancing and thesis-review rules.

[F0110] How do DCF assumptions and balance sheet characteristics vary by industry?
Asked by / question source: BMO Capital Markets SF
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
DCF value rises with higher sustainable cash flow and falls with higher discount rates. Faster growth creates value only if incremental returns exceed the cost of capital; growth that requires excessive reinvestment can destroy value. Test WACC against terminal growth or exit multiple, then separately stress revenue growth, margins, CapEx and working capital. Keep taxes and cash-flow timing consistent. No universal ranking exists for the impact of a one-percentage-point change in different assumptions: compare changes using the actual base values, forecast duration and proportion of value in the terminal period.

[F0112] How does an amount of depreciation flow through the three accounting statements with x tax rate.
Asked by / question source: BMO Capital Markets SF
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
For an incremental depreciation expense d and tax rate t, assuming an immediately usable tax deduction: EBIT and pre-tax income decrease d; net income decreases d(1-t). On the indirect cash-flow statement, add back the non-cash depreciation d, so CFO and cash rise d*t. Net PP&E falls d and retained earnings fall d(1-t); the balance sheet balances. Reverse these signs for a decrease in depreciation. If depreciation is not tax deductible or no current tax benefit is usable, cash does not rise by the tax shield; address deferred taxes separately. Depreciation allocates a capital asset’s cost over its useful life, rather than measuring its market value.

[F0113] Walk from revenue to unlevered free cash flow and explain each adjustment.
Asked by / question source: BMO Capital Markets SF; Citi Technology SF; Houlihan Lokey NY; Houlihan Lokey Restructuring LA; J.P. Morgan (compiled interview notes); M&I 400 Questions Guide (2025), p. 95; Shea & Co
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Unlevered free cash flow = EBIT*(1-t) + D&A - CapEx - increase in operating NWC. From EBITDA, subtract D&A to obtain EBIT, apply operating cash taxes, add D&A back, then subtract investment and working-capital needs. From revenue, first subtract operating expenses to reach EBIT. From net income, add after-tax interest and remove non-operating earnings before adjusting for non-cash expenses and reinvestment. FCFF excludes financing flows and is discounted at WACC. Use cash taxes and other operating adjustments where accounting taxes differ.

[F0114] How do you value an apple tree?
Asked by / question source: BMO Capital Markets SF; Citi Technology SF
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Forecast fruit volume times selling price, subtract harvesting, maintenance, land/operating costs, taxes and any required reinvestment, and discount the resulting cash flows for the tree’s economic life. Include any residual sale value and replacement/replanting costs consistently. A perpetuity only makes sense for a sustainably maintained operation, not an individual tree assumed to live forever. For constant annual end-year cash C for N years, PV = C*[1-(1+r)^(-N)]/r.

[F0115] If two companies with the same revenue, ebitda, cogs, etc were trading at different multiples, why might that be?
Asked by / question source: BMO Capital Markets SF; Canaccord Genuity NY Technology; Evercore (compiled interview notes); J.P. Morgan (compiled interview notes)
Also covers: F1712, F1837, F1851
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Identical current statements do not guarantee identical future cash flows or risk. One may have stronger customer retention, better products, patents, management, governance, backlog, lower future reinvestment needs or less concentration. Liquidity, control rights and market expectations can also differ. If all future cash flows, risk, rights and information are truly identical, intrinsic value should be identical; a price difference would then reflect market mispricing or omitted assumptions.

[F0116] How do you calculate terminal value in a DCF, and what are the advantages of each method?
Asked by / question source: BMO Capital Markets SF; Citi Technology SF; Goldman Sachs LA; J.P. Morgan (compiled interview notes); M&I 400 Questions Guide (2025), p. 95; M&I 400 Questions Guide (2025), p. 99; Morgan Stanley SF
Answer status: Guide answer
Answer origin: Supplied M&I 2025 400 IB Questions guide

ANSWER:
You can use the Multiples Method or the Gordon Growth Method (AKA Long-Term Growth Method, Perpetuity Growth Method, etc.). With the first one, you apply a Terminal Multiple to the company’s EBITDA, EBIT, NOPAT, or FCF in the final year of the forecast period. For example, if you apply a 10x TEV / EBITDA multiple to the company’s Year 10 EBITDA of $500, its Terminal Value is $5,000. With the Gordon Growth Method, you assign a “Terminal Growth Rate” to the company’s Free Cash Flows in the Terminal Period and assume they’ll grow at that rate forever. Terminal Value = Final Year Free Cash Flow * (1 + Terminal Growth Rate) / (Discount Rate – Terminal Growth Rate) The Gordon Growth Method is better from a theoretical perspective because growth always slows down over time; all companies’ cash flows eventually grow more slowly than GDP. If you use the Multiples Method, it’s easy to pick a multiple that makes no logical sense because it implies a growth rate that’s too high. However, many bankers still use and prefer the Multiples Method because it’s “easier” or because they don’t understand the issues with Terminal Multiples.

This growth rate should be below the country’s long-term GDP growth rate and in line with other macroeconomic variables like inflation. For example, if you’re in a developed country where the expected long-term GDP growth rate is 3%, you might use numbers ranging from 1% to 2% for the Terminal Growth Rates.

[F0121] Explain the credit rating and leverage of a company you previously worked on.
Asked by / question source: BNP Paribas Leveraged Finance
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Credit underwriting asks whether cash flow can pay obligations in downside scenarios and what lenders recover if it cannot. Assess business resilience, leverage, interest coverage, fixed-charge coverage, free cash flow, liquidity and maturity/refinancing risk. Review collateral, guarantees and covenant headroom. Expected credit loss is approximately PD * LGD * exposure, though valuation also includes timing and risk premiums. The “3 Cs” are commonly character, capacity and capital, with collateral and conditions added in a five-C framework. Maintenance covenants are tested periodically; incurrence covenants when specified actions occur. Do not set leverage from EBITDA alone: cyclicality, cash conversion, CapEx and rates can make equal leverage ratios very different risks.

[F0129] Walk me through a merger model and accretion/dilution analysis.
Asked by / question source: BNP Paribas NY; Centerview Partners NY; Citi Technology SF; Financial Technology Partners SF; M&I 400 Questions Guide (2025), p. 108; Morgan Stanley Singapore; UBS NY; William Blair CHI
Answer status: Guide answer
Answer origin: Supplied M&I 2025 400 IB Questions guide

ANSWER:
In a merger model, you start by projecting the financial statements of the Buyer and Seller. Then, you estimate the Purchase Price and the mix of Cash, Debt, and Stock used to fund the deal. You create a Sources & Uses schedule and Purchase Price Allocation schedule to estimate the after-effects of the deal on the financial statements. Then, you combine the Balance Sheets of the Buyer and Seller, reflecting the Cash, Debt, and Stock used, new Goodwill created, and any write-ups and write-downs. You then combine the Income Statements, reflecting the Foregone Interest on Cash, Interest Paid on New Debt, and Synergies. The Combined Net Income equals the Combined Pre-Tax Income times (1 – Buyer’s Tax Rate), and the Combined EPS equals the Combined Net Income divided by (Buyer’s Existing Share Count + New Shares Issued in the Deal). The EPS accretion/dilution equals the percentage difference between this Combined EPS and the Buyer’s standalone EPS.

[F0140] What are revenue / cost drivers of a coffee shop?
Asked by / question source: Bain Capital Credit; Bank of America NY
Also covers: F0187
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

[F0145] Calculate the price of a ticket for an airline based on a few figures about the airline and could then ask the associate for more information which he could choose to provide or not.
Asked by / question source: Bain Capital Credit
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:

Separate variable costs from fixed costs to model contribution margin, operating leverage and break-even volume. For a pharmacy use prescription volumes, reimbursement/mix, dispensing margin and payer terms; roofing uses crew capacity, projects, ticket size and repair/replacement mix; software/telecom uses subscribers, ARPU, churn and network/service costs; a food outlet uses footfall, conversion, ticket and opening days. Forecast working capital, maintenance/growth CapEx and taxes. Value sustainable after-tax cash flow and cross-check peers; local concentration, regulation and reinvestment can explain different multiples despite similar current profits.

[F0150] Where in the capital structure would you choose to invest?
Asked by / question source: Bain Capital Credit
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Credit underwriting asks whether cash flow can pay obligations in downside scenarios and what lenders recover if it cannot. Assess business resilience, leverage, interest coverage, fixed-charge coverage, free cash flow, liquidity and maturity/refinancing risk. Review collateral, guarantees and covenant headroom. Expected credit loss is approximately PD * LGD * exposure, though valuation also includes timing and risk premiums. The “3 Cs” are commonly character, capacity and capital, with collateral and conditions added in a five-C framework. Maintenance covenants are tested periodically; incurrence covenants when specified actions occur. Do not set leverage from EBITDA alone: cyclicality, cash conversion, CapEx and rates can make equal leverage ratios very different risks.

[F0151] What are the drivers for a 5 year cagr in a random dental healthcare company?
Asked by / question source: Bain Capital Credit
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Revenue CAGR = (ending revenue/beginning revenue)^(1/years)-1; for five years use the exponent 1/5. Dental revenue growth can come from practices/chairs, clinician capacity, visits per clinician, utilization, procedures per visit, net pricing and payer mix, plus acquisitions. EBITDA growth also depends on labor, rent, supplies and central overhead. Separate organic growth from acquired growth and ensure the ending metric is consistent.

[F0157] How you think about risk management are always potentially tricky and reveal a lot about a candidates understanding of these roles.
Asked by / question source: Balyasny Asset Management
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
VaR is a loss threshold at a specified confidence level and horizon; it does not describe losses beyond that threshold. Expected shortfall/CVaR measures average loss in the selected tail, subject to modeling conventions. RAROC compares risk-adjusted profit with economic capital; the capital and expected-loss definitions must be specified. CAR often means regulatory capital/risk-weighted assets, but confirm the acronym. Key-rate duration measures sensitivity at individual maturity nodes rather than assuming a parallel yield-curve shift. Combine statistical measures with stress scenarios, liquidity analysis, concentration limits and model-risk review.

Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
The SVB episode illustrates liquidity, counterparty and interest-rate concentration risk. A hedge fund should diversify operational cash and financing counterparties, monitor collateral and settlement exposures, stress deposit/credit-line access and examine hidden duration risk in portfolio companies. It may create investment opportunities, but a trade requires dated prices and legal terms. A general hedge-fund opinion is not determined by one bank failure.

[F0160] What makes a stock price move?
Asked by / question source: Balyasny Asset Management
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
A share price moves when the market revises what it expects the company to produce, what it requires in return, or both. First, expected cash flows: earnings and revisions to guidance, new products or contracts, margin and cost changes, competitive wins and losses, capital allocation, and anything that changes the long-run growth or reinvestment path. Second, the discount rate: the risk-free rate, credit spreads, the equity risk premium and company-specific risk such as leverage, cyclicality or litigation; this is why prices can fall on no company news when rates rise. Third, the gap between results and what was already priced in - a company can report record earnings and fall because expectations were higher, which is why the move tracks the surprise rather than the level. On top of those, flows and market structure move prices in the short run: index inclusion, large buyers or sellers, short positioning, options hedging, liquidity and sentiment. Separate a price move from a change in value: the mechanical effects of a dividend, a buyback or a split change the price without changing what the business is worth per dollar of claim.

[F0165] Would you prefer to pay down $1 of debt or increase operating income by $1, and why?
Asked by / question source: Bank of America CHI
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
At a constant enterprise-value multiple M, a sustainable $1 increase in EBIT can add about M dollars to EV, before reinvestment and other effects. Repaying $1 of debt with existing cash reduces both debt and cash and does not mechanically create $1 of equity value: net debt is unchanged. Debt repayment may reduce interest and distress risk. Compare the actual cash cost and durability of the earnings improvement with the risk reduction from repayment.

[F0168] What would you say are the two most important macro indicators and how would they affect a company's dcf?
Asked by / question source: Bank of America CHI
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Value equals the present value of expected cash flows. For an operating company, forecast FCFF from revenue, margins, taxes, reinvestment and working capital, discount at WACC, and add a consistently estimated terminal value. EV = sum[FCFF_t/(1+WACC)^t] + TV_N/(1+WACC)^N. Bridge to equity by adding excess cash/non-operating assets and subtracting debt, preferred claims and NCI; divide by diluted shares if needed. For a tree or other asset, forecast sale proceeds less maintenance, taxes and reinvestment over its actual economic life. A level end-of-year perpetuity is C/r; a growing one is next-period C/(r-g). Cash flow today is not the same as next-period cash flow.

[F0169] In which direction do you expect interest rates to move?
Asked by / question source: Bank of America CHI
Answer status: Framework — dated research required
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:

Separate the risk-free curve from credit spreads, and near-term shocks from long-term fundamentals. Use dated central-bank releases, filings and official economic series for facts, then state a base case, downside case and key indicators. Historical crisis questions should identify the actual period; do not describe an “upcoming crisis” as certain. For currency exposure, match cash flows and liabilities by currency where possible and assess forward/option hedges, costs and residual basis risk.
