[F0510] Price a bond from its terms. [Specific terms not recorded.]
Asked by / question source: Ducera Partners NY
Answer status: Method / conditional answer — source details needed
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
The source omits inputs needed for a unique conclusion. A bond pays contractual coupons and principal, subject to default. Price = sum[coupon_t/(1+y)^t] + principal/(1+y)^N for annual payments. YTM is the discount rate that equates those promised payments to price, not a guaranteed realized return. Current yield = annual coupon/current price. Yield to call substitutes the call date and call price for maturity. Coupon is set on face value; yield depends on price. For a one-year bond, YTM = (coupon + redemption - price)/price. For multi-year bonds solve the equation rather than using coupon/price. Distressed debt may require probability-weighted recoveries, not just promised-payment YTM.

[F0513] How would you value that (pointing out the window) office building?
Asked by / question source: Eastdil Secured SF; Lazard LA
Also covers: F1083
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Estimate stabilized net operating income from rents/occupancy and operating expenses, excluding financing and depreciation. A simple unlevered property value is NOI/capitalization rate; reconcile it to DCF and comparable sales. Account for tenant credit, location, lease duration, vacancy, tenant improvements, leasing commissions and maintenance CapEx. Equity value subtracts debt and other claims. For REITs, FFO adjusts net income for specified real-estate depreciation and disposition items; AFFO generally deducts recurring maintenance capital expenditures from FFO and adjusts non-cash rent and other items; definitions vary by issuer. Hotels often have higher operational volatility than long-lease residential assets, but cap rates depend on quality, market and growth rather than a universal ranking.

[F0514] Explain the M&A valuation and acquisition process.
Asked by / question source: Ernst & Young M&A
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
For sell-side M&A: clarify objectives, value the company, prepare marketing materials, contact qualified buyers, manage indications and diligence, negotiate final bids and agreements, then obtain approvals and close. Buy-side work starts with strategy, target screening and approach, followed by valuation, diligence, financing and negotiation. A pitch book presents the client situation, strategic alternatives, market/valuation work, execution plan and bank credentials. An IPO adds readiness work, underwriting/diligence, registration, investor marketing, bookbuilding, pricing and listing. A greenshoe permits an overallotment option to help manage issuance and stabilization under its terms; it is not a guarantee against price declines. Fees, confidentiality and regulatory obligations vary by transaction.

[F0515] If your friend has $100 she wants to invest (nothing left uninvested), would you recommend her to invest in stocks or options of a particular security?
Asked by / question source: Ernst & Young M&A
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
For ordinary long-term ownership, stock gives an ongoing equity claim without an option's expiry risk. A long option offers leverage but can expire worthless and requires a view on timing and volatility. With no objective, horizon or risk tolerance supplied, neither is universally correct; do not equate spending the entire $100 with a requirement to take maximum risk. Fractional shares may make stock ownership possible, depending on access.

[F0516] How would you price said call option if the price of the underlying had a 50% chance of going up to $120 or down to 50?
Asked by / question source: Ernst & Young M&A
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
The strike, current stock price, maturity and risk-free rate are missing. Payoffs are max(120-K,0) and max(50-K,0). If 50% is explicitly a risk-neutral probability, value is 0.5*(up payoff+down payoff)/(1+r). Otherwise derive q=[(1+r)S0-50]/70 and use the risk-neutral weighted payoffs. A real-world 50/50 probability alone does not determine an arbitrage-free option price.

[F0518] Which two financial statements would you choose, and why?
Asked by / question source: Ernst & Young M&A
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
The appropriate statement depends on the purpose. The balance sheet shows financial position and obligations at a date; the income statement shows profitability over time; the cash-flow statement shows liquidity generation and funding. If forced to pick one for debt repayment, the cash-flow statement is useful, but debt maturities and collateral still require the balance sheet and notes. With two consecutive balance sheets plus an income statement and supporting schedules, you can approximate cash flows, although acquisitions, FX and other non-cash changes complicate the reconstruction. No single statement fully captures financial health.

[F0528] Given P/E 20, EV/EBITDA 10, INT 20, r_interest 5%, Dep 20, Mkt Cap 200m, find the effective tax rate.
Asked by / question source: Evercore Generalist
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Assuming no cash and no other EV claims: net income = 200/20 = 10; debt = 20/5% = 400; EV = 600; EBITDA = 600/10 = 60; EBIT = 60-20 = 40; EBT = 40-20 = 20. Tax expense = 20-10 = 10, so effective tax rate = 50%. Cash or other omitted adjustments would change the result.

[F0529] Compare EV/EBITDA and P/E.
Asked by / question source: Evercore Generalist; J.P. Morgan (compiled interview notes)
Also covers: F1903
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Choose companies with similar business model, geography, growth, margins, risk and capital intensity. Calculate consistent enterprise/equity values and calendarized historical or forecast metrics, normalize unusual items, and apply a justified peer range to the target metric. EV/Revenue divided by EV/EBITDA equals EBITDA margin when periods and EV are consistent. P/E uses equity value/net income; EV/EBITDA uses operating value/pre-interest earnings, so taxes and financing can produce different rankings. Higher multiples can reflect growth, stronger returns, recurring revenue or lower risk, not automatically overvaluation. Negative EBITDA makes its multiple unhelpful; revenue multiples require a credible path to margins. Share price alone is not comparable across firms because share counts differ.

[F0530] What are the 3 most important considerations in an LBO?
Asked by / question source: Evercore Generalist
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
An LBO buys a company using sponsor equity and debt serviced by the target’s cash flows. Set entry EV and equity purchase price, build sources and uses including fees/refinancing, forecast operations and cash generation, model debt interest/amortization and the cash sweep, then estimate exit EV and subtract exit net debt and other claims. Sponsor MOIC = proceeds/invested equity; with one entry and exit, IRR = MOIC^(1/years)-1. Returns come from operating growth, deleveraging, entry/exit valuation and distributions. More leverage increases both upside and default risk. Favor resilient cash conversion, manageable CapEx, credible improvements and a defensible purchase price. Strategic buyers may pay more for synergies; sponsors may offer certainty, speed, rollover equity or management continuity.

[F0532] Would management want an M&A if it is not accretive?

[F0533] Would you rather a business increase sales by increasing number of units sold or increasing price?
Asked by / question source: Evercore Generalist
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Compare incremental contribution profit, not revenue alone. A price increase can add profit with little extra volume cost but may reduce demand/churn; more units adds variable costs and may require capacity and working capital. Use price elasticity, customer value, competition and spare capacity. Inelastic demand and strong differentiation may support price increases; excess capacity and price-sensitive demand may favor profitable volume growth.

[F0534] Company A purchases company B for $800mm using 50% cash, 50% debt. Company B has $800mm in assets, $300mm in liabilities. What happens to company A's balance sheet at the end of the acquisition?
Asked by / question source: Evercore Generalist
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Assume the $800 million is equity purchase consideration, the target's stated assets/liabilities are already at fair value, no debt is refinanced, and ignore fees/deferred taxes. Net identifiable assets = 800-300 = 500; goodwill = 800-500 = 300. Buyer cash falls 400, acquired assets rise 800 and goodwill rises 300: net assets +700. Acquired liabilities +300 and new debt +400: liabilities +700; buyer equity is unchanged. If 800 is enterprise value instead of equity consideration, clarify the target's debt and cash first.

[F0535] Which required EVs, costs of cash/debt/equity along with price and quantity synergies.
Asked by / question source: Evercore Generalist
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Cost synergies eliminate duplicate costs such as headquarters or procurement expense. Revenue synergies arise from cross-selling, distribution or pricing improvements, usually with additional costs and execution risk. Financial/tax synergies may involve funding or tax benefits. A dollar of durable cost savings normally adds more profit than a dollar of additional revenue because new revenue has associated variable costs. Value after-tax cash benefits after implementation costs, timing and probability of delivery. Do not pay the seller for every potential synergy or double count benefits already in the base forecasts.

[F0537] $100 in debt is issued, how does it impact your P/E and EV/EBITDA?
Asked by / question source: Evercore Generalist
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
If the $100 debt proceeds remain as cash, EV and EBITDA are initially unchanged, so EV/EBITDA is unchanged. Equity value is also initially unchanged. Later, assuming the same usable tax rate t, the incremental net-income effect is (interest income on the new cash - interest expense on the new debt)*(1-t); P/E may rise if earnings fall and equity value stays constant. Interest rates and how cash is used are needed for a numerical P/E effect.

[F0539] How does a dividend impact your P/E, EV/EBITDA, and P/B ratio?
Asked by / question source: Evercore Generalist
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
For a cash dividend D with no change in the operating business, cash and common equity value each fall D; EV is unchanged because the equity decline is offset by subtracting less cash. Debt-financed dividends add a debt/cash issuance step and then the distribution. Taxes, distress risk and market signaling can change real-world value, but the mechanical dividend alone does not change operating EV.

[F0540] Company EV/EBITDA goes from 10x to 20x and EV/Sales goes from 2x to 4x. What is happening to the company and its EBITDA margins?

ANSWER:
EBITDA margin initially is 2/10 = 20%, and afterward is 4/20 = 20%. Both multiples doubled, but the EBITDA margin is unchanged. The multiples alone cannot tell whether EV rose, revenues/EBITDA fell, or both.

[F0541] Give examples of companies with betas of -1, 0 and 1.
Asked by / question source: Evercore Healthcare MP
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Beta measures covariance with the market divided by market variance, not total volatility. A payoff independent of the market can have beta near zero despite high standalone risk; a fair casino game is an example, subject to economic exposure in the actual business. A negative-beta asset tends to rise when the market falls; protective puts and some hedging strategies can have negative beta. Gold or gold miners are not guaranteed negative-beta assets. A high-crime location adds idiosyncratic risk but does not by itself determine market beta.

[F0542] Where do you think Inflation will go over the next yr?
Asked by / question source: Evercore Healthcare MP
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
A useful macro answer links growth, inflation, employment and policy to earnings, discount rates, credit and investor positioning. Higher rates generally reduce fixed-rate bond values and increase funding costs; equity effects also depend on why rates rose and on earnings expectations. The Fed’s U.S. goals are maximum employment and stable prices; its inflation objective is measured using PCE, with core PCE often watched for underlying pressure. Fiscal policy changes government spending/taxes, while monetary policy changes financial conditions. An inverted curve can signal expected easing or weak growth but is not a certain recession forecast. Give a base case, a contrary case and indicators that would change your view rather than presenting a forecast as fact.

[F0543] Company has an EV of 1000, with 200 Debt, 100 Cash, and a Drug that has a 50% probability of approval. What would the equity value be if the drug was approved?
Asked by / question source: Evercore Healthcare MP
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
If the $1,000 EV consists solely of the risk-adjusted value of one drug with a 50% binary success probability and zero failure value, successful drug EV is $2,000 and equity value = 2000-200+100 = $1,900. If $1,000 already represents success-case EV, equity is $900. Other pipeline assets, development costs, cash burn and future dilution invalidate simple doubling; clarify the valuation basis.

[F0544] How would the financial statements of Clinical Stage Healthcare company differ from a Consumer Retail Company?

A retailer usually has sales and COGS, inventory, supplier payables, leases, store assets and seasonal operating cash flow. Biotech value depends heavily on pipeline outcomes and runway; retail value depends on traffic, ticket, gross margin, inventory and store economics.

[F0545] How could a company raise capital if they are dilution sensitive and already significantly levered?

[F0546] How would you value a biotechnology company?
Asked by / question source: Evercore Healthcare MP; Lazard Healthcare SF; Morgan Stanley SF
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
For a pre-revenue drug developer, build a risk-adjusted NPV by asset: eligible patients * diagnosis/access * market share * net price, less manufacturing, commercialization, R&D, milestones, tax and investment. Weight development paths by stage-specific probabilities and deduct future development costs at the dates they are incurred. Model patent expiry and generic/biosimilar erosion rather than assuming monopoly cash flows forever. Add cash and other pipeline assets and subtract debt/claims, recognizing funding needs and dilution. Trading/transaction revenue multiples are secondary checks only when products and development stages are comparable. Avoid counting clinical failure risk both fully in probability-weighted cash flows and again through an arbitrary discount-rate premium.

[F0550] Explain conceptually how to determine whether a deal is accretive or dilutive.
Asked by / question source: Evercore Healthcare MP
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Accretion/dilution compares pro forma EPS with the buyer’s standalone EPS. Add target earnings and after-tax synergies, subtract after-tax new interest, foregone cash interest, purchase-accounting amortization and relevant ongoing costs; divide by buyer shares plus shares issued. New shares = stock consideration/buyer share price. In a simplified all-stock deal without other adjustments, a buyer with a higher P/E than the target’s purchase P/E is accretive. For debt or cash consideration, compare the target’s earnings yield with the after-tax funding/opportunity cost. EPS accretion does not prove value creation: price paid, risk and economic returns versus cost of capital still matter.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

[F0551] Explain WACC to someone without a finance background.
Asked by / question source: Evercore Healthcare MP
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
WACC = E/(D+E)*Ke + D/(D+E)*Kd*(1-t), extending the weights for preferred capital if present. Use market-value, sustainable capital weights. Ke is often estimated with CAPM; Kd is the current marginal borrowing yield for comparable risk and maturity, not necessarily an old coupon. The debt tax adjustment reflects usable interest deductibility. Match currency, inflation and risk to the cash flows. Moderate leverage can lower WACC through tax shields, but greater default risk raises required debt and equity returns; the relationship is not universally decreasing. For a private company, estimate operating risk from public peers and use a defensible target capital structure.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

[F0552] How do you calculate unlevered free cash flow?
Asked by / question source: Evercore Healthcare MP; J.P. Morgan Fixed Income; J.P. Morgan Research; Lazard LA; LionTree
Also covers: F0952
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Unlevered free cash flow (FCFF) = EBIT(1-t) + D&A - CapEx - increase in operating NWC, with other adjustments for operating cash items as needed. It is available to all capital providers and is discounted at WACC. Levered free cash flow to equity (FCFE) deducts after-tax interest and incorporates net borrowing: FCFE = FCFF - interest(1-t) + debt issued - principal repaid. From net income, add non-cash expenses, subtract investment and operating NWC increases, and include net borrowing. Definitions of reported “FCF” vary, so identify whether the interviewer means CFO minus CapEx, FCFF or FCFE. EBITDA is not cash flow because it omits taxes, investment and working capital.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

[F0553] Why do you tax-affect EBIT rather than net income when calculating unlevered free cash flow?
Asked by / question source: Evercore Healthcare MP
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
FCFF belongs to debt and equity providers, so use after-tax operating profit EBIT*(1-t) before financing expense. Net income already deducts interest and taxes; applying another (1-t) to net income would generally double-tax it and retain a financing deduction. If starting from net income, add after-tax interest and adjust non-operating items before adding non-cash costs and subtracting reinvestment.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

[F0554] Explain how cash is treated when bridging enterprise value and equity value.
Asked by / question source: Evercore Healthcare MP
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Equity value is the value attributable to common shareholders; for a public company it is diluted share count times share price. Operating EV = equity value + debt + preferred stock + NCI - excess cash - other separately valued non-operating assets, with consistent lease/pension adjustments where relevant. EV pairs with unlevered operating metrics; equity value pairs with net income or FCFE. Raising debt and holding the proceeds as cash normally leaves operating EV unchanged: debt and cash rise equally. A dividend reduces equity and cash together, also leaving operating EV unchanged absent signaling, tax or operational effects. Spending cash on an operating asset can change EV because value has moved from non-operating cash into operations; value creation still depends on the asset’s economics.

[F0556] A company has 10x debt/EBITDA and a 10% cost of debt. What is its interest coverage ratio? [The notes do not specify whether coverage uses EBIT or EBITDA.]
Asked by / question source: Evercore Healthcare MP
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Debt/EBITDA = 10 and interest = 10% of debt, so interest/EBITDA = 1. EBITDA/interest coverage is 1.0x. EBIT/interest is lower if D&A is positive and cannot be calculated without D&A.

[F0560] Would a one-dollar change in revenue, COGS or CapEx affect a DCF the most and why?
Asked by / question source: Evercore Healthcare MP
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
For a one-time change today, with immediate usable tax effects and no other changes, +$1 CapEx reduces current FCFF by $1, +$1 cash COGS reduces it by (1-t), and +$1 revenue raises it by incremental after-tax contribution profit, at most (1-t) if no incremental cost. CapEx has later depreciation tax shields and possible operating benefits. A recurring change or different timing can reverse a simple ranking; compare full discounted lifetime effects.

[F0562] What's the beta of... (they would mention an object or a ticket of some kind?
Asked by / question source: Evercore Healthcare MP
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
CAPM estimates cost of equity as risk-free rate + levered beta * equity risk premium, with justified additional risk adjustments where appropriate. Estimate beta using a regression of stock excess returns on market excess returns, or bottom-up comparable-company betas. Beta reflects systematic risk; leverage, cyclicality and operating fixed costs can raise it. It is not a measure of all uncertainty or an invariant property of an industry. Historical estimates depend on window, frequency and benchmark, and CAPM’s single-factor assumptions are simplifications. Compare operating risk first, then financing; a higher-growth firm does not mechanically have a higher beta.

[F0563] How does PIK interest expense flow through the statements? Assume a 20% tax rate.
Asked by / question source: Evercore Healthcare MP; Evercore M&A NY
Also covers: F0592
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
PIK interest accrues onto principal instead of being paid in cash. Take $100 of debt at 5% cash and 5% PIK for one year, at a 20% tax rate.

• Income Statement: interest expense is $10, being $5 cash and $5 PIK, so Pre-Tax Income falls $10 and Net Income falls $8.

• Cash Flow Statement: Net Income −$8, add back the $5 of non-cash PIK, so cash falls $3 — the $5 cash coupon less the $2 tax saving.

• Balance Sheet: Cash −$3 and Debt +$5 from the accrued PIK; Retained Earnings −$8, so both sides fall $3 and balance.

• Intuition: PIK protects near-term liquidity and increases what you must repay later.

At repayment you repay principal including accrued PIK, plus any call premium. Without usable deductions, cash falls by the full $5 coupon and the tax benefit becomes a deferred tax asset.

[F0564] Walk me through how you would calculate the market size of [software product]?
Asked by / question source: Evercore Healthcare MP
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Size the market two ways and reconcile them; do not confuse market size with how good the business is. Bottom-up: count the target organisations, then the users or seats per organisation, then the annual price per seat. For a mid-market HR tool, perhaps 200,000 companies in the target geography and size band, an average of 300 employees each, and $8 per employee per month gives 200,000 * 300 * $96, or roughly $5.8 billion a year. Adjust for the share of those companies that are realistic buyers rather than assuming full penetration. Top-down: start from total software or IT spending in the geography, narrow to the relevant category using industry research, and cross-check against the disclosed revenue of the known vendors plus an estimate for the long tail - if the three largest players report a combined $2 billion and hold perhaps half the category, the served market is around $4 billion. Separate the total addressable market from the serviceable market your product can actually reach given segment, geography and integrations, and from the obtainable share you could realistically win against incumbents. State the geography, the period and whether you are counting licence revenue only or services too, avoid double counting seats bought through resellers, and name the assumption the answer is most sensitive to, usually price per seat or penetration.

[F0569] How do you adjust cash-flow discounting exponents for the mid-year convention and different cash-flow timing assumptions in a DCF?
Asked by / question source: Evercore Healthcare MP
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
The mid-year convention approximates cash flow arriving evenly through the year. Discount full-year forecast cash flows at exponents 0.5, 1.5, 2.5, etc., rather than 1, 2, 3. This raises their present value at a positive discount rate. Treat stub periods and terminal value consistently with when cash is received and when the terminal value is measured; do not mechanically use a half-year exponent for every terminal-value formulation. Discrete end-of-year payments should remain at their actual dates.

[F0571] When should you use an exit multiple versus Gordon growth for terminal value?
Asked by / question source: Evercore Healthcare MP; Stephens
Also covers: F1546
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
The perpetuity-growth method is TV at year N = FCF_(N+1)/(WACC-g), with WACC greater than sustainable long-term growth g. The exit-multiple method is terminal metric (often EBITDA) times a defensible terminal multiple. Discount TV from its measurement date. Perpetuity growth is tied to long-run economics and reinvestment; exit multiples are grounded in market evidence but can embed cyclical mispricing. Check that growth, margins, reinvestment and returns on capital form a sustainable steady state. A finite-life asset or expiring drug may need a runoff value rather than a perpetual terminal value. Neither method is automatically always higher or more reliable.

[F0572] Value a tree based on its cash flows. [Inputs not recorded.]
Asked by / question source: Evercore Healthcare MP
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Forecast fruit volume times selling price, subtract harvesting, maintenance, land/operating costs, taxes and any required reinvestment, and discount the resulting cash flows for the tree’s economic life. Include any residual sale value and replacement/replanting costs consistently. A perpetuity only makes sense for a sustainably maintained operation, not an individual tree assumed to live forever. For constant annual end-year cash C for N years, PV = C*[1-(1+r)^(-N)]/r.

[F0573] Would you rather invest in a 10x EV/EBITDA company or 5x EV/EBITDA? Why?
Asked by / question source: Evercore Healthcare MP
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Neither multiple alone decides. The 10x company may have superior growth, cash conversion, returns, durability or lower risk; the 5x company may be a cyclical peak or value trap. Convert EBITDA to cash flow, check debt and reinvestment, value downside and compare implied assumptions. Choose the investment with the better risk-adjusted return at its actual price.

[F0574] Which would give a lower EV/EBITDA multiple: Leasing vs. buying a vending machine?
Asked by / question source: Evercore Healthcare MP
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
There is no universal ordering without consistent accounting. A U.S.-GAAP operating lease generally lowers EBITDA through lease expense, while owning a machine produces depreciation below EBITDA; adding the same financing-like lease obligation to EV without adjusting earnings would distort the comparison. IFRS 16 and finance leases largely move expense into depreciation/interest. Compare lease-adjusted EV and operating metrics or full cash-flow economics on a consistent basis.

[F0575] How do pensions impact WACC?
Asked by / question source: Evercore Healthcare MP
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
An underfunded defined-benefit pension can be treated as a debt-like claim in the valuation bridge, with tax and funding considerations. Pension asset/liability risk and contributions may also affect business/equity risk. Do not automatically add the entire pension obligation to debt weights while leaving related pension assets and operating metrics unadjusted. A standard WACC usually uses market debt and equity; if extending it for pension risk, make all corresponding cash-flow and beta adjustments consistently.

[F0576] Value a money tree paying $100 in year 1, $200 in year 2 and continuing in that pattern. [Discount rate and horizon not recorded.]

[F0581] A company has a luxury-brand division with growing sales and flat EBITDA, and a waste-disposal division with flat revenue and growing EBITDA. How would you value the company?

Answer status: Prepared model answer

[F0582] What would you expect margins to be for a laundromat?
Asked by / question source: Evercore M&A NY
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Build revenue from operating units rather than assuming a growth rate: customers/volume * frequency/utilization * net price, plus ancillary streams. Separate variable costs from fixed costs to model contribution margin, operating leverage and break-even volume. For a pharmacy use prescription volumes, reimbursement/mix, dispensing margin and payer terms; roofing uses crew capacity, projects, ticket size and repair/replacement mix; software/telecom uses subscribers, ARPU, churn and network/service costs; a food outlet uses footfall, conversion, ticket and opening days. Forecast working capital, maintenance/growth CapEx and taxes. Value sustainable after-tax cash flow and cross-check peers; local concentration, regulation and reinvestment can explain different multiples despite similar current profits.

[F0584] A company is trading at $X per share and is being purchased at a Y% premium. You are given the amount of convertible debt, RSUs, options (and exercise price), cash, and debt the company has. What is the enterprise value of the company?
Asked by / question source: Evercore M&A NY
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Work to the offer price first, then to diluted shares, then bridge. The per-share offer price is the current price grossed up by the premium: X * (1 + Y%). Build the fully diluted share count at that offer price, not at the unaffected price. Under the treasury stock method, in-the-money options are exercised and the proceeds buy back stock, so each tranche adds options * (offer price - strike) / offer price net new shares; out-of-the-money options add nothing. RSUs are added in full, since there are no exercise proceeds. For convertible debt, compare the offer price with the conversion price: if it is in the money, apply the if-converted method, adding principal / conversion price shares and removing that principal from debt in the bridge; if it is out of the money, leave it in debt and add no shares. Never count the same convertible as both debt and shares. Diluted equity value = offer price * fully diluted shares. Then enterprise value = diluted equity value + debt (including any unconverted convertible principal) + preferred + noncontrolling interests - cash and other non-operating assets.

[F0585] How would you value a recently restructured third division in a sum-of-the-parts valuation?
Asked by / question source: Evercore M&A NY
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Value each segment using its own cash flows, peers, growth and risk rather than forcing one group multiple on dissimilar operations. Add segment operating values, subtract the PV of unallocated central costs and any separation costs, then make the consolidated EV-to-equity bridge. Avoid double counting intersegment sales, shared assets or cash/debt already included. A diversified company with a mature utility segment and a high-growth software segment is a natural SOTP example. A conglomerate discount may reflect complexity, governance or inefficient capital allocation, but should be supported rather than automatically assumed.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

[F0586] How do you take into account NOLs in an M&A transaction?
Asked by / question source: Evercore M&A NY; Lazard Healthcare SF; Lazard Technology SF
Also covers: F1066
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Deferred taxes arise when book and tax recognition differ. A DTA represents future tax relief, subject to realizability; a DTL represents future taxes from taxable temporary differences. NOLs can create DTAs, but their usable value depends on taxable profit, jurisdiction, expiration and legal restrictions. Value NOLs by forecasting actual cash-tax savings and discounting them at a rate reflecting their risk; do not automatically use face value or add a DTA to EV. In acquisitions, fair-value write-ups without tax-basis step-ups can create DTLs and increase goodwill. For U.S. ownership changes, assess Section 382 limitations rather than assuming all acquired losses can be used.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

[F0587] How would DTAs and DTLs affect Goodwill?
Asked by / question source: Evercore M&A NY
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Goodwill = consideration plus NCI/previous stake where applicable minus fair value of identifiable net assets. A recognized DTL reduces net identifiable assets and therefore increases goodwill; a recognized DTA increases them and reduces goodwill, all else equal. Tax-basis step-ups, realizability/valuation allowances and acquisition tax structure determine recognition. The cash-tax value must be modeled consistently rather than assuming every book DTA has face-value worth.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

[F0588] How is interest expense shown in DCF?
Asked by / question source: Evercore M&A NY
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
In an unlevered DCF, exclude interest expense from FCFF and discount at WACC; the debt tax shield is reflected in the after-tax cost of debt. Subtract debt in the EV-to-equity bridge. In an equity DCF, deduct after-tax interest, include net borrowing and discount FCFE at cost of equity. Deducting interest in FCFF and also using WACC would mix claims and double count financing effects.

[F0590] Two companies merge and there are no revenue synergies but the combined company has 100 million more in revenue than the sums of the revenues of the 2 individual companies. How did this happen?

[F0591] Solve for the break-even interest rate on acquisition debt that makes a transaction EPS-neutral. [Transaction inputs not recorded.]
Asked by / question source: Evercore M&A NY
Answer status: Method / conditional answer — source details needed
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
The source omits inputs needed for a unique conclusion. Assess a transaction through strategic fit, price versus standalone and synergy value, financing, execution and integration risk. Explain buyer/target businesses, consideration, purchase multiple, expected cash benefits and why a deal is preferable to organic investment. Test downside cases, regulatory constraints and ability to finance/close. More EPS or more revenue alone does not prove value creation; incremental risk-adjusted returns should exceed the cost of capital. For a named historical transaction, use the announcement, filings and investor presentations to establish terms, and distinguish the rationale known at signing from later outcomes. No unspecified deal supports a factual purchase multiple or recommendation.

[F0593] Tell me about a business in your college town -- how would you value that business?
Asked by / question source: Evercore M&A NY
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Build revenue from operating units rather than assuming a growth rate: customers/volume * frequency/utilization * net price, plus ancillary streams. Separate variable costs from fixed costs to model contribution margin, operating leverage and break-even volume. For a pharmacy use prescription volumes, reimbursement/mix, dispensing margin and payer terms; roofing uses crew capacity, projects, ticket size and repair/replacement mix; software/telecom uses subscribers, ARPU, churn and network/service costs; a food outlet uses footfall, conversion, ticket and opening days. Forecast working capital, maintenance/growth CapEx and taxes. Value sustainable after-tax cash flow and cross-check peers; local concentration, regulation and reinvestment can explain different multiples despite similar current profits.

[F0594] Compare levered and unlevered beta and explain how to move between them.
Asked by / question source: Evercore M&A NY; Houlihan Lokey NY; J.P. Morgan LA
Also covers: F0866, F0974
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Unlever comparable companies’ equity betas to remove financing risk, use a suitable peer median asset beta, and relever at the target capital structure. A common shortcut, assuming debt beta approximately zero, is beta_U = beta_L/[1+(1-t)D/E], and beta_L = beta_U[1+(1-t)D/E]. Use market-value leverage and a consistent marginal tax assumption. If debt risk is material, incorporate debt beta and a consistent tax-shield model. A private company lacks an observable stock beta, so operating comparables are the starting point; private status alone does not justify an arbitrary adjustment.

[F0595] Calculate MOIC and IRR for an LBO. [Numerical inputs not recorded.]
Asked by / question source: Evercore M&A NY
Answer status: Method / conditional answer — source details needed
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
The source omits inputs needed for a unique conclusion. An LBO buys a company using sponsor equity and debt serviced by the target’s cash flows. Set entry EV and equity purchase price, build sources and uses including fees/refinancing, forecast operations and cash generation, model debt interest/amortization and the cash sweep, then estimate exit EV and subtract exit net debt and other claims. Sponsor MOIC = proceeds/invested equity; with one entry and exit, IRR = MOIC^(1/years)-1. Returns come from operating growth, deleveraging, entry/exit valuation and distributions. More leverage increases both upside and default risk. Favor resilient cash conversion, manageable CapEx, credible improvements and a defensible purchase price. Strategic buyers may pay more for synergies; sponsors may offer certainty, speed, rollover equity or management continuity.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

[F0596] Give an example of an asset or company with a beta of zero.
Asked by / question source: Evercore M&A NY
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
CAPM estimates cost of equity as risk-free rate + levered beta * equity risk premium, with justified additional risk adjustments where appropriate. Estimate beta using a regression of stock excess returns on market excess returns, or bottom-up comparable-company betas. Beta reflects systematic risk; leverage, cyclicality and operating fixed costs can raise it. It is not a measure of all uncertainty or an invariant property of an industry. Historical estimates depend on window, frequency and benchmark, and CAPM’s single-factor assumptions are simplifications. Compare operating risk first, then financing; a higher-growth firm does not mechanically have a higher beta.

[F0597] HoldCo has $200 million of unsecured debt and holds only equity in Sub 1 and Sub 2. Sub 1 has an EV of $400 million, $200 million of secured debt and $100 million of unsecured debt. Sub 2 has an EV of $400 million and $500 million of unsecured debt. There are no intercompany guarantees. Calculate recoveries for each entity's debt. [The source omits the unit after Sub 1's EV; millions inferred from the surrounding figures.]
Asked by / question source: Evercore Restructuring
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Sub 1 EV 400 pays its 200 secured and 100 unsecured debt in full, leaving 100 equity for HoldCo. Sub 2 EV 400 pays its 500 unsecured debt at 80 cents, leaving no equity. HoldCo therefore has assets of 100 against debt of 200, giving 50% recovery. Assume no cash, costs, other claims or guarantees and contemporaneous realizable values.

[F0598] For the deal you discussed, what is a reasonable valuation and which synergies are most and least likely to be realized?
Asked by / question source: Evercore Restructuring
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Cost synergies eliminate duplicate costs such as headquarters or procurement expense. Revenue synergies arise from cross-selling, distribution or pricing improvements, usually with additional costs and execution risk. Financial/tax synergies may involve funding or tax benefits. A dollar of durable cost savings normally adds more profit than a dollar of additional revenue because new revenue has associated variable costs. Value after-tax cash benefits after implementation costs, timing and probability of delivery. Do not pay the seller for every potential synergy or double count benefits already in the base forecasts.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

[F0599] Two companies with exactly the same financial profiles have two bonds with the same YTE and par value but are trading at different values?
Asked by / question source: Evercore Restructuring
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Price, coupon, maturity and yield are linked by one equation, so fixing the yield and the par value forces the difference into the other two. A bond's price is the present value of its coupons and principal discounted at its YTM, so two bonds with the same YTM and the same par value trade at different prices when their coupon rates differ, their maturities differ, or their payment frequency or day-count conventions differ. The higher-coupon bond trades at the higher price, because the same yield is being delivered through larger interim payments. A bond priced above par has a coupon above its YTM; one priced below par has a coupon below its YTM. Quoted price conventions matter too: clean versus dirty price differ by accrued interest, and a total market value also depends on the face amount outstanding. Only after those mechanical explanations are excluded should you reach for issuer-level differences such as liquidity, covenants, call features or credit, and those would normally show up in the yield rather than leaving it unchanged.

[F0601] Two companies, same coupon, both trading at par, what has the higher YTM?
Asked by / question source: Evercore Restructuring
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Neither - they have the same YTM. A bond trading exactly at par has a yield to maturity equal to its coupon rate, because the price equals the redemption amount and there is no amortized gain or loss to add to or subtract from the coupon income. Two bonds with the same coupon, both at par, therefore have the same YTM regardless of the issuers' differing business quality, and the market is telling you it requires the same yield from both. The question tests whether you know that identity rather than inviting a comparison of the two companies. Qualifications: the bonds must have the same payment frequency and day-count convention, "par" must mean a clean price of 100 rather than a dirty price including accrued interest, and if either bond is callable the relevant comparison becomes yield to worst, which can differ even when both trade at par. A credit difference between the issuers would show up as a price difference away from par, not as different yields at the same price.

[F0602] Compare the yields to maturity of the two bonds if they trade at the same discounted price. [Bond terms not recorded in this follow-up.]
Asked by / question source: Evercore Restructuring
Answer status: Method / conditional answer — source details needed
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
The source omits inputs needed for a unique conclusion. A bond pays contractual coupons and principal, subject to default. Price = sum[coupon_t/(1+y)^t] + principal/(1+y)^N for annual payments. YTM is the discount rate that equates those promised payments to price, not a guaranteed realized return. Current yield = annual coupon/current price. Yield to call substitutes the call date and call price for maturity. Coupon is set on face value; yield depends on price. For a one-year bond, YTM = (coupon + redemption - price)/price. For multi-year bonds solve the equation rather than using coupon/price. Distressed debt may require probability-weighted recoveries, not just promised-payment YTM.

[F0603] What are the main distress of the companies that need RX?

[F0605] Enterprise value of $200mm, secured debt of $100mm and unsecured debt of $150mm. What value does each tranche of debt trade at?

[F0606] What happens to WACC as the company takes more debt?
Asked by / question source: Evercore Restructuring; J.P. Morgan (compiled interview notes); Perella Weinberg Partners CHI; PJT Partners M&A
Also covers: F1336, F1395, F1794
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
WACC = E/(D+E)*Ke + D/(D+E)*Kd*(1-t), extending the weights for preferred capital if present. Use market-value, sustainable capital weights. Ke is often estimated with CAPM; Kd is the current marginal borrowing yield for comparable risk and maturity, not necessarily an old coupon. The debt tax adjustment reflects usable interest deductibility. Match currency, inflation and risk to the cash flows. Moderate leverage can lower WACC through tax shields, but greater default risk raises required debt and equity returns; the relationship is not universally decreasing. For a private company, estimate operating risk from public peers and use a defensible target capital structure.

[F0607] What bonds that will go bankrupt in 3 years with a 10 percent coupon would trade at?
Asked by / question source: Evercore Restructuring
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
A 10% coupon and default in three years do not determine price. With face value 100, annual coupons actually paid in years 1 and 2 and recovery R in year 3, one simplified price is 10/(1+r)+10/(1+r)^2+R/(1+r)^3; add any year-3 coupon only if it is actually paid/recovered under the scenario. Specify payment timing, recovery, discount rate, seniority and probability of the scenario. Promised YTM to face value can be misleading for debt expected to default.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

[F0608] Value post chapter 7 bankruptcy liquidation?
Asked by / question source: Evercore Restructuring
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
A Chapter 7 liquidation is valued asset by asset, not as a going concern, so the earnings-based methods used for an operating company do not apply. Start from the balance sheet and estimate gross recoveries on each asset class under a forced or orderly sale, applying recovery rates that reflect how saleable each one is: cash at or near 100%, receivables at a discount for collectability and aging, inventory well below book depending on whether it is finished goods or work in process, PP&E at market or scrap value rather than book, and intangibles and goodwill at little or nothing, since brand and going-concern value largely evaporate when operations stop. Then subtract the costs of the process itself - trustee and professional fees, wind-down and severance costs, lease rejection and contract breakage - because these are administrative claims paid ahead of creditors. Distribute what remains down the statutory priority: secured creditors against their collateral first, then superpriority and administrative claims, then priority unsecured claims such as certain employee and tax obligations, then general unsecured creditors pro rata, with equity last and almost always receiving nothing. Compare the result with the going-concern or reorganization value, because liquidation value is normally the floor that makes a Chapter 11 plan worth pursuing instead.

[F0611] Give me some reasons that equity value cannot go below zero and often doesn't trade at zero.
Asked by / question source: Evercore Restructuring
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Ordinary limited-liability shares cannot have a negative trading price because holders are generally not obligated to fund the company’s debt beyond their investment. Equity can still trade above zero when current asset value is below debt because shareholders retain an option on a recovery in value and may benefit from volatility or restructuring negotiations. That does not guarantee a recovery, and options/exotic obligations or commitments outside the share itself require separate analysis.

[F0612] If a company doesn't have any debt and is trying to raise some, how much would you recommend it raise?
Asked by / question source: Evercore Restructuring
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Credit underwriting asks whether cash flow can pay obligations in downside scenarios and what lenders recover if it cannot. Assess business resilience, leverage, interest coverage, fixed-charge coverage, free cash flow, liquidity and maturity/refinancing risk. Review collateral, guarantees and covenant headroom. Expected credit loss is approximately PD * LGD * exposure, though valuation also includes timing and risk premiums. The “3 Cs” are commonly character, capacity and capital, with collateral and conditions added in a five-C framework. Maintenance covenants are tested periodically; incurrence covenants when specified actions occur. Do not set leverage from EBITDA alone: cyclicality, cash conversion, CapEx and rates can make equal leverage ratios very different risks.

[F0613] How that looks each year accounting for depreciation and PIK interest. Assume a 20% tax rate.
Asked by / question source: Evercore Restructuring
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
PIK interest accrues onto principal instead of being paid in cash. Take $100 of debt at 5% cash and 5% PIK for one year, at a 20% tax rate.

• Income Statement: interest expense is $10, being $5 cash and $5 PIK, so Pre-Tax Income falls $10 and Net Income falls $8.

• Cash Flow Statement: Net Income −$8, add back the $5 of non-cash PIK, so cash falls $3 — the $5 cash coupon less the $2 tax saving.

• Balance Sheet: Cash −$3 and Debt +$5 from the accrued PIK; Retained Earnings −$8, so both sides fall $3 and balance.

• Intuition: PIK protects near-term liquidity and increases what you must repay later.

At repayment you repay principal including accrued PIK, plus any call premium. Without usable deductions, cash falls by the full $5 coupon and the tax benefit becomes a deferred tax asset.

Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Debt = 10*100 = 1,000; annual interest = 10%*1,000 = 100. EBITDA/interest = 1.0x. EBIT-based coverage requires depreciation/amortization.

[F0615] You're a financial sponsor and you buy an asset for $100; 5 years later you sell it for $100 and you're ecstatic. Why?
Asked by / question source: Evercore Restructuring
Answer status: Prepared model answer

[F0616] A company has $200 million enterprise value, $100 million secured debt and $150 million unsecured debt. If collateral for the secured debt is worth only $50 million, what does each tranche trade at?

[F0617] A company with positive EBITDA of over $50mm for 10 years goes bankrupt. How is that possible?

[F0621] Throughout the year you raise $100 of debt with a 10% interest rate; 5% is PIK and 5% is cash interest. Walk me through the effects on all three statements after one year. Assume a 20% tax rate.
Asked by / question source: Evercore Restructuring
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Assume the full $100 is outstanding from the start of the year. Interest is $10 in total, $5 cash and $5 PIK, at a 20% tax rate.

• At issuance: Cash +$100 and Debt +$100, a financing inflow, no income effect.

• Income Statement: interest expense $10, so Pre-Tax Income falls $10 and Net Income falls $8.

• Cash Flow Statement: Net Income −$8, add back the $5 of non-cash PIK, so operating cash flow is −$3 for the year. Including the issuance, cash is up $97.

• Balance Sheet: Cash +$97 and Debt $105 after the PIK accretes, with Retained Earnings −$8, so both sides are up $97 and balance.

• Intuition: you raised $100 and paid out $5 of cash coupon less $2 of tax relief.

If the debt is drawn through the year rather than on day one, time-weight the interest.

[F0622] Starting with EBIT, calculate a company's cash burn. [Numerical inputs not recorded.]
Asked by / question source: Evercore Restructuring
Answer status: Method / conditional answer — source details needed
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
The source omits inputs needed for a unique conclusion. EBITDA = revenue - cash operating expenses before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization; EBIT = EBITDA - D&A. Net income also includes interest, taxes and non-operating items. EBITDA helps compare operating performance across financing and depreciation conventions, but is not cash flow: it ignores CapEx, working capital and cash taxes. A business can have positive EBITDA yet run out of cash because of reinvestment, interest, maturities, working-capital needs or one-time payments. EBIT can be more meaningful for asset-heavy businesses because depreciation captures part of asset consumption. Evaluate adjusted EBITDA add-backs critically and avoid adding recurring costs back simply because management labels them exceptional.

[F0623] You're playing a game, theres $2 in a pot. If you flip heads, you get to keep the $2, but if you flip tails, the pot doubles; the game does not end until you flip heads. What is the value of the game? Would you play if I charged you $10,000?
Asked by / question source: Evercore Restructuring
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
This is the St. Petersburg paradox. A first head on toss n pays 2^n dollars with probability 2^-n, so each possible n contributes $1 to expected payout; with unlimited rounds and funding the mathematical expectation diverges. A real willingness to pay is finite because wealth, risk aversion, payout caps, time and counterparty solvency matter. Infinite expected value does not make a $10,000 entry fee sensible for every person.

[F0626] HoldCo owns 75% of OpCo 1 and all of OpCo 2. OpCo 1 has EBITDA of $60 million, an 8x multiple and $300 million debt. OpCo 2 has EBITDA of $40 million, a 10x multiple and $500 million debt. OpCo 1 guarantees OpCo 2's debt. Compare buying HoldCo stock at $0.50 per share with 100 shares outstanding versus OpCo 2 debt at 90 cents on the dollar with a 10% coupon and one-year maturity. Consider MOIC and time value of money. [Units of the HoldCo share count are ambiguous in the source.]
Asked by / question source: Evercore Restructuring
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Work each borrower's own assets first, then add the guarantee claim. OpCo 1: EBITDA 60 at 8x gives an enterprise value of 480 against 300 of debt, so its debt is covered in full and 180 of residual equity is left. OpCo 2: EBITDA 40 at 10x gives 400 against 500 of debt, so it is short 100 and its equity is worthless. Because OpCo 1 guarantees OpCo 2's debt, that 100 deficiency becomes a claim at OpCo 1, where it ranks alongside OpCo 1's other unsecured creditors and is paid out of the 180 of residual value. OpCo 2's lenders therefore recover in full: 400 from their own borrower and 100 under the guarantee. OpCo 1's residual equity falls to 80, and HoldCo's 75% of that is 60, with nothing from OpCo 2, so HoldCo's equity is worth 60. On the two investments: the stock costs 100 shares times $0.50, and taking the share count in millions to match the EBITDA figures, that is 50 against 60 of value, roughly 1.2x. The OpCo 2 debt costs 90 and pays 100 of principal plus the 10% coupon at maturity in one year, so 110 against 90, about 1.22x. The debt is the better risk-adjusted purchase: a similar multiple earned over a known one-year horizon rather than an unspecified equity holding period, and a contractual claim that sits ahead of both HoldCo's equity and the guarantee. Confirm the guarantee's ranking at OpCo 1, whether it is secured or structurally subordinated, and the HoldCo share-count units before relying on these figures.

[F0627] Why could bonds of the same class, recovery and YTM trade at different market values?
Asked by / question source: Evercore Restructuring
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Bonds can have identical quoted YTM but different coupons, maturity, call terms or cash-flow schedules, producing different prices. Aggregate market value also depends on face amount outstanding. Same class and recovery percentage do not necessarily mean identical interim payments or default timing. If all contractual and expected cash flows, quantities, risk and liquidity are identical, price should be identical absent a temporary market dislocation.

[F0628] Walk through buying back $100 million of bonds at 106 with a 33% tax rate.
Asked by / question source: Evercore Restructuring
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Repurchasing $100 million of face at 106 costs $106 million and creates a $6 million extinguishment loss, at the stated 33% tax rate.

• Income Statement: a $6m loss on extinguishment, so Pre-Tax Income falls $6m and Net Income falls $4.02m.

• Cash Flow Statement: Net Income −$4.02m, and the $106m paid retires debt, so the $100m of principal is a financing outflow while the $6m premium follows the applicable policy. Total cash falls $104.02m — the $106m paid less $1.98m of tax relief.

• Balance Sheet: Cash −$104.02m and Debt −$100m, against Retained Earnings −$4.02m, so both sides fall $104.02m and balance.

• Intuition: you paid a $6m premium to retire the debt and got a third of it back in tax, so the economic cost is about $4m.

Buying debt back below par reverses this into a taxable gain. Unamortised issuance costs and original issue discount also run through the loss, and the gain may be sheltered by NOLs.

[F0635] Company A with P/E blank acquired company B with a P/E of blank.
Asked by / question source: Evercore SF
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Choose companies with similar business model, geography, growth, margins, risk and capital intensity. Calculate consistent enterprise/equity values and calendarized historical or forecast metrics, normalize unusual items, and apply a justified peer range to the target metric. EV/Revenue divided by EV/EBITDA equals EBITDA margin when periods and EV are consistent. P/E uses equity value/net income; EV/EBITDA uses operating value/pre-interest earnings, so taxes and financing can produce different rankings. Higher multiples can reflect growth, stronger returns, recurring revenue or lower risk, not automatically overvaluation. Negative EBITDA makes its multiple unhelpful; revenue multiples require a credible path to margins. Share price alone is not comparable across firms because share counts differ.

[F0636] If company A paid in blank % stock and blank % debt, would it be an accretive or dilutive acquisition?
Asked by / question source: Evercore SF
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Accretion/dilution compares pro forma EPS with the buyer’s standalone EPS. Add target earnings and after-tax synergies, subtract after-tax new interest, foregone cash interest, purchase-accounting amortization and relevant ongoing costs; divide by buyer shares plus shares issued. New shares = stock consideration/buyer share price. In a simplified all-stock deal without other adjustments, a buyer with a higher P/E than the target’s purchase P/E is accretive. For debt or cash consideration, compare the target’s earnings yield with the after-tax funding/opportunity cost. EPS accretion does not prove value creation: price paid, risk and economic returns versus cost of capital still matter.

[F0640] Please explain how you calculate the Internal Rate of Return (IRR) of a private company, given certain cash flows.
Asked by / question source: Evercore Strategic Defense & Shareholder Advisory
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
MOIC = total cash proceeds/total invested capital and does not account for timing. With a single entry and exit, annualized return or IRR = (exit proceeds/entry investment)^(1/years)-1. With interim cash flows, solve 0 = sum[CF_t/(1+r)^t]; use dated cash flows for XIRR. Earlier distributions generally increase IRR at the same MOIC. MOIC can favor a larger long-held gain while IRR favors rapid capital return; assess both alongside risk and absolute profit. ROE is accounting net income/average book equity and is not the same as an investment IRR.

[F0642] How would you build out the three financial statements for a company that pays royalties?
Asked by / question source: Financial Technology Partners SF
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
First distinguish a company paying royalties from one receiving them. A payer generally records contractual royalties as COGS or operating expense as the related sales/activity occurs, with a payable until cash settlement; an upfront license may be capitalized/amortized if the applicable rules require it. Forecast royalties from the contract’s revenue base, rate, minimums, milestones and term. [F0643] How do you calculate equity value for a private company without public financials?
Asked by / question source: Financial Technology Partners SF
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Equity value is the value attributable to common shareholders; for a public company it is diluted share count times share price. Operating EV = equity value + debt + preferred stock + NCI - excess cash - other separately valued non-operating assets, with consistent lease/pension adjustments where relevant. EV pairs with unlevered operating metrics; equity value pairs with net income or FCFE. Raising debt and holding the proceeds as cash normally leaves operating EV unchanged: debt and cash rise equally. A dividend reduces equity and cash together, also leaving operating EV unchanged absent signaling, tax or operational effects. Spending cash on an operating asset can change EV because value has moved from non-operating cash into operations; value creation still depends on the asset’s economics.

[F0646] What is the effect on the balance sheet of a ten dollar decrease of deffered revenue? Assume a 20% tax rate.
Asked by / question source: Financial Technology Partners SF
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Assume the $10 decrease is revenue earned on a prior customer prepayment, no associated costs, 20% tax rate.

• Income Statement: Revenue +$10, so Net Income is up $8.

• Cash Flow Statement: Net Income +$8 less the $10 fall in Deferred Revenue, so cash falls $2 if the tax is paid now. No new customer cash arrives.

• Balance Sheet: Deferred Revenue −$10 and Cash −$2, with Retained Earnings +$8, so both sides fall $2 and balance.

• Intuition: the only movement is the $2 of tax on revenue whose cash was collected earlier.

If instead the decrease is a refund, cash and the liability both fall $10 and no revenue is recognised. The reason for the decrease decides the answer.

[F0647] How would that track through the three statements, what happens to free cash, and overall financials?
Asked by / question source: Financial Technology Partners SF
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:

Reconcile net income to CFO using non-cash items and operating working-capital changes, then add investing and financing flows. Update cash, the relevant balance-sheet accounts and retained earnings, and verify assets = liabilities + equity. The numerical result requires amounts, timing, tax treatment and financing terms; an incomplete prompt does not support a unique set of balances. Separate initial recognition, subsequent operations and eventual repayment/disposal.

[F0648] Does an LBO typically produce a higher or lower valuation compared to a DCF?
Asked by / question source: Financial Technology Partners SF
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Core methods are public trading comparables, precedent transactions and DCF. An LBO is a sponsor’s return-constrained price analysis; asset-based/liquidation value and sum-of-the-parts are additional approaches. Trading comps reflect current minority market prices; precedents reflect historical deal conditions, control and possible synergies; DCF reflects forecast cash generation and risk. Precedents often exceed trading comps, and LBO prices can be lower than strategic values, but there is no guaranteed ranking or universal valuation floor. Select methods suited to the business, compare their assumptions and present a range rather than averaging incompatible outputs.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

[F0649] What did your excel sheet start off with in the DCF?
Asked by / question source: Financial Technology Partners SF
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Value equals the present value of expected cash flows. For an operating company, forecast FCFF from revenue, margins, taxes, reinvestment and working capital, discount at WACC, and add a consistently estimated terminal value. EV = sum[FCFF_t/(1+WACC)^t] + TV_N/(1+WACC)^N. Bridge to equity by adding excess cash/non-operating assets and subtracting debt, preferred claims and NCI; divide by diluted shares if needed. For a tree or other asset, forecast sale proceeds less maintenance, taxes and reinvestment over its actual economic life. A level end-of-year perpetuity is C/r; a growing one is next-period C/(r-g). Cash flow today is not the same as next-period cash flow.

[F0651] How did you get to an operating income?
Asked by / question source: Financial Technology Partners SF
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Start with revenue, subtract COGS for gross profit, operating expenses and D&A for operating income/EBIT, then interest and non-operating items for pre-tax income, and taxes for net income. Add back D&A to EBIT for EBITDA. Examine growth, gross and operating margin, recurring versus unusual items and conversion into cash. Statements must be analyzed together: balance sheets show financing and working-capital requirements, and cash-flow statements test whether earnings produce liquidity. A financial-statement exercise without the transaction amounts or schedules cannot yield unique numbers.

[F0652] What are the components in net working capital?
Asked by / question source: Financial Technology Partners SF
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
For valuation, operating NWC usually equals non-cash operating current assets minus non-debt operating current liabilities. An increase uses cash and is subtracted from FCFF; a decrease releases cash. Receivables and inventory tie up cash, while supplier payables and customer advances finance operations. DSO = average AR/revenue * days; inventory days = average inventory/COGS * days; DPO = average AP/COGS * days (purchases may be better when available). Cash conversion cycle = DSO + inventory days - DPO. A higher DPO can improve cash flow but may also signal supplier stress; evaluate industry terms and overdue balances.

[F0654] What is deferred revenue and what type of companies do we typically see it in? Assume a 20% tax rate.
Asked by / question source: Financial Technology Partners SF; Shea & Co
Also covers: F1708
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Cash arrives before the service is delivered, so it sits as a liability until earned. Take $100 collected upfront for a service delivered evenly over a year, no delivery costs, 20% tax rate.

• At collection: no income-statement effect. Cash +$100 and Deferred Revenue +$100, so the balance sheet balances with no change in equity.

• Income Statement, as delivered: Revenue +$100, so Pre-Tax Income is up $100 and Net Income is up $80.

• Cash Flow Statement: Net Income +$80, and the $100 decrease in Deferred Revenue is a negative, so cash falls $20.

• Balance Sheet: Cash −$20 and Deferred Revenue −$100, so assets fall $20 while liabilities fall $100 and Retained Earnings rises $80; both sides fall $20 and balance.

• Intuition: the company already holds the cash, so recognition only moves the obligation into earnings and triggers the $20 of tax.

Straight-line delivery over N months recognises contract value / N each month. Bookings, billings, revenue and cash collection are four different things, and tax recognition can differ from book.

[F0655] How do you calculate gross and net retention on a company?
Asked by / question source: Financial Technology Partners SF
Also covers: F0656
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
For the same opening customer cohort, gross revenue retention = (opening recurring revenue - churn - contraction)/opening recurring revenue. Net revenue retention adds expansion revenue to the numerator. Exclude revenue from brand-new customers; use a consistent period and treatment of reactivations/FX. Gross retention is normally at most 100%; net retention can exceed 100% when expansion exceeds losses.

[F0657] Walk me through the three statements, buying CapEx with debt?
Asked by / question source: Financial Technology Partners SF
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
At purchase, capitalize an asset at cost C. A cash-funded purchase reduces cash C and increases PP&E C, with no immediate income-statement expense; report C as investing outflow. Debt funding adds a financing inflow and debt liability; new equity funding adds paid-in capital. Subsequently depreciate (cost-residual value)/useful life for straight-line depreciation and recognize interest on debt. Net income falls by after-tax depreciation and interest; add back depreciation in CFO, and classify principal repayments as financing. The exact annual cash and retained-earnings changes require the useful life, tax rate, financing terms and purchase date. An impairment is a separate write-down, not routine CapEx.

[F0659] How do you value a SaaS company.
Asked by / question source: Financial Technology Partners SF
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
For SaaS, focus on recurring revenue quality: ARR/MRR, net and gross retention, churn, customer concentration, contract duration, gross margin and sales efficiency. NRR includes expansion less churn/contraction; GRR excludes expansion. Estimate cohort lifetime value from contribution profit and retention, compare it with fully loaded CAC, and test CAC payback. The Rule of 40 adds revenue growth percentage and a consistently defined profit-margin percentage; it is a heuristic, not a valuation formula. Value with DCF and growth/margin-adjusted EV/revenue or EV/ARR; profitable firms can use EV/EBITDA. Annual prepayments support cash conversion, but deferred revenue is an obligation. Sustainable returns matter more than growth at any cost.
