[F0660] Explain the effects of changes in accounts receivable and accounts payable on the three statements. Assume a 20% tax rate. [Additional scenario input not recorded.]
Asked by / question source: Financial Technology Partners SF
Answer status: Method / conditional answer — source details needed
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Take the two sides separately, each at a 20% tax rate.

• Receivables, on a $100 credit sale with no cost: Revenue +$100 and Net Income +$80; AR rises $100, which is a negative in operating cash flow, so cash falls $20; assets rise $80 against Retained Earnings +$80. Collection later moves $100 from AR into cash with no new income.

• Payables, on a $10 expense received but unpaid: Operating Expenses +$10 and Net Income −$8; AP rises $10, a positive, so cash rises $2; AP +$10 against Retained Earnings −$8 leaves both sides up $2. Paying it later reduces cash and AP by $10 with no new expense.

• Intuition: receivables mean you owe tax on cash you have not collected; payables mean you have taken a deduction on cash you have not paid. They work in opposite directions, which is why the cash conversion cycle nets them.

Ask whether the question describes a new sale or purchase, a delayed collection or payment, or a write-off, because each gives a different answer.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

[F0661] A company's revenue is stagnant but it has a positive ending cash-flow balance. Explain where the cash may be coming from or going. [The source recalls the question incompletely.]
Asked by / question source: Financial Technology Partners SF
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Cash can rise while revenue is flat because cash flow and revenue are different things; walk the three sections of the cash flow statement and find the source. In operating cash flow: non-cash charges such as depreciation, amortisation, impairments and stock-based compensation reduce net income without consuming cash and are added back, so a heavily depreciating business can generate cash on flat sales; working capital can release cash if receivables are collected faster, inventory is run down or payables and deferred revenue are stretched, and customer prepayments bring cash in ahead of the revenue; cash taxes can also fall through loss carryforwards or timing. In investing: selling assets, a division or investments brings in cash, and simply cutting capital expenditure below depreciation preserves it. In financing: new borrowing or an equity issue raises cash, and suspending dividends or buybacks retains it. The useful follow-up is which of these repeats. Non-cash add-backs and genuine margin or working-capital improvement are repeatable; asset sales, a one-off working-capital release, deferred capex and new borrowing are not, and the last two can mean the business is harvesting itself or levering up rather than performing. Ask for the cash flow statement and compare operating cash flow with net income and with capital expenditure over several periods.

[F0664] How to value a company with negative net income and negative Ebitda?
Asked by / question source: Financial Technology Partners SF
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Negative net income and EBITDA make historical P/E and EV/EBITDA unsuitable as straightforward valuation anchors; they do not automatically make the business worthless. Identify whether losses are temporary, growth-related or structural. Forecast revenue, sustainable margins, taxes, reinvestment and funding in base, upside and downside scenarios, then discount the resulting cash flows. Include cash burn before profitability and the risk the business fails to reach that stage. Use EV/revenue or forward positive-earnings multiples only with genuinely comparable economics and a credible profitability path. Add excess cash and subtract debt/other claims to reach equity consistently, accounting for financing needs without double counting them. If no viable going concern remains, examine realizable asset value and the claim waterfall instead.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

[F0665] What could be the reason that sometimes a company could have positive EBITDA but negative cashflow?
Asked by / question source: Financial Technology Partners SF
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
EBITDA = revenue - cash operating expenses before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization; EBIT = EBITDA - D&A. Net income also includes interest, taxes and non-operating items. EBITDA helps compare operating performance across financing and depreciation conventions, but is not cash flow: it ignores CapEx, working capital and cash taxes. A business can have positive EBITDA yet run out of cash because of reinvestment, interest, maturities, working-capital needs or one-time payments. EBIT can be more meaningful for asset-heavy businesses because depreciation captures part of asset consumption. Evaluate adjusted EBITDA add-backs critically and avoid adding recurring costs back simply because management labels them exceptional.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

[F0666] What is enterprise value?
Asked by / question source: Financial Technology Partners SF; KKR; LionTree; Raymond James NY
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Equity value is the value attributable to common shareholders; for a public company it is diluted share count times share price. Operating EV = equity value + debt + preferred stock + NCI - excess cash - other separately valued non-operating assets, with consistent lease/pension adjustments where relevant. EV pairs with unlevered operating metrics; equity value pairs with net income or FCFE. Raising debt and holding the proceeds as cash normally leaves operating EV unchanged: debt and cash rise equally. A dividend reduces equity and cash together, also leaving operating EV unchanged absent signaling, tax or operational effects. Spending cash on an operating asset can change EV because value has moved from non-operating cash into operations; value creation still depends on the asset’s economics.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

[F0667] How are non controlling interests taken in consideration while calculating the equity value of a company?
Asked by / question source: Financial Technology Partners SF
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
When a parent controls a subsidiary, its statements consolidate 100% of the subsidiary’s operations even if ownership is below 100%; noncontrolling interest represents the outside owners’ claim. Therefore, add the market value of NCI in the EV bridge when EBITDA includes 100% of subsidiary EBITDA. Parent equity value includes only the parent’s economic share. In the income statement, distinguish consolidated net income from net income attributable to the parent; NCI is separately presented within equity. A nonconsolidated equity-method associate generally contributes investment income rather than full EBITDA, so treat its investment value separately and avoid double counting. Debt recoveries must respect entity boundaries and guarantees.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

[F0668] A customer prepays $120 for a one-year magazine subscription delivered monthly. Explain deferred revenue and the financial statement effects over the year. Assume a 20% tax rate.
Asked by / question source: Financial Technology Partners SF
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
A $120 annual subscription delivered monthly, no delivery costs, 20% tax rate.

• At receipt: Cash +$120 and Deferred Revenue +$120, with no income-statement effect.

• Income Statement, each month: recognise $120 / 12 = $10 of revenue, so monthly Net Income is $8.

• Cash Flow Statement, each month: Net Income +$8 less the $10 reduction in the liability, so cash falls $2 — the tax on that month's revenue.

• Balance Sheet: Deferred Revenue falls $10 a month to zero after twelve months, by which point $120 of revenue has been recognised and $24 of tax paid.

• Intuition: the company holds the full $120 from day one and gives $24 of it back in tax across the year.

[F0669] Why could two companies with identical balance sheets and income statements have different P/E ratios?
Asked by / question source: Financial Technology Partners SF
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Identical current statements do not guarantee identical future cash flows or risk. One may have stronger customer retention, better products, patents, management, governance, backlog, lower future reinvestment needs or less concentration. Liquidity, control rights and market expectations can also differ. If all future cash flows, risk, rights and information are truly identical, intrinsic value should be identical; a price difference would then reflect market mispricing or omitted assumptions.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

[F0670] Compare DCF, public comparables and precedent transactions.
Asked by / question source: Financial Technology Partners SF
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Core methods are public trading comparables, precedent transactions and DCF. An LBO is a sponsor’s return-constrained price analysis; asset-based/liquidation value and sum-of-the-parts are additional approaches. Trading comps reflect current minority market prices; precedents reflect historical deal conditions, control and possible synergies; DCF reflects forecast cash generation and risk. Precedents often exceed trading comps, and LBO prices can be lower than strategic values, but there is no guaranteed ranking or universal valuation floor. Select methods suited to the business, compare their assumptions and present a range rather than averaging incompatible outputs.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

[F0672] Why is the LBO the baseline valuation?
Asked by / question source: Financial Technology Partners SF
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
An LBO buys a company using sponsor equity and debt serviced by the target’s cash flows. Set entry EV and equity purchase price, build sources and uses including fees/refinancing, forecast operations and cash generation, model debt interest/amortization and the cash sweep, then estimate exit EV and subtract exit net debt and other claims. Sponsor MOIC = proceeds/invested equity; with one entry and exit, IRR = MOIC^(1/years)-1. Returns come from operating growth, deleveraging, entry/exit valuation and distributions. More leverage increases both upside and default risk. Favor resilient cash conversion, manageable CapEx, credible improvements and a defensible purchase price. Strategic buyers may pay more for synergies; sponsors may offer certainty, speed, rollover equity or management continuity.

[F0673] What sort of things would you look for in a prospective fund manager relationship?
Asked by / question source: GCM Grosvenor
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
An asset manager invests client capital within mandates and earns fees, often based on assets under management and sometimes performance. Analyze investment process, team stability, risk controls, capacity, alignment, track record versus an appropriate benchmark, fees and operational infrastructure. For PE managers, management fees support recurring fee-related earnings and carried interest depends on realizations and fund terms. Value a manager through forecast fee earnings and risk-adjusted performance fees, not by treating all client AUM as the manager’s assets. Claims about a named manager’s current funds or hit rate require its own disclosures; do not invent them.

[F0674] Walk me through your investment process?
Asked by / question source: GTCR
Answer status: Open-ended answer framework
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Assess the underlying cash flows, price paid, loss risk, liquidity, horizon and legal claim. Debt offers contractual payments and priority but capped upside and default/refinancing risk; equity is residual and has uncapped upside with greater downside volatility. Compare downside recovery and expected return after fees/taxes, and avoid selecting on yield or a low price alone. For lending, examine sustainable debt service and collateral; for equity, test growth, reinvestment and competitive durability. A recommendation needs the stated investor constraints and actual instrument/company data.

[F0677] What do you consider a good private equity investment?
Asked by / question source: GTCR
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
A PE fund raises commitments from limited partners, calls capital for investments, supports portfolio companies and distributes exit proceeds. The manager earns management fees and, subject to the agreement/hurdle, carried interest on gains. A fund of funds invests in underlying funds, offering diversification and access with an additional fee layer. Secondaries transfer existing fund interests or assets; GP-led continuation deals may offer investors liquidity or a rollover choice. Buyers assess NAV quality, unfunded commitments, concentration, remaining duration and price discounts/premiums. Secondaries can reduce blind-pool risk and duration, but do not automatically deliver higher IRR or MOIC; timing, pricing, leverage and asset performance determine returns.

[F0678] Estimate a valuation multiple for an unfamiliar business using qualitative questions about unit economics, total addressable market and penetration, without asking for comparable-company multiples. [Business description not recorded.]
Asked by / question source: GTCR
Answer status: Method / conditional answer — source details needed
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Derive an implied multiple from fundamentals instead of asking for comparable-company multiples. Ask about market size and penetration, growth runway, customer retention, pricing, contribution margins, fixed costs, required CapEx/working capital and business risk. Convert these into forecast cash flows and discount them. Then divide the resulting enterprise value by the matching revenue or EBITDA measure to obtain an implied multiple. As a simplified sustainable-growth illustration, EV/EBITDA_1 = (FCFF_1/EBITDA_1)/(WACC-g), where both flow measures refer to next year and WACC exceeds g. Cash conversion must include taxes and the reinvestment required to support g. A changing-growth business needs an explicit forecast before its terminal period. No unique multiple can be calculated without the omitted business inputs, but the method does not require peer multiples.

[F0690] Calculate post-transaction accretion or dilution. [Deal inputs not recorded.]
Asked by / question source: Goldman Sachs HK
Answer status: Method / conditional answer — source details needed
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
The source omits inputs needed for a unique conclusion. Accretion/dilution compares pro forma EPS with the buyer’s standalone EPS. Add target earnings and after-tax synergies, subtract after-tax new interest, foregone cash interest, purchase-accounting amortization and relevant ongoing costs; divide by buyer shares plus shares issued. New shares = stock consideration/buyer share price. In a simplified all-stock deal without other adjustments, a buyer with a higher P/E than the target’s purchase P/E is accretive. For debt or cash consideration, compare the target’s earnings yield with the after-tax funding/opportunity cost. EPS accretion does not prove value creation: price paid, risk and economic returns versus cost of capital still matter.

[F0691] If I raised a 100,000 bond with interest payments of 10% every year over 5 years. What will happen to the financial statements?
Asked by / question source: Goldman Sachs HK
Answer status: Method / conditional answer — source details needed
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
At issuance of a 100,000 bond at par, cash and debt rise 100,000; financing cash flow is +100,000. Each full year, cash interest is 10,000. Assuming a usable tax deduction at t, NI and net cash fall 10,000(1-t), with interest classification under applicable standards. At maturity, repay 100,000 through financing cash flow and eliminate the debt. The use of proceeds, fees and tax timing are not supplied.

[F0692] If I was a client looking to raise debt and equity and I am highly leveraged, what would you as a banker tell them?
Asked by / question source: Goldman Sachs HK
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Credit underwriting asks whether cash flow can pay obligations in downside scenarios and what lenders recover if it cannot. Assess business resilience, leverage, interest coverage, fixed-charge coverage, free cash flow, liquidity and maturity/refinancing risk. Review collateral, guarantees and covenant headroom. Expected credit loss is approximately PD * LGD * exposure, though valuation also includes timing and risk premiums. The “3 Cs” are commonly character, capacity and capital, with collateral and conditions added in a five-C framework. Maintenance covenants are tested periodically; incurrence covenants when specified actions occur. Do not set leverage from EBITDA alone: cyclicality, cash conversion, CapEx and rates can make equal leverage ratios very different risks.

[F0695] What is the Black-Scholes option pricing model and describe the mechanism?
Asked by / question source: Goldman Sachs HK
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Black-Scholes prices a European option in continuous time, assuming the underlying follows a lognormal random walk with constant volatility, frictionless continuous trading and a constant risk-free rate. For a European call on a non-dividend-paying stock, C = S*N(d1) - K*exp(-r*T)*N(d2), where d1 = [ln(S/K) + (r + sigma^2/2)*T]/(sigma*sqrt(T)), d2 = d1 - sigma*sqrt(T), and N() is the cumulative standard normal distribution. The inputs are spot price S, strike K, time to expiry T, risk-free rate r, volatility sigma and any dividend yield. The mechanism is replication and no arbitrage rather than forecasting: a continuously rebalanced holding of N(d1) shares funded with borrowing reproduces the option's payoff, so the option must cost what that portfolio costs, which is why the stock's own expected return never appears in the formula. Read the two terms as a discounted expected payoff under the risk-neutral measure, where N(d2) is the risk-neutral probability of finishing in the money and N(d1) is the option's delta. A put follows from put-call parity: P = C - S + K*exp(-r*T). A higher spot price raises a call's value and lowers a put's, with delta measuring the rate of change and gamma its curvature; more volatility and more time raise both calls and puts. The model's weaknesses are its constant-volatility and lognormal assumptions, which is why observed implied volatility varies across strikes and maturities, and it does not handle early exercise on American options or discrete dividends without adjustment.

[F0696] If account payable decreases by 10, what's the change for 3 sheets?
Asked by / question source: Goldman Sachs HK
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
If an existing $10 supplier payable is paid, cash and AP each fall $10. No new expense or income is recognized. CFO falls $10 through the AP change. If the payable disappears for another reason, such as forgiveness or reclassification, the accounting differs.

[F0697] Why might two companies have identical EV/EBITDA multiples but different P/E multiples?
Asked by / question source: Goldman Sachs LA
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
EV/EBITDA compares operating value with earnings before financing, tax and D&A; P/E compares common equity value with net income available to common shareholders. Therefore equal EV/EBITDA can coexist with different leverage, cash, interest costs, D&A, tax rates and non-operating items, producing different P/E ratios. Define B as debt + preferred stock + NCI - excess cash - other non-operating assets. Then equity value = EV-B, so P/E = [(EV/EBITDA) - B/EBITDA]/(common net income/EBITDA). For example, two unlevered, cash-free companies can each have EV=1,000 and EBITDA=100, hence EV/EBITDA=10x. With no D&A or other items, tax rates of 20% and 40% give net income of 80 and 60, and P/E of 12.5x and 16.67x. This is a mechanical example holding EV fixed, not a claim that taxes have no effect on intrinsic EV.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

[F0698] Is the cost of debt always cheaper than the cost of equity? Are there any situations where the cost of debt is higher?
Asked by / question source: Goldman Sachs LA
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Normally debt is cheaper, for two reasons: lenders sit ahead of shareholders and have contractual payments, so they require less return for the same business, and interest is usually tax-deductible, which lowers the after-tax cost further. But it is not a law. The comparison can invert in distress: a bond yielding 20% to maturity is promising a high return to compensate for a real chance of default, and once leverage is that high the equity may be a small residual stub that a naive CAPM estimate prices at a lower expected return than the debt. Be careful what you are comparing. A promised yield to maturity is not an expected return, because it assumes full repayment; the expected return on distressed debt is lower than its quoted yield once you probability-weight recoveries. The clean statement is that for the same company at a sustainable capital structure, debt is cheaper, and that raising leverage pushes both costs up, which is why the all-debt structure does not minimise WACC.

[F0699] How I would cost everything in a newly built stadium in LA, complete with financing and all.
Asked by / question source: Goldman Sachs LA
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Build revenue from operating units rather than assuming a growth rate: customers/volume * frequency/utilization * net price, plus ancillary streams. Separate variable costs from fixed costs to model contribution margin, operating leverage and break-even volume. For a pharmacy use prescription volumes, reimbursement/mix, dispensing margin and payer terms; roofing uses crew capacity, projects, ticket size and repair/replacement mix; software/telecom uses subscribers, ARPU, churn and network/service costs; a food outlet uses footfall, conversion, ticket and opening days. Forecast working capital, maintenance/growth CapEx and taxes. Value sustainable after-tax cash flow and cross-check peers; local concentration, regulation and reinvestment can explain different multiples despite similar current profits.

[F0701] If a company is pre-revenue, pre-EBITDA, what does its capital structure look like?
Asked by / question source: Goldman Sachs LA
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Debt avoids immediate ownership dilution and can provide a usable tax shield, but imposes interest, maturity and covenant obligations. Equity has no mandatory repayment and absorbs downside but dilutes owners and normally demands a higher return. Choose a sustainable mix using downside cash generation, collateral, funding horizon, liquidity and market access. Issuing debt and retaining cash raises both equally without initial earnings effects. Issuing primary equity raises cash and paid-in equity; neither immediately creates operating profit. Distressed or pre-revenue businesses may need equity even when debt looks nominally cheaper.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

[F0702] How do you calculate its WACC?
Asked by / question source: Goldman Sachs LA
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
WACC = E/(D+E)*Ke + D/(D+E)*Kd*(1-t), extending the weights for preferred capital if present. Use market-value, sustainable capital weights. Ke is often estimated with CAPM; Kd is the current marginal borrowing yield for comparable risk and maturity, not necessarily an old coupon. The debt tax adjustment reflects usable interest deductibility. Match currency, inflation and risk to the cash flows. Moderate leverage can lower WACC through tax shields, but greater default risk raises required debt and equity returns; the relationship is not universally decreasing. For a private company, estimate operating risk from public peers and use a defensible target capital structure.

For a private company, estimate operating risk from public peers and use a defensible target capital structure.

[F0705] If the company raise $100 debt to repurchase 10 shares. The annual interest rate on debt is 10%. The marginal tax rate is 40%, and the effective interest rate is 30%. what happens to EPS after year 1?
Asked by / question source: Goldman Sachs LA
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
The number of original shares and original net income are missing. Repurchase price = 100/10 = $10 per share; annual interest is $10. Using the marginal 40% tax rate, after-tax financing cost is $6, so new EPS = (NI-6)/(N-10). It is accretive if original EPS exceeds $0.60. The 30% figure is described ambiguously and should not replace the marginal tax rate without clarification.

[F0706] Walk through the three-statement effects of an asset purchase financed by PIK debt, immediately and after one year. Assume a 20% tax rate. [Amounts and rates not recorded.]
Asked by / question source: Goldman Sachs LA
Answer status: Method / conditional answer — source details needed
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
The source omits the amounts and rates, so work from a clean example. PIK interest accrues onto principal instead of being paid in cash. Take $100 of debt at 5% cash and 5% PIK for one year, at a 20% tax rate.

• Income Statement: interest expense is $10, being $5 cash and $5 PIK, so Pre-Tax Income falls $10 and Net Income falls $8.

• Cash Flow Statement: Net Income −$8, add back the $5 of non-cash PIK, so cash falls $3 — the $5 cash coupon less the $2 tax saving.

• Balance Sheet: Cash −$3 and Debt +$5 from the accrued PIK; Retained Earnings −$8, so both sides fall $3 and balance.

• Intuition: PIK protects near-term liquidity and increases what you must repay later.

At repayment you repay principal including accrued PIK, plus any call premium. Without usable deductions, cash falls by the full $5 coupon and the tax benefit becomes a deferred tax asset.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

[F0707] How would you adjust a DCF to use levered versus unlevered cash flows?
Asked by / question source: Goldman Sachs LA
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Value equals the present value of expected cash flows. For an operating company, forecast FCFF from revenue, margins, taxes, reinvestment and working capital, discount at WACC, and add a consistently estimated terminal value. EV = sum[FCFF_t/(1+WACC)^t] + TV_N/(1+WACC)^N. Bridge to equity by adding excess cash/non-operating assets and subtracting debt, preferred claims and NCI; divide by diluted shares if needed. For a tree or other asset, forecast sale proceeds less maintenance, taxes and reinvestment over its actual economic life. A level end-of-year perpetuity is C/r; a growing one is next-period C/(r-g). Cash flow today is not the same as next-period cash flow.

[F0709] What questions would you ask to evaluate the fairness of an acquisition offer when advising the buyer?
Asked by / question source: Goldman Sachs LA
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Assess a transaction through strategic fit, price versus standalone and synergy value, financing, execution and integration risk. Explain buyer/target businesses, consideration, purchase multiple, expected cash benefits and why a deal is preferable to organic investment. Test downside cases, regulatory constraints and ability to finance/close. More EPS or more revenue alone does not prove value creation; incremental risk-adjusted returns should exceed the cost of capital. For a named historical transaction, use the announcement, filings and investor presentations to establish terms, and distinguish the rationale known at signing from later outcomes. No unspecified deal supports a factual purchase multiple or recommendation.

[F0710] An LBO target has $100 million of EBITDA, a 10x entry multiple, 6x leverage and $80 million of annual levered free cash flow for five years. The exit multiple is 10x. Calculate ending equity value and IRR. [EBITDA growth and debt repayment assumptions are not stated.]
Asked by / question source: Goldman Sachs LA
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Assume constant EBITDA, no fees, and all $80 million annual cash flow repays debt. Entry EV = 10*100 = 1,000; debt = 600; sponsor equity = 400. Five years repay 400, leaving debt 200. Exit EV = 1,000; exit equity = 800. MOIC = 2.0x; five-year IRR = 2^(1/5)-1 = 14.87%. Growth, dividends, cash interest interactions or different debt repayment assumptions change the answer.

[F0713] What can you tell me about bonds?
Asked by / question source: Goldman Sachs NY Financing; Nomura Global Markets
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
A bond pays contractual coupons and principal, subject to default. Price = sum[coupon_t/(1+y)^t] + principal/(1+y)^N for annual payments. YTM is the discount rate that equates those promised payments to price, not a guaranteed realized return. Current yield = annual coupon/current price. Yield to call substitutes the call date and call price for maturity. Coupon is set on face value; yield depends on price. For a one-year bond, YTM = (coupon + redemption - price)/price. For multi-year bonds solve the equation rather than using coupon/price. Distressed debt may require probability-weighted recoveries, not just promised-payment YTM.

[F0715] Explain the structure and purpose of a securitization.
Asked by / question source: Goldman Sachs NY Financing
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Securitization pools financial assets and allocates their cash flows to securities with different priorities. Senior tranches have greater protection; junior/equity tranches absorb losses first and seek higher returns. Model collateral defaults, recoveries, prepayments, rates, servicing and waterfall triggers. Mortgage investors face extension risk when rates rise and prepayments slow, and contraction/reinvestment risk when rates fall. In a CMO, a Z/accrual tranche defers current interest while earlier tranches receive cash. A quoted spread must compensate for expected losses, duration/option risk, liquidity and model uncertainty; no universal spread follows without collateral and structure details.

[F0719] What spread would you bid for a portfolio of these phones?
Asked by / question source: Goldman Sachs NY Financing
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Price this as an asset-backed pool, not as an asset allocation. The spread must cover expected loss plus a return for the risks you cannot diversify away. Start with the collateral: used phones lose value quickly and unevenly by model, condition, storage and carrier lock, so estimate recovery per unit in both an orderly and a forced sale. Build expected loss as probability of non-payment times loss given default times exposure, where loss given default is driven by that resale value net of collection, refurbishment, storage and shipping costs. Then add premia for what remains: concentration in a few models or a single obsolescence cycle, correlation between defaults and a falling secondhand market, the short and uncertain duration of the cash flows, the practicality of servicing and repossession, fraud, and the illiquidity of the position itself. Benchmark the result against observable spreads on comparable consumer or equipment ABS of similar tenor, rating and collateral quality, and demand more where the loss history is thinner. Finally, state where in the structure you are bidding: a senior tranche with subordination beneath it, excess spread and a reserve account justifies a far tighter spread than a first-loss piece on the same pool. No single number follows without the pool's loss history, the structure and the current market level.

[F0720] How would you value this specific type of fund manager?

Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:

For PE managers, management fees support recurring fee-related earnings and carried interest depends on realizations and fund terms. Value a manager through forecast fee earnings and risk-adjusted performance fees, not by treating all client AUM as the manager’s assets. Claims about a named manager’s current funds or hit rate require its own disclosures; do not invent them.

[F0723] What is a leveraged buyout and what are the steps to complete a model.
Asked by / question source: Goldman Sachs NY Financing
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
An LBO buys a company using sponsor equity and debt serviced by the target’s cash flows. Set entry EV and equity purchase price, build sources and uses including fees/refinancing, forecast operations and cash generation, model debt interest/amortization and the cash sweep, then estimate exit EV and subtract exit net debt and other claims. Sponsor MOIC = proceeds/invested equity; with one entry and exit, IRR = MOIC^(1/years)-1. Returns come from operating growth, deleveraging, entry/exit valuation and distributions. More leverage increases both upside and default risk. Favor resilient cash conversion, manageable CapEx, credible improvements and a defensible purchase price. Strategic buyers may pay more for synergies; sponsors may offer certainty, speed, rollover equity or management continuity.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

[F0724] If a company with a higher PE multiple purchases a company with a lower PE multiple is the transaction accretive or dilutive?
Asked by / question source: Goldman Sachs NY Financing
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Accretion/dilution compares pro forma EPS with the buyer’s standalone EPS. Add target earnings and after-tax synergies, subtract after-tax new interest, foregone cash interest, purchase-accounting amortization and relevant ongoing costs; divide by buyer shares plus shares issued. New shares = stock consideration/buyer share price. In a simplified all-stock deal without other adjustments, a buyer with a higher P/E than the target’s purchase P/E is accretive. For debt or cash consideration, compare the target’s earnings yield with the after-tax funding/opportunity cost. EPS accretion does not prove value creation: price paid, risk and economic returns versus cost of capital still matter.

[F0725] How would you explain the difference between bank debt and high yield debt to your grandmother?
Asked by / question source: Goldman Sachs NY Financing
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Debt is differentiated by issuer/guarantor, collateral, lien priority, contractual seniority, maturity, amortization and covenants. Revolvers and senior secured loans typically have floating rates and security; institutional term loans often have limited amortization. High-yield bonds commonly have fixed coupons, bullet maturities and call protection; they may be secured or unsecured. Subordinated/mezzanine debt ranks behind senior obligations and may include PIK or warrants. A leveraged loan is lending to an already highly levered or below-investment-grade borrower. Do not assume every revolver automatically outranks every term loan: inspect the lien and intercreditor documents.

[F0726] How to choose tax rate in merger model?
Asked by / question source: Goldman Sachs NY
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Use the buyer/combined business’s expected marginal cash tax rates for incremental income, synergies and deductible financing costs, considering jurisdictions, NOLs and interest limits. Use target/buyer jurisdiction-specific rates for items where necessary. Historical effective tax rate may contain one-off items and is not automatically the right forward rate. Purchase-accounting deferred taxes and tax-basis step-ups need separate treatment.

[F0727] What are the advantages and disadvantages of the main valuation methods?
Asked by / question source: Evercore (compiled interview notes); Goldman Sachs NY; Greenhill NY
Also covers: F0785
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Core methods are public trading comparables, precedent transactions and DCF. An LBO is a sponsor’s return-constrained price analysis; asset-based/liquidation value and sum-of-the-parts are additional approaches. Trading comps reflect current minority market prices; precedents reflect historical deal conditions, control and possible synergies; DCF reflects forecast cash generation and risk. Precedents often exceed trading comps, and LBO prices can be lower than strategic values, but there is no guaranteed ranking or universal valuation floor. Select methods suited to the business, compare their assumptions and present a range rather than averaging incompatible outputs.

[F0728] How would you value a manufacturing company?
Asked by / question source: Goldman Sachs NY
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Choose between an intrinsic cash-flow valuation, market comparables, precedent transactions and, when relevant, asset-based or LBO analysis. Match the numerator to the claimant: EV with pre-interest operating metrics and equity with net income/FCFE. Normalize earnings, align periods and distinguish growth from capital intensity and risk. A private company requires reliable financials and suitable public/deal benchmarks; lack of information increases uncertainty rather than justifying an arbitrary precise value. Use a range with scenario/sensitivity analysis and reconcile results to the business’s cash-generation capacity.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

[F0729] Why multiples are different in different industries?
Asked by / question source: Goldman Sachs NY
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Choose companies with similar business model, geography, growth, margins, risk and capital intensity. Calculate consistent enterprise/equity values and calendarized historical or forecast metrics, normalize unusual items, and apply a justified peer range to the target metric. EV/Revenue divided by EV/EBITDA equals EBITDA margin when periods and EV are consistent. P/E uses equity value/net income; EV/EBITDA uses operating value/pre-interest earnings, so taxes and financing can produce different rankings. Higher multiples can reflect growth, stronger returns, recurring revenue or lower risk, not automatically overvaluation. Negative EBITDA makes its multiple unhelpful; revenue multiples require a credible path to margins. Share price alone is not comparable across firms because share counts differ.

[F0731] What is the least important of the three financial statements to look at?
Asked by / question source: Goldman Sachs NY
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
The appropriate statement depends on the purpose. The balance sheet shows financial position and obligations at a date; the income statement shows profitability over time; the cash-flow statement shows liquidity generation and funding. If forced to pick one for debt repayment, the cash-flow statement is useful, but debt maturities and collateral still require the balance sheet and notes. With two consecutive balance sheets plus an income statement and supporting schedules, you can approximate cash flows, although acquisitions, FX and other non-cash changes complicate the reconstruction. No single statement fully captures financial health.

[F0735] You have two companies with the same P/E ratio. What makes their EV/EBITDA different?
Asked by / question source: Goldman Sachs NY
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
The same P/E does not imply the same operating valuation multiple. Let B = debt + preferred stock + NCI - excess cash - other non-operating assets. Since EV = common equity value + B and common equity value = (P/E)*common net income, EV/EBITDA = (P/E)*(common net income/EBITDA) + B/EBITDA. D&A, interest, taxes and non-operating items change net income relative to EBITDA; leverage, cash and other claims change the bridge. For example, at 15x P/E, common net income of 100 implies equity value of 1,500. If EBITDA is 200, net debt of zero gives EV/EBITDA=7.5x, while net debt of 500 gives 10x, with no other bridge items. The example takes those net-income figures as given; it does not assume identical interest expense or other earnings inputs.

[F0740] Value an apple tree producing $100 in revenue a year. Now value it if it was 100, 200, 300, 400... with a 10% discount rate.
Asked by / question source: Goldman Sachs TMT SF
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Revenue is not cash flow: subtract costs, taxes and investment first. If the stated figures are actually net annual cash flows and life is infinite, $100/year at 10% is worth $1,000. For $100, $200, $300, ... at successive year-ends, PV = 100*1.1/0.1^2 = $11,000. Finite tree life, biological constraints and changing risk would reduce or otherwise change this stylized result.

[F0742] Given merger details - what number in revenue synergies would you need in order to be accreative - VERY HARD?
Asked by / question source: Goldman Sachs TMT SF
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Cost synergies eliminate duplicate costs such as headquarters or procurement expense. Revenue synergies arise from cross-selling, distribution or pricing improvements, usually with additional costs and execution risk. Financial/tax synergies may involve funding or tax benefits. A dollar of durable cost savings normally adds more profit than a dollar of additional revenue because new revenue has associated variable costs. Value after-tax cash benefits after implementation costs, timing and probability of delivery. Do not pay the seller for every potential synergy or double count benefits already in the base forecasts.

[F0744] You have an apartment (2-bedrooms) given to you for 2mm, how would you assess its fair value?
Asked by / question source: Goldman Sachs TMT SF
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
The stated 2 million price is not proof of fair value. Compare recent similar apartment sales adjusted for location, size, condition, tenure and building costs; estimate achievable net rent and apply a supported cap rate or DCF. Deduct required renovations and assess legal restrictions, vacancy and liquidity. Two bedrooms alone cannot establish the value.

[F0746] Explain the price-to-earnings (P/E) multiple.
Asked by / question source: Goldman Sachs TMT SF
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Choose companies with similar business model, geography, growth, margins, risk and capital intensity. Calculate consistent enterprise/equity values and calendarized historical or forecast metrics, normalize unusual items, and apply a justified peer range to the target metric. EV/Revenue divided by EV/EBITDA equals EBITDA margin when periods and EV are consistent. P/E uses equity value/net income; EV/EBITDA uses operating value/pre-interest earnings, so taxes and financing can produce different rankings. Higher multiples can reflect growth, stronger returns, recurring revenue or lower risk, not automatically overvaluation. Negative EBITDA makes its multiple unhelpful; revenue multiples require a credible path to margins. Share price alone is not comparable across firms because share counts differ.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

[F0747] When would a DCF give you a higher valuation then the other three methods?
Asked by / question source: Goldman Sachs TMT SF
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Value equals the present value of expected cash flows. For an operating company, forecast FCFF from revenue, margins, taxes, reinvestment and working capital, discount at WACC, and add a consistently estimated terminal value. EV = sum[FCFF_t/(1+WACC)^t] + TV_N/(1+WACC)^N. Bridge to equity by adding excess cash/non-operating assets and subtracting debt, preferred claims and NCI; divide by diluted shares if needed. For a tree or other asset, forecast sale proceeds less maintenance, taxes and reinvestment over its actual economic life. A level end-of-year perpetuity is C/r; a growing one is next-period C/(r-g). Cash flow today is not the same as next-period cash flow.

[F0758] For a company with no revenues, what is the cost of equity?
Asked by / question source: Goldman Sachs TMT SF
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
WACC = E/(D+E)*Ke + D/(D+E)*Kd*(1-t), extending the weights for preferred capital if present. Use market-value, sustainable capital weights. Ke is often estimated with CAPM; Kd is the current marginal borrowing yield for comparable risk and maturity, not necessarily an old coupon. The debt tax adjustment reflects usable interest deductibility. Match currency, inflation and risk to the cash flows. Moderate leverage can lower WACC through tax shields, but greater default risk raises required debt and equity returns; the relationship is not universally decreasing. For a private company, estimate operating risk from public peers and use a defensible target capital structure.

[F0759] Would you rather have higher lease expenses or depreciation expenses?
Asked by / question source: Goldman Sachs TMT SF
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Neither is inherently preferable. A lease conserves upfront cash and can provide flexibility but creates contractual obligations; ownership needs capital upfront and exposes the owner to residual-value risk. Compare after-tax discounted lease payments with purchase, maintenance and resale cash flows, and ensure service terms match. Expense presentation alone is not an economic benefit; accounting differs under ASC 842 and IFRS 16.

[F0760] Given pre-merger financials and post-merger accretion, solve for the tax rate. [Inputs not recorded.]

Answer status: Method / conditional answer — source details needed
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
The source omits inputs needed for a unique conclusion. Accretion/dilution compares pro forma EPS with the buyer’s standalone EPS. [F0775] How are the three financial statements linked?
Asked by / question source: Deloitte Corporate Finance; Evercore Private Capital Markets & Debt Advisory; Greenhill NY; J.P. Morgan Finance and Business Management; KeyBanc NY; Lazard LA; M&I 400 Questions Guide (2025), p. 50; TD Securities SF; Wells Fargo NY; Wells Fargo Public Finance
Also covers: F0433, F1036, F1579, F1648
Answer status: Guide answer
Answer origin: Supplied M&I 2025 400 IB Questions guide

ANSWER:
To link the statements, make Net Income from the Income Statement the top line of the Cash Flow Statement. Then, adjust this Net Income number for non-cash items such as Depreciation & Amortization. Next, reflect changes to operational Balance Sheet items such as Accounts Receivable, which may increase or reduce the company’s cash flow. This gets you to Cash Flow from Operations. Next, include the investing and financing activities, which may increase or reduce cash flow, and sum up Cash Flow from Operations, Investing, and Financing to get the net change in cash and ending cash balance. Cash at the bottom of the CFS becomes Cash on the Balance Sheet, and Net Income, Stock Issuances/Repurchases, Stock-Based Compensation, and Dividends link into Common Shareholders’ Equity. Next, link the separate line items on the CFS to their corresponding Balance Sheet line items; for example, CapEx and Depreciation link into Net PP&E. On the Assets side of the Balance Sheet, subtract CFS links; add them on the L&E side. Finally, check that Assets equals Liabilities plus Equity at the end.
Supporting reference: https://www.sec.gov/about/reports-publications/beginners-guide-financial-statements

[F0776] How has coronavirus impacted the PE world/made it difficult for sponsors to buyout companies?
Asked by / question source: Greenhill NY
Answer status: Prepared model answer

Some businesses benefited from digital demand while travel and hospitality faced severe stress. This is a qualitative historical explanation, not a claim that all sponsors or all 2020 periods experienced the same conditions.

[F0778] How do you value a lemonade stand?
Asked by / question source: Greenhill NY
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Build revenue from operating units rather than assuming a growth rate: customers/volume * frequency/utilization * net price, plus ancillary streams. Separate variable costs from fixed costs to model contribution margin, operating leverage and break-even volume. For a pharmacy use prescription volumes, reimbursement/mix, dispensing margin and payer terms; roofing uses crew capacity, projects, ticket size and repair/replacement mix; software/telecom uses subscribers, ARPU, churn and network/service costs; a food outlet uses footfall, conversion, ticket and opening days. Forecast working capital, maintenance/growth CapEx and taxes. Value sustainable after-tax cash flow and cross-check peers; local concentration, regulation and reinvestment can explain different multiples despite similar current profits.

[F0780] Let's say Apple is buying $100 worth of new iPod factories with debt. How are all 3 statements affected at the start of "Year 1," before anything else happens?
Asked by / question source: Greenhill NY
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
At acquisition of the factories, PP&E increases $100 and debt increases $100. The cash-flow statement shows +100 financing and -100 investing, leaving cash unchanged. No depreciation, interest or income effect occurs before time passes, ignoring fees.

[F0781] After a company buys $100 of factories entirely with debt, walk through the first year's statements assuming 10% interest, 10% annual depreciation and no principal repayment. [Tax rate not recorded in this report.]
Asked by / question source: Greenhill NY
Answer status: Method / conditional answer — source details needed
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Depreciation is 10% of $100, so $10, and interest is 10% of $100, so $10. Tax rate 20%, no principal repaid.

• Income Statement: $10 of depreciation and $10 of interest, so Pre-Tax Income falls $20 and Net Income falls $16.

• Cash Flow Statement: Net Income −$16, add back the $10 of depreciation, so cash falls $6.

• Balance Sheet: Cash −$6 and Net PP&E −$10 (from $100 to $90), so assets fall $16; Debt stays at $100 and Retained Earnings falls $16, so both sides fall $16 and balance.

• Intuition: the $6 of cash out is the $10 cash coupon less $4 of tax relief on the $20 of deductions.

[F0782] A company bought $100 of factories entirely with debt and depreciated them at 10% annually. At the start of year 3, the factories are written down to zero and the loan must be repaid. Walk through the three statements. Assume a 20% tax rate. [Tax rate not recorded.]
Asked by / question source: Greenhill NY
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
After two full years of $10 depreciation the factory's book value is $80. Write it off and repay the $100 loan, at a 20% tax rate, assuming the loss is deductible now.

• Income Statement: an $80 non-cash write-off, so Pre-Tax Income falls $80 and Net Income falls $64.

• Cash Flow Statement: Net Income −$64, add back the $80 non-cash loss, so operating cash flow is +$16; the $100 repayment is a financing outflow, so cash falls $84 in this step.

• Balance Sheet: Cash −$84 and PP&E −$80, so assets fall $164; Debt −$100 and Retained Earnings −$64, so both sides fall $164 and balance.

• Intuition: the write-off itself moves only $16 of tax relief; the $100 repayment is what drains the cash.

If only one year had elapsed the book value would be $90 and the write-off $90, so clarify the timing. With no taxable income the loss creates no immediate cash saving.

[F0784] A 10x P/E company acquires a 15x P/E company using one-third stock, one-third debt and one-third cash. Debt costs 10%, cash yields 5% and the tax rate is 50%. Is the deal accretive or dilutive?
Asked by / question source: Greenhill NY
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Target earnings yield = 1/15 = 6.667%. Financing cost is (1/3)*(1/10) for stock dilution + (1/3)*10%*(1-50%) for debt + (1/3)*5%*(1-50%) for cash = 5.833%. Target yield exceeds blended cost, so the deal is accretive before fees, purchase accounting and synergies. Exact percentage accretion requires transaction size and buyer earnings.

[F0786] Two companies, same industry, but one has a higher ebitda multiple, why?
Asked by / question source: Greenhill NY
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Identical current statements do not guarantee identical future cash flows or risk. One may have stronger customer retention, better products, patents, management, governance, backlog, lower future reinvestment needs or less concentration. Liquidity, control rights and market expectations can also differ. If all future cash flows, risk, rights and information are truly identical, intrinsic value should be identical; a price difference would then reflect market mispricing or omitted assumptions.

[F0787] Give me 5 or more ways to boost IRR on an LBO. 5.
Asked by / question source: Greenhill NY
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
An LBO buys a company using sponsor equity and debt serviced by the target’s cash flows. Set entry EV and equity purchase price, build sources and uses including fees/refinancing, forecast operations and cash generation, model debt interest/amortization and the cash sweep, then estimate exit EV and subtract exit net debt and other claims. Sponsor MOIC = proceeds/invested equity; with one entry and exit, IRR = MOIC^(1/years)-1. Returns come from operating growth, deleveraging, entry/exit valuation and distributions. More leverage increases both upside and default risk. Favor resilient cash conversion, manageable CapEx, credible improvements and a defensible purchase price. Strategic buyers may pay more for synergies; sponsors may offer certainty, speed, rollover equity or management continuity.

[F0789] What are the most important accounting concepts to consider in a merger model?
Asked by / question source: Greenhill NY
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Accretion/dilution compares pro forma EPS with the buyer’s standalone EPS. Add target earnings and after-tax synergies, subtract after-tax new interest, foregone cash interest, purchase-accounting amortization and relevant ongoing costs; divide by buyer shares plus shares issued. New shares = stock consideration/buyer share price. In a simplified all-stock deal without other adjustments, a buyer with a higher P/E than the target’s purchase P/E is accretive. For debt or cash consideration, compare the target’s earnings yield with the after-tax funding/opportunity cost. EPS accretion does not prove value creation: price paid, risk and economic returns versus cost of capital still matter.

[F0790] In what situation would you not use an asset step up in a merger model?
Asked by / question source: Greenhill NY
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
An asset write-up is absent or limited when fair value does not exceed carrying value, the relevant assets do not require a change, or the transaction falls under a different accounting model such as a qualifying common-control transfer. Do not confuse a stock acquisition’s absence of a tax-basis step-up with book acquisition accounting: a stock deal can still require book fair-value write-ups and related DTLs. Apply the applicable business-combination rules.

[F0792] If a company is issuing a convertible bond, and it has a cost of debt of 5 percent, and a cost of equity of 10 percent, what will the coupon on the bond be?
Asked by / question source: Greenhill NY
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
You cannot determine the coupon from 5% cost of debt and 10% cost of equity alone. The convertible contains an equity option, so the coupon may be below the comparable straight-debt yield, but requires conversion price, volatility, maturity, credit risk, rates and covenants. Averaging 5% and 10% is incorrect.

[F0793] A DCF implies a value of 11, precedents imply 13 and trading comparables imply 10. What sale price would you recommend, and why?
Asked by / question source: Greenhill NY
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Treat 10, 11 and 13 as valuation indications, not votes to average. A credible seller range might be anchored around intrinsic value 11 with an aspiration toward 13 if control/synergies and market demand support it. The reservation price depends on alternatives, timing and execution certainty. Check whether all values refer to the same EV/equity basis and date.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

[F0795] Compare betas across industries.
Asked by / question source: Greenhill NY
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
CAPM estimates cost of equity as risk-free rate + levered beta * equity risk premium, with justified additional risk adjustments where appropriate. Estimate beta using a regression of stock excess returns on market excess returns, or bottom-up comparable-company betas. Beta reflects systematic risk; leverage, cyclicality and operating fixed costs can raise it. It is not a measure of all uncertainty or an invariant property of an industry. Historical estimates depend on window, frequency and benchmark, and CAPM’s single-factor assumptions are simplifications. Compare operating risk first, then financing; a higher-growth firm does not mechanically have a higher beta.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

[F0796] How does selling PP&E affect the three statements? Assume a 20% tax rate.
Asked by / question source: Greenhill NY
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Take an asset with a $100 book value sold for $120 in cash, at a 20% tax rate, with tax basis equal to book basis.

• Income Statement: a $20 gain, so Pre-Tax Income is up $20 and Net Income is up $16.

• Cash Flow Statement: Net Income +$16, less the $20 non-cash gain reversed out of operating cash flow, plus the full $120 of proceeds in investing, so cash rises $116.

• Balance Sheet: Cash +$116 and the asset −$100, so assets rise $16; Retained Earnings +$16, and both sides balance.

• Intuition: you collect $120 and pay $4 of tax on the $20 gain, so cash is up $116.

Sold below book value the gain becomes a loss: it is added back in operating cash flow and the tax saving reduces the cash outflow. A write-down is different — no proceeds arrive, so only the tax effect moves cash.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

[F0797] Compare EBIT, net income and free cash flow.
Asked by / question source: Greenhill NY
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Unlevered free cash flow (FCFF) = EBIT(1-t) + D&A - CapEx - increase in operating NWC, with other adjustments for operating cash items as needed. It is available to all capital providers and is discounted at WACC. Levered free cash flow to equity (FCFE) deducts after-tax interest and incorporates net borrowing: FCFE = FCFF - interest(1-t) + debt issued - principal repaid. From net income, add non-cash expenses, subtract investment and operating NWC increases, and include net borrowing. Definitions of reported “FCF” vary, so identify whether the interviewer means CFO minus CapEx, FCFF or FCFE. EBITDA is not cash flow because it omits taxes, investment and working capital.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

[F0798] Why might enterprise value not reconcile to equity market value plus debt minus cash? What other adjustments might be needed?
Asked by / question source: Greenhill NY
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Equity value is the value attributable to common shareholders; for a public company it is diluted share count times share price. Operating EV = equity value + debt + preferred stock + NCI - excess cash - other separately valued non-operating assets, with consistent lease/pension adjustments where relevant. EV pairs with unlevered operating metrics; equity value pairs with net income or FCFE. Raising debt and holding the proceeds as cash normally leaves operating EV unchanged: debt and cash rise equally. A dividend reduces equity and cash together, also leaving operating EV unchanged absent signaling, tax or operational effects. Spending cash on an operating asset can change EV because value has moved from non-operating cash into operations; value creation still depends on the asset’s economics.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

[F0799] How should cash be treated in the WACC formula?
Asked by / question source: Greenhill NY
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Standard WACC uses market-value equity and debt weights for the operating business; do not treat excess cash as a source of financing or automatically subtract it from debt while leaving beta and weights unchanged. Excess cash can depress observed equity beta, so a detailed approach can separate cash and operating asset risk. Match the WACC, cash flows and leverage convention and add excess cash separately in the EV-to-equity bridge.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

[F0800] A company has EV/Sales of 2x and EV/EBITDA of 5x. What is its EBITDA margin?
Asked by / question source: Greenhill NY
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
EBITDA margin = (EV/Sales)/(EV/EBITDA) = 2/5 = 40%.

[F0801] A company whose revenue comes from a man gambling in vegas?
Asked by / question source: Greenhill NY
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
If the sole revenue source is a person gambling in a negative-expected-value casino game, a positive revenue forecast without costs/losses is misleading. Value expected net payouts less stakes, expenses and funding, accounting for survival and risk. Random outcomes can have near-zero market beta while retaining extreme total risk. Sustainable skill or a genuine edge would need evidence; luck does not justify perpetual growth.

[F0804] How do deferred tax assets and liabilities affect valuation and accounting?
Asked by / question source: Greenhill NY
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Deferred taxes arise when book and tax recognition differ. A DTA represents future tax relief, subject to realizability; a DTL represents future taxes from taxable temporary differences. NOLs can create DTAs, but their usable value depends on taxable profit, jurisdiction, expiration and legal restrictions. Value NOLs by forecasting actual cash-tax savings and discounting them at a rate reflecting their risk; do not automatically use face value or add a DTA to EV. In acquisitions, fair-value write-ups without tax-basis step-ups can create DTLs and increase goodwill. For U.S. ownership changes, assess Section 382 limitations rather than assuming all acquired losses can be used.

[F0805] What business investment would you make in your hometown?
Asked by / question source: Guggenheim Partners
Answer status: Open-ended answer framework
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:

Compare your view with what the current price seems to imply. Cover revenue quality, margins, reinvestment, cash conversion, balance-sheet risk and management capital allocation. A good business is not automatically a good investment at any price. For a short, include borrow cost, squeeze risk and loss limits; for a long, say what would invalidate the thesis. Without a specified company and current price, a particular target price or trade recommendation would be fabricated.

[F0811] What is the duration of a 10yr zero coupon bond?
Asked by / question source: Guggenheim Partners
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Macaulay duration is exactly 10 years for a 10-year zero-coupon bond. With annual compounding at yield y, modified duration is 10/(1+y). The two definitions should not be confused.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

[F0812] What is the price of a 10yr zero coupon bond if rates sell off 200bps?
Asked by / question source: Guggenheim Partners
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
For face value F and initial annual yield y, new price after a 200-basis-point selloff is F/(1+y+0.02)^10. Initial yield and face value are missing. Price falls; approximate percentage change is -Dmod*0.02, with convexity improving accuracy.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

[F0813] What if rates rally 200 bps then what is the price?
Asked by / question source: Guggenheim Partners
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
For face value F and initial annual yield y, new price after a 200-basis-point rally is F/(1+y-0.02)^10, using consistent compounding. Initial yield and face value are missing. Price rises, generally by more than it falls for an equal upward yield shift because a plain bond has positive convexity.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

[F0814] What is convexity?
Asked by / question source: Guggenheim Partners
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
A bond’s price is the PV of coupons plus principal discounted at the required yield. Price moves inversely to yield. Macaulay duration is the cash-flow-PV-weighted average payment time; modified duration approximates percentage price sensitivity: change in price/price ≈ -Dmod * change in yield. Convexity improves the approximation for larger moves. A zero-coupon bond’s Macaulay duration equals its maturity; modified duration differs by the compounding adjustment. Longer maturity and lower coupon usually increase rate sensitivity. Credit spreads, embedded options and liquidity can move price independently of the risk-free curve.

[F0819] Walk me through the line items on the income statement sheet.
Asked by / question source: Guggenheim Partners
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Start with revenue, subtract COGS for gross profit, operating expenses and D&A for operating income/EBIT, then interest and non-operating items for pre-tax income, and taxes for net income. Add back D&A to EBIT for EBITDA. Examine growth, gross and operating margin, recurring versus unusual items and conversion into cash. Statements must be analyzed together: balance sheets show financing and working-capital requirements, and cash-flow statements test whether earnings produce liquidity. A financial-statement exercise without the transaction amounts or schedules cannot yield unique numbers.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

[F0820] How does accretion/dilution change under different financing mixes?
Asked by / question source: Guggenheim Partners NY
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Accretion/dilution compares pro forma EPS with the buyer’s standalone EPS. Add target earnings and after-tax synergies, subtract after-tax new interest, foregone cash interest, purchase-accounting amortization and relevant ongoing costs; divide by buyer shares plus shares issued. New shares = stock consideration/buyer share price. In a simplified all-stock deal without other adjustments, a buyer with a higher P/E than the target’s purchase P/E is accretive. For debt or cash consideration, compare the target’s earnings yield with the after-tax funding/opportunity cost. EPS accretion does not prove value creation: price paid, risk and economic returns versus cost of capital still matter.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

[F0821] Explain how to calculate EBITDA without using numerical inputs.
Asked by / question source: Guggenheim Partners NY
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
EBITDA = revenue - cash operating expenses before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization; EBIT = EBITDA - D&A. Net income also includes interest, taxes and non-operating items. EBITDA helps compare operating performance across financing and depreciation conventions, but is not cash flow: it ignores CapEx, working capital and cash taxes. A business can have positive EBITDA yet run out of cash because of reinvestment, interest, maturities, working-capital needs or one-time payments. EBIT can be more meaningful for asset-heavy businesses because depreciation captures part of asset consumption. Evaluate adjusted EBITDA add-backs critically and avoid adding recurring costs back simply because management labels them exceptional.

[F0822] A company with 15x PE multiple purchases a company in an all-stock transaction. The same company, but with a 10x PE multiple purchases a copy of the company purchased by the 15x in an all-stock transaction. Which transaction is less dilutive? Why?
Asked by / question source: Guggenheim Partners NY
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
The 15x P/E buyer has a lower earnings yield (6.67%) than the 10x buyer (10%). It issues fewer shares/less earnings dilution per dollar of consideration, so its otherwise identical all-stock deal is more accretive or less dilutive. Whether either deal is actually accretive depends on the target's purchase P/E and other adjustments.

[F0823] Acquirer with an optimal capital structure buys another company. Which has a higher cost of capital, 100% stock for stock deal or 100% debt?
Asked by / question source: Guggenheim Partners NY
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Starting from an optimum does not establish which financing choice produces higher post-deal WACC. An all-debt deal can push leverage above optimum and raise distress/required returns; an all-stock deal can move it below optimum and reduce the tax shield. The target's size, operating risk, leverage and the shape of the WACC curve determine which deviation is worse. It is not valid to assume debt always lowers WACC.

[F0824] What are the differences between EV/Rev, EV/EBITDA, PE, and in what situations would you use each?
Asked by / question source: Guggenheim Partners NY
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Choose companies with similar business model, geography, growth, margins, risk and capital intensity. Calculate consistent enterprise/equity values and calendarized historical or forecast metrics, normalize unusual items, and apply a justified peer range to the target metric. EV/Revenue divided by EV/EBITDA equals EBITDA margin when periods and EV are consistent. P/E uses equity value/net income; EV/EBITDA uses operating value/pre-interest earnings, so taxes and financing can produce different rankings. Higher multiples can reflect growth, stronger returns, recurring revenue or lower risk, not automatically overvaluation. Negative EBITDA makes its multiple unhelpful; revenue multiples require a credible path to margins. Share price alone is not comparable across firms because share counts differ.

[F0827] What is a dividend recap and why do PE firms employ them?
Asked by / question source: Guggenheim Partners NY
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
A dividend recapitalization raises new debt and distributes proceeds to shareholders. It returns cash to the sponsor without selling the business and can improve sponsor IRR through earlier distributions. The company has more debt and interest expense, increasing refinancing, covenant and default risk. It does not create operating value by itself. Include the interim dividend, remaining debt and exit equity in sponsor cash flows, avoiding double counting.
