[F0828] If tax rate rises, what will be the impact on enterprise value?
Asked by / question source: Guggenheim Partners NY
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
A higher corporate tax rate generally lowers after-tax operating cash flow, reducing operating EV, while increasing the value of usable interest tax shields and changing after-tax WACC. Depreciation deductions, NOLs, jurisdiction mix and financing can offset part of the effect. Recalculate cash flows and discount rate consistently; it is not valid to claim a universal dollar impact without inputs.

[F0831] What is less dilutive from an ownership standpoint for an acquiring company?
Asked by / question source: Guggenheim Partners NY

ANSWER:

[F0832] Walkthrough an LBO model. Was given purchase multiple, type of debt and exit multiple. Had to provide the MoM and IRR.
Asked by / question source: Guggenheim Partners NY
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
An LBO buys a company using sponsor equity and debt serviced by the target’s cash flows. Set entry EV and equity purchase price, build sources and uses including fees/refinancing, forecast operations and cash generation, model debt interest/amortization and the cash sweep, then estimate exit EV and subtract exit net debt and other claims. Sponsor MOIC = proceeds/invested equity; with one entry and exit, IRR = MOIC^(1/years)-1. Returns come from operating growth, deleveraging, entry/exit valuation and distributions. More leverage increases both upside and default risk. Favor resilient cash conversion, manageable CapEx, credible improvements and a defensible purchase price. Strategic buyers may pay more for synergies; sponsors may offer certainty, speed, rollover equity or management continuity.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

[F0833] $1000 PPE, $500 debt w/10% interest, $500 debt w/5% PIK interest, GAAP depr SL over 10y, MACRS depr $200 in y1 => walk through the 3 statements in y0 and y1 (all mental math)?
Asked by / question source: Guggenheim Partners NY
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Book depreciation is $1,000 / 10 = $100; tax depreciation is $200. Cash interest is 10% of $500 = $50 and PIK is 5% of $500 = $25. Tax rate 20%.

• At purchase: PP&E +$1,000 and Debt +$1,000, no net cash movement.

• Income Statement: $100 of depreciation plus $75 of interest, so book Pre-Tax Income falls $175 and Net Income falls $140.

• Taxes: taxable income falls $275, being $200 of tax depreciation and $75 of interest, so cash taxes fall $55 while book tax falls $35. The $20 difference creates a deferred tax liability.

• Cash Flow Statement: the only cash items are the $50 cash coupon out and $55 of tax saved, so cash rises $5.

• Balance Sheet: Cash +$5 and PP&E −$100, so assets fall $95; Debt +$25 from the PIK, a DTL of +$20 and Retained Earnings −$140 also sum to −$95, so both sides balance.

• Intuition: accelerated tax depreciation defers $20 of tax into a liability and is what turns the year cash-positive.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

[F0835] How would you value a company with negative EBITDA?
Asked by / question source: Guggenheim Partners NY; UBS NY
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
A negative EBITDA denominator makes a conventional EV/EBITDA comparison economically unhelpful. Determine why EBITDA is negative and whether the business can generate sustainable positive cash flow. Use a scenario DCF that includes losses, CapEx, working capital, funding requirements and failure risk before reaching normalized profitability. A revenue multiple or a forward positive-EBITDA multiple may provide a cross-check if peers have comparable growth, margins, capital needs and risk; do not assume all revenue deserves the same multiple. If the business cannot remain a going concern, use asset/recovery analysis instead. When reconciling earnings, unadjusted EBITDA adds back interest, taxes and D&A, not every non-cash expense; SBC and other adjustments require separate identification.

[F0836] Calculate an investment's rate of return. [Inputs not recorded.]
Asked by / question source: Guggenheim Partners NY
Answer status: Method / conditional answer — source details needed
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
The source omits inputs needed for a unique conclusion. Assess the underlying cash flows, price paid, loss risk, liquidity, horizon and legal claim. Debt offers contractual payments and priority but capped upside and default/refinancing risk; equity is residual and has uncapped upside with greater downside volatility. Compare downside recovery and expected return after fees/taxes, and avoid selecting on yield or a low price alone. For lending, examine sustainable debt service and collateral; for equity, test growth, reinvestment and competitive durability. A recommendation needs the stated investor constraints and actual instrument/company data.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

[F0837] How does depreciation impact your DCF?
Asked by / question source: Guggenheim Partners NY
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
In an unlevered DCF, FCFF = EBIT(1-t) + D&A - CapEx - change in operating NWC. Additional tax-deductible depreciation d reduces EBIT but is added back, increasing cash flow by d*t, provided the tax shield is currently usable. Earlier tax depreciation therefore generally increases present value by bringing tax savings forward. Changing book depreciation alone while cash taxes stay unchanged does not create cash value: deferred taxes offset the accounting change. Also distinguish a depreciation-method change from new CapEx, which has its own cash cost.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

[F0838] If I wasn't using the mid-year convention and then decided to use it, how do you think the percentage of present value from the terminal value would be affected?
Asked by / question source: Guggenheim Partners NY
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
It depends on how terminal value timing is treated. If moving to mid-year discounting multiplies both explicit-period cash-flow PV and terminal PV by the same factor, the terminal share of total PV is unchanged. If only explicit cash flows move half a year earlier while terminal value remains at the same date, explicit PV rises and the terminal share falls. Specify the perpetuity/exiting-multiple convention and cash-flow dates instead of assuming one universal answer.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

[F0840] If we originally have a company that has 1⁄3 debt to equity value and now the debt to equity value increased to 3, how do you think that will impact your WACC?
Asked by / question source: Guggenheim Partners NY
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
D/E changes from 1/3 to 3: debt weight goes from 25% to 75%, and equity weight from 75% to 25%. Holding Ke and after-tax Kd fixed, WACC falls if debt is cheaper. In reality greater leverage raises equity risk and can raise debt spreads and distress costs, so WACC may fall initially and then rise. The two leverage ratios alone do not establish the new WACC.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

[F0841] Would taking on more debt always reduce your WACC?
Asked by / question source: Guggenheim Partners NY
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
WACC = E/(D+E)*Ke + D/(D+E)*Kd*(1-t), extending the weights for preferred capital if present. Use market-value, sustainable capital weights. Ke is often estimated with CAPM; Kd is the current marginal borrowing yield for comparable risk and maturity, not necessarily an old coupon. The debt tax adjustment reflects usable interest deductibility. Match currency, inflation and risk to the cash flows. Moderate leverage can lower WACC through tax shields, but greater default risk raises required debt and equity returns; the relationship is not universally decreasing. For a private company, estimate operating risk from public peers and use a defensible target capital structure.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

[F0842] How do you calculate the net return on invested equity in an LBO?
Asked by / question source: Guggenheim Partners NY
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
An LBO buys a company using sponsor equity and debt serviced by the target’s cash flows. Set entry EV and equity purchase price, build sources and uses including fees/refinancing, forecast operations and cash generation, model debt interest/amortization and the cash sweep, then estimate exit EV and subtract exit net debt and other claims. Sponsor MOIC = proceeds/invested equity; with one entry and exit, IRR = MOIC^(1/years)-1. Returns come from operating growth, deleveraging, entry/exit valuation and distributions. More leverage increases both upside and default risk. Favor resilient cash conversion, manageable CapEx, credible improvements and a defensible purchase price. Strategic buyers may pay more for synergies; sponsors may offer certainty, speed, rollover equity or management continuity.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

[F0843] What does it mean when a dividend recap is levered vs unlevered?
Asked by / question source: Guggenheim Partners NY
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
For a cash dividend D with no change in the operating business, cash and common equity value each fall D; EV is unchanged because the equity decline is offset by subtracting less cash. Debt-financed dividends add a debt/cash issuance step and then the distribution. Taxes, distress risk and market signaling can change real-world value, but the mechanical dividend alone does not change operating EV.

[F0844] Company A has a P/E of 10x and Company B has a P/E of 15x. If A acquires B using all debt, is the acquisition accretive or dilutive?
Asked by / question source: Guggenheim Partners NY
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
You cannot answer from the two P/E multiples alone, because in an all-debt deal the buyer's own multiple is not the financing cost — no shares are issued. The comparison is between what the target's earnings yield and what the debt costs after tax. Company B at a 15x purchase multiple yields 1 / 15 = 6.67%. The deal is accretive if the after-tax interest rate on the new debt is below 6.67%, and dilutive above it. At a 20% tax rate that breaks even at a pre-tax coupon of 6.67% / 0.80 = 8.3%, so borrowing below roughly 8% accretes and borrowing above it dilutes. Two things the shortcut leaves out: purchase-accounting amortisation of written-up intangibles reduces pro forma earnings and pushes the breakeven rate lower, while synergies raise the target's effective yield and push it higher. And accretion is not value creation — a deal funded with cheap debt can add to EPS while still overpaying and adding leverage risk.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

[F0845] Calculate a company's tax rate from revenue, expenses, interest and D&A. Assume a 20% tax rate. [Inputs not recorded.]
Asked by / question source: Houlihan Lokey Healthcare
Answer status: Method / conditional answer — source details needed
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
The question asks for the tax rate, so do not assume one — derive it. Build down the income statement to pre-tax income, then divide the tax charge into it. Revenue less operating expenses and D&A gives EBIT; EBIT less interest gives Pre-Tax Income; the effective tax rate is Income Tax Expense / Pre-Tax Income. For example, with $500 of revenue, $300 of operating expenses, $50 of D&A and $25 of interest, Pre-Tax Income is $125, and a $25 tax charge is a 20% effective rate. Distinguish three rates that are easily confused: the statutory rate set by law, the effective rate from the income statement, which permanent differences move away from statutory, and the cash tax rate, which is cash taxes paid over pre-tax income and differs again because of timing differences and deferred taxes. For valuation use a forward-looking marginal or cash rate rather than a historical effective rate that may carry one-off items. The source does not record the figures, so substitute them into Income Tax Expense / Pre-Tax Income.

[F0846] Calculate an exit valuation multiple after changes in revenue and EBITDA margins. [Inputs incomplete in source.]
Asked by / question source: Houlihan Lokey Healthcare
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Choose companies with similar business model, geography, growth, margins, risk and capital intensity. Calculate consistent enterprise/equity values and calendarized historical or forecast metrics, normalize unusual items, and apply a justified peer range to the target metric. EV/Revenue divided by EV/EBITDA equals EBITDA margin when periods and EV are consistent. P/E uses equity value/net income; EV/EBITDA uses operating value/pre-interest earnings, so taxes and financing can produce different rankings. Higher multiples can reflect growth, stronger returns, recurring revenue or lower risk, not automatically overvaluation. Negative EBITDA makes its multiple unhelpful; revenue multiples require a credible path to margins. Share price alone is not comparable across firms because share counts differ.

[F0852] What is the present value of $100 received annually for five years with no growth and a 5% discount rate?

Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

[F0853] Explain the Gordon Growth Model, its use in terminal value, and alternative terminal-value methods.
Asked by / question source: Houlihan Lokey Industrials
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
The perpetuity-growth method is TV at year N = FCF_(N+1)/(WACC-g), with WACC greater than sustainable long-term growth g. The exit-multiple method is terminal metric (often EBITDA) times a defensible terminal multiple. Discount TV from its measurement date. Perpetuity growth is tied to long-run economics and reinvestment; exit multiples are grounded in market evidence but can embed cyclical mispricing. Check that growth, margins, reinvestment and returns on capital form a sustainable steady state. A finite-life asset or expiring drug may need a runoff value rather than a perpetual terminal value. Neither method is automatically always higher or more reliable.

[F0854] Walk me through the 4 methods of valuation and rank them based on the value they might give.
Asked by / question source: Houlihan Lokey Industrials
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Core methods are public trading comparables, precedent transactions and DCF. An LBO is a sponsor’s return-constrained price analysis; asset-based/liquidation value and sum-of-the-parts are additional approaches. Trading comps reflect current minority market prices; precedents reflect historical deal conditions, control and possible synergies; DCF reflects forecast cash generation and risk. Precedents often exceed trading comps, and LBO prices can be lower than strategic values, but there is no guaranteed ranking or universal valuation floor. Select methods suited to the business, compare their assumptions and present a range rather than averaging incompatible outputs.

[F0855] Why as well as how I looked at working capital and why it's important.
Asked by / question source: Houlihan Lokey Industrials
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
For valuation, operating NWC usually equals non-cash operating current assets minus non-debt operating current liabilities. An increase uses cash and is subtracted from FCFF; a decrease releases cash. Receivables and inventory tie up cash, while supplier payables and customer advances finance operations. DSO = average AR/revenue * days; inventory days = average inventory/COGS * days; DPO = average AP/COGS * days (purchases may be better when available). Cash conversion cycle = DSO + inventory days - DPO. A higher DPO can improve cash flow but may also signal supplier stress; evaluate industry terms and overdue balances.

[F0856] Explain the Black-Scholes model and how stock prices affect option values.
Asked by / question source: Houlihan Lokey Industrials
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Black-Scholes prices a European option in continuous time, assuming the underlying follows a lognormal random walk with constant volatility, frictionless continuous trading and a constant risk-free rate. For a European call on a non-dividend-paying stock, C = S*N(d1) - K*exp(-r*T)*N(d2), where d1 = [ln(S/K) + (r + sigma^2/2)*T]/(sigma*sqrt(T)), d2 = d1 - sigma*sqrt(T), and N() is the cumulative standard normal distribution. The inputs are spot price S, strike K, time to expiry T, risk-free rate r, volatility sigma and any dividend yield. The mechanism is replication and no arbitrage rather than forecasting: a continuously rebalanced holding of N(d1) shares funded with borrowing reproduces the option's payoff, so the option must cost what that portfolio costs, which is why the stock's own expected return never appears in the formula. Read the two terms as a discounted expected payoff under the risk-neutral measure, where N(d2) is the risk-neutral probability of finishing in the money and N(d1) is the option's delta. A put follows from put-call parity: P = C - S + K*exp(-r*T). A higher spot price raises a call's value and lowers a put's, with delta measuring the rate of change and gamma its curvature; more volatility and more time raise both calls and puts. The model's weaknesses are its constant-volatility and lognormal assumptions, which is why observed implied volatility varies across strikes and maturities, and it does not handle early exercise on American options or discrete dividends without adjustment.

[F0860] How could a company increase FCF without increasing net income?
Asked by / question source: Houlihan Lokey NY
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

[F0861] Explain the practical construction and technical assumptions of a financial model you have built.
Asked by / question source: Houlihan Lokey NY
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:

Reconcile net income to CFO using non-cash items and operating working-capital changes, then add investing and financing flows. Update cash, the relevant balance-sheet accounts and retained earnings, and verify assets = liabilities + equity. The numerical result requires amounts, timing, tax treatment and financing terms; an incomplete prompt does not support a unique set of balances. Separate initial recognition, subsequent operations and eventual repayment/disposal.

[F0862] How does an increase in current liabilities affect FCFF.
Asked by / question source: Houlihan Lokey NY
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
An increase in operating current liabilities (accounts payable, accrued expenses, deferred revenue) reduces operating net working capital, which releases cash and therefore increases FCFF, because FCFF subtracts the increase in operating NWC. A decrease does the reverse. Two cautions: the item must be an operating, non-debt liability - an increase in short-term borrowings or the current portion of long-term debt is financing, so it does not affect FCFF at all - and if the liability rose because an expense was accrued rather than paid, record the expense effect on EBIT first and then the offsetting working-capital change, rather than counting the cash benefit alone.

[F0863] What is Levered beta?
Asked by / question source: Houlihan Lokey NY
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Unlever comparable companies’ equity betas to remove financing risk, use a suitable peer median asset beta, and relever at the target capital structure. A common shortcut, assuming debt beta approximately zero, is beta_U = beta_L/[1+(1-t)D/E], and beta_L = beta_U[1+(1-t)D/E]. Use market-value leverage and a consistent marginal tax assumption. If debt risk is material, incorporate debt beta and a consistent tax-shield model. A private company lacks an observable stock beta, so operating comparables are the starting point; private status alone does not justify an arbitrary adjustment.

[F0864] Tell me by how much the deal was accretive or dilutive?
Asked by / question source: Houlihan Lokey NY
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Accretion/dilution compares pro forma EPS with the buyer’s standalone EPS. Add target earnings and after-tax synergies, subtract after-tax new interest, foregone cash interest, purchase-accounting amortization and relevant ongoing costs; divide by buyer shares plus shares issued. New shares = stock consideration/buyer share price. In a simplified all-stock deal without other adjustments, a buyer with a higher P/E than the target’s purchase P/E is accretive. For debt or cash consideration, compare the target’s earnings yield with the after-tax funding/opportunity cost. EPS accretion does not prove value creation: price paid, risk and economic returns versus cost of capital still matter.

[F0865] Why are financial institutions not valued based on EBITDA?
Asked by / question source: Houlihan Lokey NY
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
For banks and similar lenders, interest is a core operating input and debt/deposits fund earning assets, so excluding interest to calculate EBITDA removes a central part of the business economics. EV and debt separation are less meaningful than for an industrial company. Use equity DCF/dividend/residual-income models and P/E or price/tangible book, considering credit losses, capital and returns on equity.

[F0867] How does $10 increase in debt affect enterprise value?

ANSWER:

[F0868] Walk from revenue to levered free cash flow.
Asked by / question source: Houlihan Lokey Restructuring LA
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Unlevered free cash flow (FCFF) = EBIT(1-t) + D&A - CapEx - increase in operating NWC, with other adjustments for operating cash items as needed. It is available to all capital providers and is discounted at WACC. Levered free cash flow to equity (FCFE) deducts after-tax interest and incorporates net borrowing: FCFE = FCFF - interest(1-t) + debt issued - principal repaid. From net income, add non-cash expenses, subtract investment and operating NWC increases, and include net borrowing. Definitions of reported “FCF” vary, so identify whether the interviewer means CFO minus CapEx, FCFF or FCFE. EBITDA is not cash flow because it omits taxes, investment and working capital.

[F0869] How could you increase a DCF valuation?
Asked by / question source: Houlihan Lokey Restructuring LA; Intrepid LA
Also covers: F0918
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
DCF value rises with higher sustainable cash flow and falls with higher discount rates. Faster growth creates value only if incremental returns exceed the cost of capital; growth that requires excessive reinvestment can destroy value. Test WACC against terminal growth or exit multiple, then separately stress revenue growth, margins, CapEx and working capital. Keep taxes and cash-flow timing consistent. No universal ranking exists for the impact of a one-percentage-point change in different assumptions: compare changes using the actual base values, forecast duration and proportion of value in the terminal period.

[F0871] How does $10 of interest expense flow through the three financial statements? Assume a 20% tax rate.
Asked by / question source: Houlihan Lokey Restructuring LA
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Ten dollars of interest expense, paid in cash, at a 20% tax rate.

• Income Statement: interest sits below EBIT, so Pre-Tax Income falls $10 and Net Income falls $8.

• Cash Flow Statement: Net Income −$8 and there is nothing to add back, because the interest was paid, so cash falls $8.

• Balance Sheet: Cash −$8 against Retained Earnings −$8, so both sides fall $8 and balance. Debt principal does not change — this is the coupon, not a repayment.

• Intuition: $10 leaves the business and $2 comes back as tax relief, so the net cost is $8.

Under U.S. GAAP cash interest is an operating outflow; IFRS allows a policy choice. If the interest is accrued rather than paid, an interest payable rises and cash does not move yet; if it is PIK, it accretes onto principal and is added back as non-cash.

[F0873] Explain bond valuation and creditor recovery waterfalls.
Asked by / question source: Houlihan Lokey Restructuring LA
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
A bond’s value is the present value of expected coupons and principal, discounted consistently for rates, credit and liquidity; price generally falls as required yield rises. In distress, contractual payments may be replaced by expected recoveries. Build a legal-entity waterfall: collateral supports secured claims first, eligible deficiencies join the appropriate unsecured pool, pari passu claims share pro rata, and equity gets only the residual. Model default timing, administrative costs, guarantees and claim priority rather than applying a single recovery percentage to all debt.

[F0874] If a company's capital structure is 50% debt, 50% equity and return on assets is 10%, return on debt is 5%, what is return on equity?
Asked by / question source: Houlihan Lokey Restructuring LA
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
If 10% is an unlevered asset return before financing/tax and debt and equity are each 50%, then 10% = 0.5*5% + 0.5*Re, so Re = 15%, ignoring tax. Accounting ROA defined using net income is different; with net-income ROA of 10% and equity/assets of 50%, ROE would be 20%. Clarify which return definition the prompt uses.

[F0875] Walk from EBITDA to unlevered free cash flow.
Asked by / question source: Houlihan Lokey Restructuring LA; William Blair SF
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Unlevered free cash flow = EBIT*(1-t) + D&A - CapEx - increase in operating NWC. From EBITDA, subtract D&A to obtain EBIT, apply operating cash taxes, add D&A back, then subtract investment and working-capital needs. From revenue, first subtract operating expenses to reach EBIT. From net income, add after-tax interest and remove non-operating earnings before adjusting for non-cash expenses and reinvestment. FCFF excludes financing flows and is discounted at WACC. Use cash taxes and other operating adjustments where accounting taxes differ.

[F0876] Walk through multiple years of inventory, debt, PIK interest and debt amortization. Assume a 20% tax rate. [Inputs not recorded.]
Asked by / question source: Houlihan Lokey Restructuring LA
Answer status: Method / conditional answer — source details needed
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
The source omits the amounts, so work a clean case: $100 of inventory bought with $100 of debt at 5% cash and 5% PIK, 20% annual amortisation of the original principal, sold the following year for $200, at a 20% tax rate.

• Year 1, at purchase: Inventory +$100 and Debt +$100, so cash does not move and nothing hits the income statement.

• Year 2 Income Statement: Revenue $200 and COGS $100, less $5 of cash interest and $5 of PIK, so Pre-Tax Income is $90 and Net Income is $72.

• Year 2 Cash Flow Statement: Net Income $72, plus $5 of PIK added back, plus the $100 release of inventory, gives $177 of operating cash flow; the $20 amortisation is a financing outflow, so cash rises $157.

• Year 2 Balance Sheet: inventory falls to zero, Debt ends at $85 after $5 of accretion and $20 of repayment, and Retained Earnings rises $72 — both sides up $57 from the post-purchase position.

• Intuition: the inventory came back as $100 of cash, the $100 of margin cost $18 of tax, and $25 went out as coupon and principal.

[F0877] A company has enterprise value of $500, $75 secured debt and $225 unsecured debt. Calculate equity value. If enterprise value falls to $250, what are the values of equity and each debt tranche?

[F0878] How a company goes into distress, what the possible routes for a company in distress are and why each of them matter/their advantages and disadvantages and what they do for creditors and the debtor, and the bankruptcy process.
Asked by / question source: Houlihan Lokey Restructuring LA
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Start with a 13-week cash-flow forecast, covenant/maturity review and entity-by-entity capital structure. Options include operational fixes, asset sales, new capital, maturity extensions, debt exchanges, out-of-court restructuring and court proceedings. U.S. Chapter 11 permits reorganization under court oversight, potentially with DIP financing and a plan; Chapter 7 generally liquidates assets through a trustee. A prepack requires sufficient creditor agreement in advance and may not suit contested claims or complex operational changes. A Section 363 sale is a court-supervised asset sale subject to required protections and approval. Compare going-concern versus liquidation value, creditor recoveries, speed, financing needs, execution risk and stakeholder incentives.

[F0879] Walk through the statements when inventory is purchased with debt in year 1 and sold in year 2, including cash and PIK interest. Assume a 20% tax rate. [Amounts and rates not recorded.]
Asked by / question source: Houlihan Lokey Restructuring LA
Answer status: Method / conditional answer — source details needed
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
The source omits the amounts and rates, so work from a clean example. PIK interest accrues onto principal instead of being paid in cash. Take $100 of debt at 5% cash and 5% PIK for one year, at a 20% tax rate.

• Income Statement: interest expense is $10, being $5 cash and $5 PIK, so Pre-Tax Income falls $10 and Net Income falls $8.

• Cash Flow Statement: Net Income −$8, add back the $5 of non-cash PIK, so cash falls $3 — the $5 cash coupon less the $2 tax saving.

• Balance Sheet: Cash −$3 and Debt +$5 from the accrued PIK; Retained Earnings −$8, so both sides fall $3 and balance.

• Intuition: PIK protects near-term liquidity and increases what you must repay later.

At repayment you repay principal including accrued PIK, plus any call premium. Without usable deductions, cash falls by the full $5 coupon and the tax benefit becomes a deferred tax asset.

[F0880] How does cash flow from operations differ from unlevered free cash flow?
Asked by / question source: Houlihan Lokey Restructuring LA
Also covers: F0893
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Under U.S. GAAP, CFO generally starts from earnings after interest and includes operating working-capital changes and non-cash adjustments. FCFF is cash available to all capital providers after operating taxes and reinvestment, before financing. A common bridge is FCFF = CFO + after-tax interest - CapEx, with adjustments for non-operating items and tax/classification differences. CFO alone omits CapEx and is not identical to UFCF.

[F0882] What is the difference between operating lease accounting and capital lease accounting?
Asked by / question source: Evercore (compiled interview notes); Houlihan Lokey Restructuring LA
Also covers: F0898, F1880
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Both U.S. GAAP and IFRS generally place a lessee’s right-of-use asset and lease liability on the balance sheet, subject to exceptions. Under ASC 842, operating leases normally produce a single straight-line lease expense and operating cash payments; finance leases produce amortization plus interest, with principal in financing cash flow. IFRS 16 largely uses a single lessee model with depreciation plus interest. Finance-lease principal repayments are a financing outflow, while operating-lease payments under ASC 842 sit entirely in operating cash flow; interest classification follows the applicable reporting rules. For valuation, match the earnings metric and lease treatment: do not add lease liabilities to EV while using an earnings denominator that already deducts the same financing-like lease cost without a consistent adjustment.
Supporting reference: https://www.ifrs.org/issued-standards/list-of-standards/ifrs-16-leases/
Supporting reference: https://fasb.org/projects/current-projects/leases-398331

[F0883] You have a bond trading at 80 with a 12% coupon rate. What is the YTM if you assume it will be redeemed at par in 5 years?
Asked by / question source: Houlihan Lokey Restructuring LA
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Solve 80 = 12*(1-(1+y)^-5)/y + 100/(1+y)^5. Annual YTM is approximately 18.46%. A rough estimate is [12+(100-80)/5]/[(100+80)/2] = 17.78%; identify that as an approximation rather than an exact result.

[F0887] A company has EBITDA of 100 and trades at a 7x multiple, with $300 of senior debt and $600 of subordinated debt. What does each tranche trade at? If I offered you 500 for the subordinated notes, would you take the deal?
Asked by / question source: Houlihan Lokey Restructuring LA
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Enterprise value is 100 * 7 = 700. The senior debt of 300 is covered in full, so it is worth par, 100 cents. That leaves 400 for the 600 of subordinated debt, a 66.67% recovery, or about 67 cents. On the offer: 500 for the whole 600 face position is about 83 cents, well above the ~67 cents the waterfall supports, so yes, sell. You are being paid above the value of the claim. Before agreeing, pin down what 500 means — a cash price for the entire position, a price per 100 of face, or a face amount being exchanged — because the three give very different answers. Then check the things the simplified waterfall ignores: cash on the balance sheet, structural seniority and which entity each claim sits at, administrative and professional costs that come ahead of creditors, intercreditor terms, and how long realisation would take, since a 67-cent recovery two years out is worth less than 67 cents today.

[F0888] What would be the value of the debt if the debt matures in one year and is zero coupon?
Asked by / question source: Houlihan Lokey Restructuring LA
Answer status: Method / conditional answer — source details needed
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:

For risky debt, use a consistent credit-adjusted yield or probability-weighted recoveries with an appropriate discount rate. Face value and rate are not supplied, so no unique price can be calculated.

[F0889] Assess liquidity from a complex capital structure including an asset-based lending facility. [Inputs not recorded.]
Asked by / question source: Houlihan Lokey Restructuring LA
Answer status: Method / conditional answer — source details needed
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
The source omits inputs needed for a unique conclusion. Debt avoids immediate ownership dilution and can provide a usable tax shield, but imposes interest, maturity and covenant obligations. Equity has no mandatory repayment and absorbs downside but dilutes owners and normally demands a higher return. Choose a sustainable mix using downside cash generation, collateral, funding horizon, liquidity and market access. Issuing debt and retaining cash raises both equally without initial earnings effects. Issuing primary equity raises cash and paid-in equity; neither immediately creates operating profit. Distressed or pre-revenue businesses may need equity even when debt looks nominally cheaper.

[F0891] What is the present value of cash flows of 50, 100, 150, 200 and so on forever? [Discount rate not recorded.]

[F0899] Which section of CF statement does interest expense go in?
Asked by / question source: Houlihan Lokey Restructuring LA
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Under the direct method, CFO lists operating cash receipts and payments; under the indirect method, it starts with net income and adjusts for non-cash items and working capital. The resulting CFO should match. Subtract non-cash/non-operating gains and add back corresponding losses included in net income, then put cash proceeds in the proper cash-flow category. Non-cash investing/financing transactions are disclosed separately. Interest paid is generally operating under U.S. GAAP; IFRS classification requires attention to the applicable standards and policy. Consistency of tax and interest treatment is essential.

[F0900] A company buys $100 of inventory with debt in year 1. The debt has 10% interest, split 5% cash and 5% PIK, and 20% amortization. In year 2 the company sells the inventory for $200, amortizes debt and pays interest. Walk through both years' three statements. Assume a 20% tax rate. [Tax rate not recorded.]
Asked by / question source: Houlihan Lokey Restructuring LA
Answer status: Method / conditional answer — source details needed
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Assume the purchase at the start of year one, a full year of interest before the sale, amortisation of 20% of the original $100 at year-end, and a 20% tax rate.

• Year one, at purchase: Inventory +$100 and Debt +$100, so no net cash movement and no income effect.

• Year two, Income Statement: Revenue $200 and COGS $100, less $5 of cash interest and $5 of PIK, so Pre-Tax Income is $90 and Net Income is $72.

• Cash Flow Statement: Net Income $72, plus $5 of PIK added back, plus the $100 release of inventory, gives operating cash flow of $177; the $20 amortisation is a financing outflow, so cash rises $157.

• Balance Sheet: Inventory falls to zero, Debt ends at $85 after $5 of PIK and $20 of repayment, and Retained Earnings rises $72; the $157 of cash against the $100 of inventory released leaves both sides up $57 from the post-purchase position and balanced.

• Intuition: the $100 of inventory came back as cash, the $100 of profit was taxed $18, and $5 of coupon and $20 of principal went out.

[F0901] At the beginning of the year, you finance 200 million dollars of inventory by taking on 200 million dollars of debt. The debt is amortized 20% at the end of the year and the interest on the debt is 5% cash, 5% paid in kind. At the end of the year you sell your inventory for 400 million dollars in revenue at 200 million dollars in cost. Walk me through how these changes impact the 3 financial statements at both the beginning and end of the year.
Asked by / question source: Houlihan Lokey Restructuring LA
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Assume the sale and the amortisation occur at year-end, interest runs on the opening $200, amortisation is 20% of the original principal, the sale is for cash, and the tax rate is 20%.

• At purchase: Inventory +$200 and Debt +$200, so the borrowing and the inventory outlay offset and cash does not move.

• Income Statement: Revenue $400 and COGS $200, less $10 of cash interest and $10 of PIK, so Pre-Tax Income is $180 and Net Income is $144.

• Cash Flow Statement: operating cash flow is $190 less the $36 of tax, so $154 — the $400 sale, less the $200 paid for inventory, less $10 of cash interest, less $36 of tax. Financing is the $200 drawn less the $40 repaid, so +$160.

• Balance Sheet: cash is up $314, inventory is zero, Debt ends at $170 after $10 of PIK and $40 of amortisation, and Retained Earnings rises $144.

• Intuition: the business turned $200 of inventory into $400 of cash, paid $36 of tax and $10 of coupon, and still owes $170.

A different amortisation base or interest timing changes the figures.

[F0904] Walk me through the financial statements at the beginning and end of a year with the purchase of an asset through debt with X% cash and X% PIK interest with X repayment. Assume a 20% tax rate.
Asked by / question source: Houlihan Lokey Restructuring LA
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
PIK interest accrues onto principal instead of being paid in cash. Take $100 of debt at 5% cash and 5% PIK for one year, at a 20% tax rate.

• Income Statement: interest expense is $10, being $5 cash and $5 PIK, so Pre-Tax Income falls $10 and Net Income falls $8.

• Cash Flow Statement: Net Income −$8, add back the $5 of non-cash PIK, so cash falls $3 — the $5 cash coupon less the $2 tax saving.

• Balance Sheet: Cash −$3 and Debt +$5 from the accrued PIK; Retained Earnings −$8, so both sides fall $3 and balance.

• Intuition: PIK protects near-term liquidity and increases what you must repay later.

At repayment you repay principal including accrued PIK, plus any call premium. Without usable deductions, cash falls by the full $5 coupon and the tax benefit becomes a deferred tax asset.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

[F0905] You sell the asset for X at the end of the period.
Asked by / question source: Houlihan Lokey Restructuring LA
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
For a sale of an asset with book value B for proceeds P, the gain/loss is P-B and after-tax income is (P-B)(1-t), if tax basis equals book basis. Remove the gain or add back the loss in CFO; report gross proceeds P in investing cash flow. Cash rises P-t(P-B), the asset falls B and retained earnings change by after-tax gain/loss. A non-cash impairment W reduces assets and income; add W back in CFO. Cash rises W*t only if a current tax deduction is usable; otherwise recognize any appropriate deferred-tax effect. Losing cash directly is different: cash falls and shareholders bear the loss; operating enterprise value need not change if the loss has no operational implications.

[F0906] What section of the cash flow statement does PIK interest expense go in?
Asked by / question source: Houlihan Lokey Restructuring LA
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
PIK interest is interest expense on the income statement but no current cash payment occurs. Under the indirect cash-flow method, add the non-cash PIK expense back to net income in CFO; cash tax effects remain separate. Capitalizing it increases debt and is a non-cash financing movement, not a new cash financing inflow. When principal is eventually repaid, the cash repayment follows the applicable debt classification.

[F0921] What are financing synergies and how is that achieved?
Asked by / question source: Intrepid LA
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Financing synergies are reductions in financing cost or improved access/capacity after combination, such as lower borrowing spreads, more efficient liquidity use or reduced expected distress costs. Diversification can sometimes support more debt, but not all apparent benefits are value creation and lower funding rates may reflect risk transferred among claimants. Value actual incremental after-tax cash benefits net of fees and avoid double counting them in both cash flows and WACC.

A good business is not automatically a good investment at any price. For a short, include borrow cost, squeeze risk and loss limits; for a long, say what would invalidate the thesis. Without a specified company and current price, a particular target price or trade recommendation would be fabricated.

[F0925] When the price of a bond goes up, what happens to the interest rate?
Asked by / question source: J.P. Morgan Asset Management
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
A bond’s price is the PV of coupons plus principal discounted at the required yield. Price moves inversely to yield. Macaulay duration is the cash-flow-PV-weighted average payment time; modified duration approximates percentage price sensitivity: change in price/price ≈ -Dmod * change in yield. Convexity improves the approximation for larger moves. A zero-coupon bond’s Macaulay duration equals its maturity; modified duration differs by the compounding adjustment. Longer maturity and lower coupon usually increase rate sensitivity. Credit spreads, embedded options and liquidity can move price independently of the risk-free curve.

[F0927] Can cost of equity be less than cost of debt?
Asked by / question source: J.P. Morgan CHI
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
WACC = E/(D+E)*Ke + D/(D+E)*Kd*(1-t), extending the weights for preferred capital if present. Use market-value, sustainable capital weights. Ke is often estimated with CAPM; Kd is the current marginal borrowing yield for comparable risk and maturity, not necessarily an old coupon. The debt tax adjustment reflects usable interest deductibility. Match currency, inflation and risk to the cash flows. Moderate leverage can lower WACC through tax shields, but greater default risk raises required debt and equity returns; the relationship is not universally decreasing. For a private company, estimate operating risk from public peers and use a defensible target capital structure.

[F0928] If Coke is trading at 14x, and then goes to 16x, would you still buy the stock?

Specify whether 14x/16x means P/E, EV/EBITDA or another measure.

[F0930] How do oil and gas prices affect companies' revenue and profit?
Asked by / question source: J.P. Morgan CHI
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Upstream producers generally benefit from higher realized oil/gas prices if volumes and costs are unchanged; prices can also change royalties, taxes, drilling activity and hedging outcomes. Refiners depend on crack spreads rather than crude price alone. Midstream revenue may be more contracted/volume-based but still has counterparty and utilization risk. Fuel-intensive consumers can suffer higher costs unless they pass them through. Identify the business model before assigning a profit effect.

[F0933] What is specifically on JPMorgan's balance sheet?
Asked by / question source: J.P. Morgan Finance and Business Management
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
A bank's balance sheet is the business, not a support schedule for it, so read it from the funding side first. Assets are overwhelmingly financial: cash and reserves at the central bank, loans to consumers and corporates net of an allowance for credit losses, investment securities held to maturity or available for sale, trading assets and derivatives, securities borrowed and reverse repos, plus goodwill and intangibles from past acquisitions. Liabilities are mostly customer deposits, which are the cheapest and stickiest funding, plus long-term debt, short-term borrowings, repos and trading liabilities. Equity is common shareholders' equity plus preferred stock. Two things to say that show you understand a bank rather than a company: the balance sheet drives the income statement, because net interest income is the spread between what the earning assets yield and what the funding costs, so loan and deposit growth and the rate on each are the forecast drivers; and the size and mix are constrained by regulation, since risk-weighted assets and the CET 1 ratio limit how much the bank can lend and how much it can distribute. That is also why enterprise value is not used for banks: you cannot separate operating from financing activity when the financing is the operation.

[F0934] The bank receives a million dollars, what line in the balance sheet does this go on?
Asked by / question source: J.P. Morgan Finance and Business Management
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Cash/reserves rise by $1 million. The offset depends on the source: a customer deposit increases deposit liabilities; a loan to the bank increases borrowings; a share issuance increases equity; earned fee revenue affects profit/equity. Receiving cash alone does not identify the offset.

[F0936] What would you do with excess cash if your company is already doing well?
Asked by / question source: J.P. Morgan Finance and Business Management
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Five uses of cash are reinvestment in operations/CapEx, acquisitions, debt repayment, dividends and share repurchases. First reserve required operating liquidity; then choose incremental projects whose risk-adjusted returns exceed their cost of capital. Avoid overpaying for acquisitions or own shares. Debt reduction can lower distress/refinancing risk. Excess unrestricted cash is usually added separately in the EV-to-equity bridge at approximately face value, adjusted for access/tax issues. An interest tax shield equals deductible interest times the applicable tax rate, subject to actual tax capacity and legal limits.

[F0944] 100 people in line. The first person opens every single closet. The second person closes the ones that are multiples of 2 (2nd, 4th ...). The third person closes very open closet and opens every closed closet that is a multiple of 3...and so on so forth.
Asked by / question source: J.P. Morgan Fixed Income
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Assuming all 100 doors begin closed and person n toggles every nth door, a door ends open only if it has an odd number of divisors. Only perfect squares have odd divisor counts, so 1,4,9,16,25,36,49,64,81,100 remain open: ten doors.

[F0954] What risks affect mortgage-backed securities?
Asked by / question source: J.P. Morgan Fixed Income
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Securitization pools financial assets and allocates their cash flows to securities with different priorities. Senior tranches have greater protection; junior/equity tranches absorb losses first and seek higher returns. Model collateral defaults, recoveries, prepayments, rates, servicing and waterfall triggers. Mortgage investors face extension risk when rates rise and prepayments slow, and contraction/reinvestment risk when rates fall. In a CMO, a Z/accrual tranche defers current interest while earlier tranches receive cash. A quoted spread must compensate for expected losses, duration/option risk, liquidity and model uncertainty; no universal spread follows without collateral and structure details.

[F0959] Walk me through delta hedging.
Asked by / question source: J.P. Morgan Fixed Income
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Delta hedging offsets the first-order sensitivity of an option position to the underlying. For N options with delta d and contract multiplier m, hedge by holding approximately -N*d*m units of the underlying for a long option position. Delta changes with price, time and volatility, so the hedge must be rebalanced and still has gamma, vega, gap, transaction-cost and liquidity risk. It is not a guarantee of a risk-free profit.

[F0962] As CFO of a new airline with no revenue yet, what information would you request to forecast next year's revenue?
Asked by / question source: J.P. Morgan Fixed Income
Answer status: Framework — dated research required
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Build revenue from operating units rather than assuming a growth rate: customers/volume * frequency/utilization * net price, plus ancillary streams. Separate variable costs from fixed costs to model contribution margin, operating leverage and break-even volume. For a pharmacy use prescription volumes, reimbursement/mix, dispensing margin and payer terms; roofing uses crew capacity, projects, ticket size and repair/replacement mix; software/telecom uses subscribers, ARPU, churn and network/service costs; a food outlet uses footfall, conversion, ticket and opening days. Forecast working capital, maintenance/growth CapEx and taxes. Value sustainable after-tax cash flow and cross-check peers; local concentration, regulation and reinvestment can explain different multiples despite similar current profits.

[F0968] How can you take a view / trade on both the slope an curvature of the yield curve?
Asked by / question source: J.P. Morgan Fixed Income
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
A steepener benefits from the selected long-minus-short yield spread widening; a flattener benefits from narrowing. Use duration/DV01-matched bond or swap legs to reduce outright rate exposure, recognizing residual curve and basis risk. A butterfly compares an intermediate-maturity belly with short/long wings to express curvature. Define the exact tenors, long/short positions, carry and stress scenarios; yield-curve shape alone does not establish an attractive trade.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

[F0969] What is a credit default swap?
Asked by / question source: J.P. Morgan Fixed Income; PJT Partners RSSG NY
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
A credit default swap transfers specified reference-entity credit risk. The protection buyer pays premiums, and the protection seller makes a contractual payment if a defined credit event occurs, commonly linked to loss on the reference obligation through cash or physical settlement. Key terms include reference entity, obligation, seniority, maturity and credit-event definitions. CDS adds counterparty, basis and documentation risks; it does not eliminate all risk.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

[F0970] Why are credit default swaps widely used?
Asked by / question source: J.P. Morgan Fixed Income
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
CDS lets investors hedge credit exposure without selling the cash bond, express a credit view, or separate credit risk from interest-rate exposure. It can improve trading flexibility, but premiums, bond-CDS basis, liquidity, collateral and counterparty risk matter. Protection is limited to the contract’s defined events and obligations, so it is not equivalent to insuring every possible economic loss.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

[F0971] What roles do the issuer and buyer of a credit default swap play within the agreement?
Asked by / question source: J.P. Morgan Fixed Income
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
The CDS protection buyer pays a running premium and sometimes an upfront amount to transfer specified credit-event risk. The protection seller receives that compensation and owes the contractual settlement if a covered event occurs. The reference company usually is not a party to the CDS; calling it the CDS "issuer" can be misleading. Distinguish the underlying debt issuer from the seller of protection.

[F0973] Calculate a portfolio's return and explain how changing the constituent stocks' expected returns and standard deviations affects the result and risk. [Numerical inputs not recorded.]
Asked by / question source: J.P. Morgan Fixed Income
Answer status: Method / conditional answer — source details needed
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

[F0975] How to value a lemon tree?
Asked by / question source: J.P. Morgan LA
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Forecast fruit volume times selling price, subtract harvesting, maintenance, land/operating costs, taxes and any required reinvestment, and discount the resulting cash flows for the tree’s economic life. Include any residual sale value and replacement/replanting costs consistently. A perpetuity only makes sense for a sustainably maintained operation, not an individual tree assumed to live forever. For constant annual end-year cash C for N years, PV = C*[1-(1+r)^(-N)]/r.

Also covers: F0161

ANSWER:

Distinguish revenue growth from profitable growth and accounting earnings from cash. For an unspecified case, ask for the missing company, period and figures before giving a numerical conclusion; do not fabricate a company-specific result.

[F0977] When should a valuation use terminal value versus the asset's finite life?
Asked by / question source: J.P. Morgan LA
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
The perpetuity-growth method is TV at year N = FCF_(N+1)/(WACC-g), with WACC greater than sustainable long-term growth g. The exit-multiple method is terminal metric (often EBITDA) times a defensible terminal multiple. Discount TV from its measurement date. Perpetuity growth is tied to long-run economics and reinvestment; exit multiples are grounded in market evidence but can embed cyclical mispricing. Check that growth, margins, reinvestment and returns on capital form a sustainable steady state. A finite-life asset or expiring drug may need a runoff value rather than a perpetual terminal value. Neither method is automatically always higher or more reliable.

[F0978] Explain your discount-rate assumptions, including the forecast horizon and seasonal effects.
Asked by / question source: J.P. Morgan LA
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Match discount rate to the cash-flow claimant, currency, inflation convention and operating/financing risk. Forecast until the business reaches a defensible steady state or asset life ends. Model seasonal cash flows and working-capital peaks explicitly; use actual dates or a justified mid-year convention. Do not pick a longer forecast merely to obtain a preferred value.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

[F0979] How would you assign a beta (and some question to probe my understanding of how beta works?
Asked by / question source: J.P. Morgan LA
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
CAPM estimates cost of equity as risk-free rate + levered beta * equity risk premium, with justified additional risk adjustments where appropriate. Estimate beta using a regression of stock excess returns on market excess returns, or bottom-up comparable-company betas. Beta reflects systematic risk; leverage, cyclicality and operating fixed costs can raise it. It is not a measure of all uncertainty or an invariant property of an industry. Historical estimates depend on window, frequency and benchmark, and CAPM’s single-factor assumptions are simplifications. Compare operating risk first, then financing; a higher-growth firm does not mechanically have a higher beta.

[F0985] If you are a foreign investor in U.S. Treasuries, how does appreciation or depreciation of your currency against the dollar affect your return?
Asked by / question source: J.P. Morgan Research
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
A foreign investor’s home-currency return equals (1+USD asset return)*(1+USD appreciation versus home currency)-1, ignoring hedge costs and taxes. If the home currency depreciates against the dollar, converting dollar proceeds back generally boosts home-currency return; home-currency appreciation reduces it. A currency hedge changes this through forward pricing, fees and basis risk.

[F0986] What factors impact mortgage bonds?
Asked by / question source: J.P. Morgan Research
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Securitization pools financial assets and allocates their cash flows to securities with different priorities. Senior tranches have greater protection; junior/equity tranches absorb losses first and seek higher returns. Model collateral defaults, recoveries, prepayments, rates, servicing and waterfall triggers. Mortgage investors face extension risk when rates rise and prepayments slow, and contraction/reinvestment risk when rates fall. In a CMO, a Z/accrual tranche defers current interest while earlier tranches receive cash. A quoted spread must compensate for expected losses, duration/option risk, liquidity and model uncertainty; no universal spread follows without collateral and structure details.

[F0988] What is the probability that at least one of ten randomly selected Manhattan apartments is in the top ten by price? [Total population not recorded.]
Asked by / question source: J.P. Morgan Research
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
This is a sampling-probability question rather than a valuation question. Let N be the total number of Manhattan apartments and treat the ten most expensive as a fixed set. Drawing ten apartments without replacement, the chance that none is in the top ten is the number of ways to choose all ten from the other N-10, divided by the ways to choose any ten: C(N-10,10) / C(N,10). The question asks for the complement, so P(at least one) = 1 - C(N-10,10) / C(N,10). Equivalently, multiply the sequential misses: 1 - [(N-10)/N] * [(N-11)/(N-1)] * ... * [(N-19)/(N-9)]. When N is large relative to the sample, each draw has about a 10/N chance of hitting the top ten, so the answer is approximately 100/N: at roughly 850,000 apartments that is about 0.012%, or one in 8,500. Sampling with replacement would instead give 1 - (1 - 10/N)^10, which is almost identical for large N. The total apartment count is not recorded in the source, so state your assumption for N and show the formula rather than guessing a figure.

[F0989] What makes an LBO circular?
Asked by / question source: J.P. Morgan SF
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Interest depends on debt balances; debt repayment depends on cash available; cash available depends on net income after interest. Using average debt therefore creates a circular link. Resolve it with controlled iteration, an algebraic solution or a transparent approximation such as beginning-balance interest, and include a circularity switch. Ensure the result converges and repayment/minimum-cash constraints still hold.

[F0990] How do NOLs affect your DCF valuation?
Asked by / question source: J.P. Morgan SF; Morgan Stanley MP
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
NOLs can reduce future cash taxes and increase DCF value when usable. Forecast taxable income, utilization limits and timing, then discount the actual tax savings. Either include them directly in cash taxes or value and add them separately; do not do both. Their value may be far below face amount times tax rate because of delayed use, expiration, ownership-change limits or insufficient future income.

[F0991] If you had to find comps for a business that was very niche or specialized without very clear cut public competitors, how would you go about compiling a list together?
Asked by / question source: J.P. Morgan SF
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Choose companies with similar business model, geography, growth, margins, risk and capital intensity. Calculate consistent enterprise/equity values and calendarized historical or forecast metrics, normalize unusual items, and apply a justified peer range to the target metric. EV/Revenue divided by EV/EBITDA equals EBITDA margin when periods and EV are consistent. P/E uses equity value/net income; EV/EBITDA uses operating value/pre-interest earnings, so taxes and financing can produce different rankings. Higher multiples can reflect growth, stronger returns, recurring revenue or lower risk, not automatically overvaluation. Negative EBITDA makes its multiple unhelpful; revenue multiples require a credible path to margins. Share price alone is not comparable across firms because share counts differ.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

[F0992] How would you value a healthcare startup?
Asked by / question source: J.P. Morgan SF
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
For a pre-revenue drug developer, build a risk-adjusted NPV by asset: eligible patients * diagnosis/access * market share * net price, less manufacturing, commercialization, R&D, milestones, tax and investment. Weight development paths by stage-specific probabilities and deduct future development costs at the dates they are incurred. Model patent expiry and generic/biosimilar erosion rather than assuming monopoly cash flows forever. Add cash and other pipeline assets and subtract debt/claims, recognizing funding needs and dilution. Trading/transaction revenue multiples are secondary checks only when products and development stages are comparable. Avoid counting clinical failure risk both fully in probability-weighted cash flows and again through an arbitrary discount-rate premium.

[F0993] Why a company would choose not to delay debt repayments, given that the time value of money means that money is worth more now than later.
Asked by / question source: J.P. Morgan SF
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Delaying debt repayment may trigger default, penalties, covenant breach or lost lender access. Even when contractually permitted, keeping debt costs interest and preserves refinancing risk; repayment can earn an effective return equal to the avoided after-tax cost. Compare that benefit with investment opportunities, required liquidity and prepayment penalties. Time value alone is not a reason to ignore contractual obligations.

[F0994] How do you valuate companies in eCommerce space?
Asked by / question source: J.P. Morgan SF
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Choose between an intrinsic cash-flow valuation, market comparables, precedent transactions and, when relevant, asset-based or LBO analysis. Match the numerator to the claimant: EV with pre-interest operating metrics and equity with net income/FCFE. Normalize earnings, align periods and distinguish growth from capital intensity and risk. A private company requires reliable financials and suitable public/deal benchmarks; lack of information increases uncertainty rather than justifying an arbitrary precise value. Use a range with scenario/sensitivity analysis and reconcile results to the business’s cash-generation capacity.

[F0995] How would you estimate the revenue of a hot dog stand near Time Square?
Asked by / question source: J.P. Morgan SF
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Build revenue from operating units rather than assuming a growth rate: customers/volume * frequency/utilization * net price, plus ancillary streams. Separate variable costs from fixed costs to model contribution margin, operating leverage and break-even volume. For a pharmacy use prescription volumes, reimbursement/mix, dispensing margin and payer terms; roofing uses crew capacity, projects, ticket size and repair/replacement mix; software/telecom uses subscribers, ARPU, churn and network/service costs; a food outlet uses footfall, conversion, ticket and opening days. Forecast working capital, maintenance/growth CapEx and taxes. Value sustainable after-tax cash flow and cross-check peers; local concentration, regulation and reinvestment can explain different multiples despite similar current profits.

[F0998] Why didn't you use EV/Net Income as a metric to compare competitors for Alibaba?
Asked by / question source: J.P. Morgan SF
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
EV belongs to all operating capital providers while net income is after interest and attributable to equity (after applicable NCI/preferred adjustments). EV/net income mismatches numerator and denominator and can distort comparisons across leverage. Pair EV with EBIT, EBITDA or FCFF; pair equity value with common net income or FCFE. Match consolidation scope and periods.

[F1002] What happens to EPS, PE, equity value, EV when company issues 300m in new debt?
Asked by / question source: J.P. Morgan SF
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:

Subsequently net income falls by after-tax interest net of income on retained cash, so EPS may fall and P/E rise at a fixed equity value. Use of proceeds can change the result; borrowing alone does not determine future EPS.

[F1003] Explain the business model and economics of a SaaS company.
Asked by / question source: J.P. Morgan SF
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
For SaaS, focus on recurring revenue quality: ARR/MRR, net and gross retention, churn, customer concentration, contract duration, gross margin and sales efficiency. NRR includes expansion less churn/contraction; GRR excludes expansion. Estimate cohort lifetime value from contribution profit and retention, compare it with fully loaded CAC, and test CAC payback. The Rule of 40 adds revenue growth percentage and a consistently defined profit-margin percentage; it is a heuristic, not a valuation formula. Value with DCF and growth/margin-adjusted EV/revenue or EV/ARR; profitable firms can use EV/EBITDA. Annual prepayments support cash conversion, but deferred revenue is an obligation. Sustainable returns matter more than growth at any cost.

[F1006] Walk me through the direct method of the cash flow statement" and drilled in on the specifics of the differences between indirect and direct methods of computing the cash flow statement.
Asked by / question source: J.P. Morgan SF
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Under the direct method, CFO lists operating cash receipts and payments; under the indirect method, it starts with net income and adjusts for non-cash items and working capital. The resulting CFO should match. Subtract non-cash/non-operating gains and add back corresponding losses included in net income, then put cash proceeds in the proper cash-flow category. Non-cash investing/financing transactions are disclosed separately. Interest paid is generally operating under U.S. GAAP; IFRS classification requires attention to the applicable standards and policy. Consistency of tax and interest treatment is essential.

[F1007] Walk me through how depreciation reducing by $20 impacts the three financial statements. Assume a 20% tax rate.
Asked by / question source: J.P. Morgan SF
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
A $20 decrease in depreciation, with the deduction that is lost having been usable, at a 20% tax rate.

• Income Statement: $20 less expense, so EBIT and Pre-Tax Income rise $20 and Net Income rises $16.

• Cash Flow Statement: Net Income is up $16, but you now add back $20 less of non-cash depreciation, so cash falls $4.

• Balance Sheet: Cash −$4 and Net PP&E +$20, so assets rise $16; Retained Earnings +$16, and both sides rise $16 and balance.

• Intuition: reported profit is higher but the company is $4 worse off in cash, because it gave up $4 of tax shield.

This is the standard trap: lower depreciation flatters earnings and costs cash. If only book depreciation changed and cash taxes did not, there is no cash effect and the difference sits in deferred taxes.

[F1010] Which would have a higher valuation a hospital in a metropolitan city or a hospital in the suburbs and why?
Asked by / question source: J.P. Morgan SF
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Neither location is automatically more valuable. A metropolitan hospital may have greater volume, specialized services and referral networks, but higher labor/property costs and competition. A suburban hospital may have favorable payer mix and lower costs but different demand and growth. Compare sustainable cash flow, occupancy, reimbursement, clinical capabilities, competitive position and required CapEx; equal EBITDA can still mask different investment needs.

[F1011] If there's a one hundred million bond with a 5% coupon rate what's is the yield on the bond after two years?
Asked by / question source: J.P. Morgan SF
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
A 5% coupon on 100 million pays 5 million annually. Yield after two years cannot be calculated without the then-current price and remaining maturity. If it trades at par and the terms are plain, YTM equals the 5% coupon rate. Coupon rate is not the realized investment return.

[F1015] Compare valuation methods for startups, banks and large public companies.
Asked by / question source: Jefferies; Jefferies NY
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Banks are usually valued with equity-based methods such as dividend discount, FCFE or residual income, plus P/E and price/tangible book cross-checks. Deposits and debt are operating funding, making a conventional corporate EV/EBITDA or FCFF bridge less useful. Forecast net interest income, fees, credit losses, expenses, regulatory capital and distributable earnings. Growth consumes regulatory equity, so distributions must be consistent with required capital and asset quality.
