[F1138] Calculate the investment's value and IRR. [Numerical inputs not recorded.]
Asked by / question source: LionTree
Answer status: Method / conditional answer — source details needed
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
The source omits inputs needed for a unique conclusion. MOIC = total cash proceeds/total invested capital and does not account for timing. With a single entry and exit, annualized return or IRR = (exit proceeds/entry investment)^(1/years)-1. With interim cash flows, solve 0 = sum[CF_t/(1+r)^t]; use dated cash flows for XIRR. Earlier distributions generally increase IRR at the same MOIC. MOIC can favor a larger long-held gain while IRR favors rapid capital return; assess both alongside risk and absolute profit. ROE is accounting net income/average book equity and is not the same as an investment IRR.

[F1139] Calculate enterprise value including less common adjustments. [Specific adjustments and inputs not recorded.]
Asked by / question source: LionTree
Answer status: Method / conditional answer — source details needed
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
The source omits inputs needed for a unique conclusion. Equity value is the value attributable to common shareholders; for a public company it is diluted share count times share price. Operating EV = equity value + debt + preferred stock + NCI - excess cash - other separately valued non-operating assets, with consistent lease/pension adjustments where relevant. EV pairs with unlevered operating metrics; equity value pairs with net income or FCFE. Raising debt and holding the proceeds as cash normally leaves operating EV unchanged: debt and cash rise equally. A dividend reduces equity and cash together, also leaving operating EV unchanged absent signaling, tax or operational effects. Spending cash on an operating asset can change EV because value has moved from non-operating cash into operations; value creation still depends on the asset’s economics.

[F1140] Solve a merger-model case. [Inputs not recorded.]
Asked by / question source: LionTree
Answer status: Method / conditional answer — source details needed
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
The source omits inputs needed for a unique conclusion. Assess a transaction through strategic fit, price versus standalone and synergy value, financing, execution and integration risk. Test downside cases, regulatory constraints and ability to finance/close. More EPS or more revenue alone does not prove value creation; incremental risk-adjusted returns should exceed the cost of capital. [F1141] How to get to FCF" as the way they formulated it was poor.
Asked by / question source: MUFG
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Unlevered free cash flow (FCFF) = EBIT(1-t) + D&A - CapEx - increase in operating NWC, with other adjustments for operating cash items as needed. It is available to all capital providers and is discounted at WACC. Levered free cash flow to equity (FCFE) deducts after-tax interest and incorporates net borrowing: FCFE = FCFF - interest(1-t) + debt issued - principal repaid. From net income, add non-cash expenses, subtract investment and operating NWC increases, and include net borrowing. Definitions of reported “FCF” vary, so identify whether the interviewer means CFO minus CapEx, FCFF or FCFE. EBITDA is not cash flow because it omits taxes, investment and working capital.

[F1142] What is project finance?
Asked by / question source: MUFG
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Project finance lends primarily against a project’s contracted or forecast cash flows, often through a separate entity with limited recourse. Size debt using downside debt-service coverage, construction risk, contracts, permits, counterparties and reserve needs. Municipal general-obligation bonds rely on the issuer’s pledged taxing resources, while revenue bonds rely on specified project/system revenues under their terms. Compare construction versus operating phases, rate-setting flexibility, demand, debt coverage and legal protections. Funding can combine bonds/loans, public contributions, grants and private equity; no capital structure is appropriate without the project budget and cash-flow profile.

[F1145] How the balance sheet is used for issuing loans and what to look for when issuing loans.
Asked by / question source: MUFG
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Credit underwriting asks whether cash flow can pay obligations in downside scenarios and what lenders recover if it cannot. Assess business resilience, leverage, interest coverage, fixed-charge coverage, free cash flow, liquidity and maturity/refinancing risk. Review collateral, guarantees and covenant headroom. Expected credit loss is approximately PD * LGD * exposure, though valuation also includes timing and risk premiums. The “3 Cs” are commonly character, capacity and capital, with collateral and conditions added in a five-C framework. Maintenance covenants are tested periodically; incurrence covenants when specified actions occur. Do not set leverage from EBITDA alone: cyclicality, cash conversion, CapEx and rates can make equal leverage ratios very different risks.

[F1148] How would you calculate WACC for a private company?
Asked by / question source: M&I 400 Questions Guide (2025), p. 183; Macquarie Group LA
Answer status: Guide answer
Answer origin: Supplied M&I 2025 400 IB Questions guide

ANSWER:
You still calculate the Risk-Free Rate, Equity Risk Premium, Cost of Debt, and Cost of Preferred Stock in the same ways. If you cannot determine the Cost of Debt from the firm’s filings, you could use the comparable public companies’ costs or estimate its credit default spread and add it to the Risk-Free Rate to estimate the Cost of Debt. The Cost of Equity calculation changes because private companies do not have share prices or market caps, and their Equity tends to be riskier than public companies’. So, you often use higher values for Beta when calculating the Cost of Equity (i.e., you may add a risk or illiquidity premium), and you use the median capital structure of the comparable public companies when re-levering Beta and calculating WACC. Private companies do not have easy-to-determine current capital structures or historical Betas, so you must rely on the data from comparable companies.

[F1149] Walk me through what happens on the three financial statements when PIK interest goes up by $100m? Assume 10% interest rate year 1, how to get from Revenue to FCF? Assume a 20% tax rate.
Asked by / question source: Macquarie Group LA
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Read the question first: $100 million of PIK interest expense is different from $100 million of principal bearing PIK. Take the expense reading, at a 20% tax rate.

• Income Statement: interest expense $100m, so Pre-Tax Income falls $100m and Net Income falls $80m.

• Cash Flow Statement: Net Income −$80m, add back the $100m of non-cash PIK, so cash rises $20m.

• Balance Sheet: Cash +$20m and Debt +$100m, against Retained Earnings −$80m, so both sides rise $20m and balance.

• Intuition: the charge costs no cash and saves $20m of tax, while adding $100m to what must eventually be repaid.

On the other reading — $100m of principal at a 10% PIK rate for one year — apply the same mechanics to $10m of interest: Net Income −$8m, cash +$2m, debt +$10m.

[F1150] Company A has $200 of bank debt and $300 of high-yield debt. Company B has $300 of bank debt and $200 of high-yield debt. Which company would have more expensive bank debt, and which would have more expensive high-yield debt? Why?
Asked by / question source: Macquarie Group LA
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Both have $500 total debt, but B has more senior bank debt. Assuming identical enterprise/collateral values and priority, B's bank lenders have a larger senior claim sharing the same collateral, and its high-yield debt has more senior debt ahead of it. Both tranches may therefore be riskier in B. Actual pricing requires collateral, guarantees, covenants, maturities and default probabilities; the totals alone do not fix spreads.

[F1151] Walk me through the different types of debt in detail.
Asked by / question source: Macquarie Group LA
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Debt is differentiated by issuer/guarantor, collateral, lien priority, contractual seniority, maturity, amortization and covenants. Revolvers and senior secured loans typically have floating rates and security; institutional term loans often have limited amortization. High-yield bonds commonly have fixed coupons, bullet maturities and call protection; they may be secured or unsecured. Subordinated/mezzanine debt ranks behind senior obligations and may include PIK or warrants. A leveraged loan is lending to an already highly levered or below-investment-grade borrower. Do not assume every revolver automatically outranks every term loan: inspect the lien and intercreditor documents.

[F1154] What happens to the financial statements if depreciation increases by $5? Assume a 20% tax rate.
Asked by / question source: Macquarie Group LA
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
A $5 increase in depreciation, with the deduction usable now and a 20% tax rate.

• Income Statement: EBIT and Pre-Tax Income fall $5 and Net Income falls $4.

• Cash Flow Statement: Net Income is down $4, but you add back the $5 of non-cash depreciation, so cash rises $1.

• Balance Sheet: Cash +$1 and Net PP&E −$5, so assets fall $4; Retained Earnings falls $4, and both sides fall $4 and balance.

• Intuition: the only cash movement is the $1 tax saving.

If the depreciation is not currently deductible there is no cash benefit and the difference goes to deferred taxes.

[F1155] Do you think the liquidation value of casino assets would provide debt holders a decent return on their collateral?
Asked by / question source: Macquarie Group LA
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Value the relevant legal entity and its distributable assets, then apply claims in legal priority. Secured creditors receive collateral value up to their claims; undersecured deficiencies may join the unsecured pool. Allocate any residual pool among pari passu unsecured claims pro rata; equity receives only what remains after creditor claims. Claims on different entities are not automatically pooled. A HoldCo normally owns only OpCo residual equity after OpCo liabilities, unless guarantees or direct asset claims change the result. Evaluate guarantee enforceability, collateral scope, intercreditor terms, fees and timing. Recovery/face value gives a simplified price in cents on the dollar; traded prices also discount time, uncertainty and required return.

[F1156] How does 10$ of PIK influence the three financial statements? Assume a 20% tax rate.
Asked by / question source: Miller Buckfire
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Ten dollars of PIK interest, at a 20% tax rate. PIK accrues onto principal instead of being paid.

• Income Statement: interest expense $10, so Pre-Tax Income falls $10 and Net Income falls $8.

• Cash Flow Statement: Net Income −$8, add back the $10 of non-cash PIK, so cash rises $2.

• Balance Sheet: Cash +$2 and Debt +$10 as the PIK accretes, against Retained Earnings −$8, so both sides rise $2 and balance.

• Intuition: no coupon is paid, so the only cash movement is the $2 tax saving — and the company now owes $10 more.

With no usable deduction, cash does not move at all and the benefit becomes a deferred tax asset.

[F1157] Walk me through the major lines of income statement?
Asked by / question source: Miller Buckfire
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Start with revenue, subtract COGS for gross profit, operating expenses and D&A for operating income/EBIT, then interest and non-operating items for pre-tax income, and taxes for net income. Add back D&A to EBIT for EBITDA. Examine growth, gross and operating margin, recurring versus unusual items and conversion into cash. Statements must be analyzed together: balance sheets show financing and working-capital requirements, and cash-flow statements test whether earnings produce liquidity. A financial-statement exercise without the transaction amounts or schedules cannot yield unique numbers.

[F1158] Why do you subtract net working capital to get free cashflow?
Asked by / question source: Miller Buckfire
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
For valuation, operating NWC usually equals non-cash operating current assets minus non-debt operating current liabilities. An increase uses cash and is subtracted from FCFF; a decrease releases cash. Receivables and inventory tie up cash, while supplier payables and customer advances finance operations. DSO = average AR/revenue * days; inventory days = average inventory/COGS * days; DPO = average AP/COGS * days (purchases may be better when available). Cash conversion cycle = DSO + inventory days - DPO. A higher DPO can improve cash flow but may also signal supplier stress; evaluate industry terms and overdue balances.

[F1162] Let's say the company has EBITDA of 100, and is valued at 5x. The company has a $100 senior secured term loan and $1,000 unsecured notes. What price to the unsecured notes trade at?
Asked by / question source: Miller Buckfire
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:

[F1163] What are some signs of a distressed company and some potential solutions available to that company?
Asked by / question source: Miller Buckfire; PJT Partners RSSG NY
Also covers: F1377
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Start with a 13-week cash-flow forecast, covenant/maturity review and entity-by-entity capital structure. Options include operational fixes, asset sales, new capital, maturity extensions, debt exchanges, out-of-court restructuring and court proceedings. U.S. Chapter 11 permits reorganization under court oversight, potentially with DIP financing and a plan; Chapter 7 generally liquidates assets through a trustee. A prepack requires sufficient creditor agreement in advance and may not suit contested claims or complex operational changes. A Section 363 sale is a court-supervised asset sale subject to required protections and approval. Compare going-concern versus liquidation value, creditor recoveries, speed, financing needs, execution risk and stakeholder incentives.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

[F1164] How does debt seniority affect cost of debt and valuation?
Asked by / question source: Miller Buckfire
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
WACC = E/(D+E)*Ke + D/(D+E)*Kd*(1-t), extending the weights for preferred capital if present. Use market-value, sustainable capital weights. Ke is often estimated with CAPM; Kd is the current marginal borrowing yield for comparable risk and maturity, not necessarily an old coupon. The debt tax adjustment reflects usable interest deductibility. Match currency, inflation and risk to the cash flows. Moderate leverage can lower WACC through tax shields, but greater default risk raises required debt and equity returns; the relationship is not universally decreasing. For a private company, estimate operating risk from public peers and use a defensible target capital structure.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

[F1165] Why can a DCF, precedent transactions and public comparables produce different valuation ranges?
Asked by / question source: Miller Buckfire
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Core methods are public trading comparables, precedent transactions and DCF. An LBO is a sponsor’s return-constrained price analysis; asset-based/liquidation value and sum-of-the-parts are additional approaches. Trading comps reflect current minority market prices; precedents reflect historical deal conditions, control and possible synergies; DCF reflects forecast cash generation and risk. Precedents often exceed trading comps, and LBO prices can be lower than strategic values, but there is no guaranteed ranking or universal valuation floor. Select methods suited to the business, compare their assumptions and present a range rather than averaging incompatible outputs.

[F1172] How would rising Federal Reserve rates affect the restructuring market?
Asked by / question source: Miller Buckfire
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Rising policy rates generally increase restructuring activity, with a lag, through three channels. First, debt service: most leveraged loans are floating-rate, so a higher base rate feeds directly into cash interest and compresses interest coverage even when EBITDA is flat, and a borrower at 5x leverage can drift toward its covenant levels without anything changing operationally. Second, refinancing: higher rates and wider spreads make maturity walls harder to clear, so a company that could previously refinance its way out of a problem must instead extend, exchange or restructure. Third, valuation: higher discount rates compress enterprise values, which pushes more capital structures underwater and moves the fulcrum security up the stack, changing who negotiates and who receives equity in a reorganisation. Expect covenant amendments, liability management exercises and distressed exchanges before formal filings, and more court processes where liquidity runs out first. Sponsors also have less room to support portfolio companies with cheap incremental debt, and DIP financing itself costs more. Pace and cause matter: a gradual increase alongside growth is absorbed far better than a rapid increase into a slowdown, and sectors differ by how much floating-rate debt and how much pricing power they carry.

[F1173] A bank holds $100 million of debt in a company worth $80 million. At what price would the debt trade? [Other liabilities and recovery assumptions are not recorded.]
Asked by / question source: Miller Buckfire
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
If the bank's $100 million claim is the only debt/priority claim and $80 million is distributable value, recovery is 80 cents on the dollar. The source lacks other claims and timing, so this is a simplified recovery indication, not a guaranteed trading price.

[F1174] A company with a positive EBITDA goes bankrupt, how?
Asked by / question source: Deloitte Corporate Finance; Evercore (compiled interview notes); Miller Buckfire
Also covers: F0439, F1183, F1881
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
EBITDA = revenue - cash operating expenses before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization; EBIT = EBITDA - D&A. Net income also includes interest, taxes and non-operating items. EBITDA helps compare operating performance across financing and depreciation conventions, but is not cash flow: it ignores CapEx, working capital and cash taxes. A business can have positive EBITDA yet run out of cash because of reinvestment, interest, maturities, working-capital needs or one-time payments. EBIT can be more meaningful for asset-heavy businesses because depreciation captures part of asset consumption. Evaluate adjusted EBITDA add-backs critically and avoid adding recurring costs back simply because management labels them exceptional.

[F1175] What is the difference between Chapter 7 and Chapter 11 Bankruptcy?
Asked by / question source: Evercore (compiled interview notes); Miller Buckfire
Also covers: F1869
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Start with a 13-week cash-flow forecast, covenant/maturity review and entity-by-entity capital structure. Options include operational fixes, asset sales, new capital, maturity extensions, debt exchanges, out-of-court restructuring and court proceedings. U.S. Chapter 11 permits reorganization under court oversight, potentially with DIP financing and a plan; Chapter 7 generally liquidates assets through a trustee. A prepack requires sufficient creditor agreement in advance and may not suit contested claims or complex operational changes. A Section 363 sale is a court-supervised asset sale subject to required protections and approval. Compare going-concern versus liquidation value, creditor recoveries, speed, financing needs, execution risk and stakeholder incentives.

[F1177] What are the differences between secured and unsecured debt?
Asked by / question source: Miller Buckfire
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Value the relevant legal entity and its distributable assets, then apply claims in legal priority. Secured creditors receive collateral value up to their claims; undersecured deficiencies may join the unsecured pool. Allocate any residual pool among pari passu unsecured claims pro rata; equity receives only what remains after creditor claims. Claims on different entities are not automatically pooled. A HoldCo normally owns only OpCo residual equity after OpCo liabilities, unless guarantees or direct asset claims change the result. Evaluate guarantee enforceability, collateral scope, intercreditor terms, fees and timing. Recovery/face value gives a simplified price in cents on the dollar; traded prices also discount time, uncertainty and required return.

[F1185] How much debt, expressed as a multiple of EBITDA, would you use in an LBO?
Asked by / question source: Moelis & Co. PFA NY
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Credit underwriting asks whether cash flow can pay obligations in downside scenarios and what lenders recover if it cannot. Assess business resilience, leverage, interest coverage, fixed-charge coverage, free cash flow, liquidity and maturity/refinancing risk. Review collateral, guarantees and covenant headroom. Expected credit loss is approximately PD * LGD * exposure, though valuation also includes timing and risk premiums. The “3 Cs” are commonly character, capacity and capital, with collateral and conditions added in a five-C framework. Maintenance covenants are tested periodically; incurrence covenants when specified actions occur. Do not set leverage from EBITDA alone: cyclicality, cash conversion, CapEx and rates can make equal leverage ratios very different risks.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

[F1187] How do you maximize IRR?
Asked by / question source: Moelis & Co. PFA NY
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
MOIC = total cash proceeds/total invested capital and does not account for timing. With a single entry and exit, annualized return or IRR = (exit proceeds/entry investment)^(1/years)-1. With interim cash flows, solve 0 = sum[CF_t/(1+r)^t]; use dated cash flows for XIRR. Earlier distributions generally increase IRR at the same MOIC. MOIC can favor a larger long-held gain while IRR favors rapid capital return; assess both alongside risk and absolute profit. ROE is accounting net income/average book equity and is not the same as an investment IRR.

[F1191] How would I calculate the revenue that the Starbucks earns in a week?
Asked by / question source: Morgan Stanley Investment Management
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Build revenue from operating units rather than assuming a growth rate: customers/volume * frequency/utilization * net price, plus ancillary streams. Separate variable costs from fixed costs to model contribution margin, operating leverage and break-even volume. For a pharmacy use prescription volumes, reimbursement/mix, dispensing margin and payer terms; roofing uses crew capacity, projects, ticket size and repair/replacement mix; software/telecom uses subscribers, ARPU, churn and network/service costs; a food outlet uses footfall, conversion, ticket and opening days. Forecast working capital, maintenance/growth CapEx and taxes. Value sustainable after-tax cash flow and cross-check peers; local concentration, regulation and reinvestment can explain different multiples despite similar current profits.

[F1192] Does saas software or on premises have higher margins typically: How would you model out a Saas company: Why are semiconductor companies extremely cyclical?
Asked by / question source: Morgan Stanley MP
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Mature SaaS can have high gross margins, but hosting/support costs, sales spending, churn and SBC matter; on-premises software can also have high license margins with different upfront revenue and cash timing. Model SaaS from opening ARR, new sales, expansion and churn, then delivery costs, CAC/payback, deferred revenue and investment. Semiconductors are cyclical because long capacity lead times, high fixed costs and inventory adjustments can amplify demand swings and cause shortages or oversupply.

[F1193] Walk me through a DCF, then what should I do with employee stock based compensation and what are your thoughts for the different ways to judge this versus other methods of stock based compensation.
Asked by / question source: Morgan Stanley MP
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Stock-based compensation reduces book earnings but is non-cash when recognized. The cash-flow statement adds it back; equity typically increases. In valuation it is an economic cost: either keep an expense for replacement compensation or add it back and explicitly model dilution/option value, avoiding double counting. For an option pool, specify whether managers receive a percentage of total exit equity, only gains above the sponsor’s entry equity, or value above a hurdle. Sponsor proceeds = exit equity less management proceeds; compare sponsor proceeds with sponsor investment to calculate MOIC and IRR. Vesting, strike prices, performance hurdles and tax treatment matter.

[F1194] If you had to choose between semis, software, and internet, rank which industry has the best business model What is the most interesting technology trend you follow?
Asked by / question source: Morgan Stanley MP
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
For SaaS, focus on recurring revenue quality: ARR/MRR, net and gross retention, churn, customer concentration, contract duration, gross margin and sales efficiency. NRR includes expansion less churn/contraction; GRR excludes expansion. Estimate cohort lifetime value from contribution profit and retention, compare it with fully loaded CAC, and test CAC payback. The Rule of 40 adds revenue growth percentage and a consistently defined profit-margin percentage; it is a heuristic, not a valuation formula. Value with DCF and growth/margin-adjusted EV/revenue or EV/ARR; profitable firms can use EV/EBITDA. Annual prepayments support cash conversion, but deferred revenue is an obligation. Sustainable returns matter more than growth at any cost.

[F1196] Walk me through bookings and revenue differences.
Asked by / question source: Morgan Stanley MP
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Bookings represent contractual sales commitments under the company’s definition; billings are invoices issued; revenue is recognized as performance obligations are satisfied. Cash is collected according to payment terms. Upfront billing for a year-long service may create deferred revenue that is released over the year. Bookings and ARR are non-GAAP operating metrics with company-specific definitions, so reconcile them to disclosures.

[F1197] Why would some companies be valued very highly even though very negative net income.
Asked by / question source: Morgan Stanley MP
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:

Negative current earnings may reflect early investment, non-cash charges or temporary losses, while credible future growth has value. The high valuation is justified only if risk-adjusted future returns and funding needs support it; persistent losses with no profitable unit economics do not become valuable merely because growth is high.

[F1200] How would you price a SaaS product?

[F1201] Rank the betas of a utility supplying electricity and gas to distributors, a biotechnology company that 3D-prints organs, and a business that pays you $100 on an even die roll but collects $50 on an odd roll. Explain your reasoning.
Asked by / question source: Morgan Stanley MP
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
The die payoff is independent of market returns, so its theoretical beta is zero despite risky outcomes. A regulated utility often has relatively low systematic operating risk. A speculative biotech can have large total risk, but clinical risk is often idiosyncratic; its beta is not necessarily higher than the utility's. The commonly expected order is biotech, utility, die, but justify it with market sensitivity and leverage rather than treating total volatility as beta.

[F1202] How would you explain DCF to a 10 year old?
Asked by / question source: Morgan Stanley MP
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Value equals the present value of expected cash flows. For an operating company, forecast FCFF from revenue, margins, taxes, reinvestment and working capital, discount at WACC, and add a consistently estimated terminal value. EV = sum[FCFF_t/(1+WACC)^t] + TV_N/(1+WACC)^N. Bridge to equity by adding excess cash/non-operating assets and subtracting debt, preferred claims and NCI; divide by diluted shares if needed. For a tree or other asset, forecast sale proceeds less maintenance, taxes and reinvestment over its actual economic life. A level end-of-year perpetuity is C/r; a growing one is next-period C/(r-g). Cash flow today is not the same as next-period cash flow.

A good business is not automatically a good investment at any price. For a short, include borrow cost, squeeze risk and loss limits; for a long, say what would invalidate the thesis. Without a specified company and current price, a particular target price or trade recommendation would be fabricated.

[F1206] Let's say company A has 10mm total outstanding shares at the share price of $25. It has the net income of $10. Assume that company A will acquire company B at $150mm in all-stock transaction and company B has the net income of $10. Tax rate is 20%. Will this transaction be accretive or dilutive and if so, how much?
Asked by / question source: Morgan Stanley MP
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Assume both net income amounts are $10 million. A's standalone EPS = 10m/10m = $1.00. New shares = 150m/$25 = 6m. Combined NI = 20m and shares = 16m, giving EPS $1.25: 25% accretion. The stated tax rate does not change already after-tax net income absent synergies or new financing. Ignore fees and purchase-accounting adjustments.

[F1209] Explain gross vs net retention Difference between bookings, billings, and revenue?
Asked by / question source: Morgan Stanley MP
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Gross retention = (opening cohort recurring revenue - churn - contraction)/opening recurring revenue. Net retention also includes expansion from that same cohort; exclude new customers. Bookings are contractual sales commitments, billings are invoices and revenue is recognized as service is delivered. Cash collection can precede or follow revenue. Company definitions and measurement periods must be consistent.

[F1210] Rank three companies by beta and WACC and explain your reasoning. [Company descriptions not recorded.]
Asked by / question source: Morgan Stanley MP
Answer status: Method / conditional answer — source details needed
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
The source omits inputs needed for a unique conclusion. CAPM estimates cost of equity as risk-free rate + levered beta * equity risk premium, with justified additional risk adjustments where appropriate. Estimate beta using a regression of stock excess returns on market excess returns, or bottom-up comparable-company betas. Beta reflects systematic risk; leverage, cyclicality and operating fixed costs can raise it. It is not a measure of all uncertainty or an invariant property of an industry. Historical estimates depend on window, frequency and benchmark, and CAPM’s single-factor assumptions are simplifications. Compare operating risk first, then financing; a higher-growth firm does not mechanically have a higher beta.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

[F1211] Give an example of a company where cost of debt exceeds cost of equity.
Asked by / question source: Morgan Stanley MP
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
WACC = E/(D+E)*Ke + D/(D+E)*Kd*(1-t), extending the weights for preferred capital if present. Use market-value, sustainable capital weights. Ke is often estimated with CAPM; Kd is the current marginal borrowing yield for comparable risk and maturity, not necessarily an old coupon. The debt tax adjustment reflects usable interest deductibility. Match currency, inflation and risk to the cash flows. Moderate leverage can lower WACC through tax shields, but greater default risk raises required debt and equity returns; the relationship is not universally decreasing. For a private company, estimate operating risk from public peers and use a defensible target capital structure.

[F1215] If you purchase a $100 shirt with $50 on a gift card and $50 in cash, and the shirt costed $30 to produce, please show the result on the 3 statements? Assume a 20% tax rate.
Asked by / question source: Morgan Stanley NY
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Assume the gift-card cash was received earlier and sits in Deferred Revenue. Tax rate 20%.

• Income Statement: Revenue +$100 and COGS +$30, so Pre-Tax Income is up $70 and Net Income is up $56.

• Cash Flow Statement: Net Income +$56, plus the $30 reduction in inventory, less the $50 reduction in Deferred Revenue, so cash rises $36 — the $50 collected now less $14 of tax.

• Balance Sheet: Cash +$36 and Inventory −$30, so assets rise $6; Deferred Revenue −$50 and Retained Earnings +$56 also give $6, so both sides balance.

• Intuition: only half the sale brings in new cash, because the gift-card half was collected when the card was sold. Do not count that cash twice.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

[F1216] How does a minority interest flow through the 3 statements if NI = $X?
Asked by / question source: Morgan Stanley NY
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
When a parent controls a subsidiary, its statements consolidate 100% of the subsidiary’s operations even if ownership is below 100%; noncontrolling interest represents the outside owners’ claim. Therefore, add the market value of NCI in the EV bridge when EBITDA includes 100% of subsidiary EBITDA. Parent equity value includes only the parent’s economic share. In the income statement, distinguish consolidated net income from net income attributable to the parent; NCI is separately presented within equity. A nonconsolidated equity-method associate generally contributes investment income rather than full EBITDA, so treat its investment value separately and avoid double counting. Debt recoveries must respect entity boundaries and guarantees.

[F1218] Is an acquisition accretive or dilutive when the target has a lower P/E than the buyer? Explain the relevant financing assumptions.
Asked by / question source: Morgan Stanley SF
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Accretion/dilution compares pro forma EPS with the buyer’s standalone EPS. Add target earnings and after-tax synergies, subtract after-tax new interest, foregone cash interest, purchase-accounting amortization and relevant ongoing costs; divide by buyer shares plus shares issued. New shares = stock consideration/buyer share price. In a simplified all-stock deal without other adjustments, a buyer with a higher P/E than the target’s purchase P/E is accretive. For debt or cash consideration, compare the target’s earnings yield with the after-tax funding/opportunity cost. EPS accretion does not prove value creation: price paid, risk and economic returns versus cost of capital still matter.

[F1219] How do you value the terminal value of an asset, what are the financial multiples in the deal you talk about, have a public stock, know the investors of the firm?
Asked by / question source: Morgan Stanley SF
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
The perpetuity-growth method is TV at year N = FCF_(N+1)/(WACC-g), with WACC greater than sustainable long-term growth g. The exit-multiple method is terminal metric (often EBITDA) times a defensible terminal multiple. Discount TV from its measurement date. Perpetuity growth is tied to long-run economics and reinvestment; exit multiples are grounded in market evidence but can embed cyclical mispricing. Check that growth, margins, reinvestment and returns on capital form a sustainable steady state. A finite-life asset or expiring drug may need a runoff value rather than a perpetual terminal value. Neither method is automatically always higher or more reliable.

[F1220] How would you evaluate the cash flow of an apple tree and how would you determine the appropriate discount rate to use ?
Asked by / question source: Morgan Stanley SF
Answer status: Open-ended answer framework
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Describe the customer problem, revenue model, unit economics, competitive advantage and addressable market. Evaluate growth and retention, margins, customer/supplier concentration, pricing power, regulatory exposure and required reinvestment. Reconcile reported earnings with cash generation and balance-sheet funding. In diligence, verify key claims against filings/contracts, cohort or customer data and independent industry evidence; stress downside assumptions. Recommend an action only after comparing its incremental cash return and risk with alternatives. If the business is unspecified, this is an analysis framework rather than a factual claim about a particular firm.

[F1221] Build a DCF in 30 minutes. [Case inputs not recorded.]
Asked by / question source: Morgan Stanley SF
Answer status: Method / conditional answer — source details needed
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
The source omits inputs needed for a unique conclusion. Value equals the present value of expected cash flows. For an operating company, forecast FCFF from revenue, margins, taxes, reinvestment and working capital, discount at WACC, and add a consistently estimated terminal value. EV = sum[FCFF_t/(1+WACC)^t] + TV_N/(1+WACC)^N. Bridge to equity by adding excess cash/non-operating assets and subtracting debt, preferred claims and NCI; divide by diluted shares if needed. For a tree or other asset, forecast sale proceeds less maintenance, taxes and reinvestment over its actual economic life. A level end-of-year perpetuity is C/r; a growing one is next-period C/(r-g). Cash flow today is not the same as next-period cash flow.

[F1222] What is one tech M&A deal you think would be interesting to see happen in the next year.

More EPS or more revenue alone does not prove value creation; incremental risk-adjusted returns should exceed the cost of capital. No unspecified deal supports a factual purchase multiple or recommendation.

[F1223] What are the 4 financial statements and how are they linked.
Asked by / question source: Morgan Stanley SF
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
The income statement measures performance over a period; net income flows into retained earnings and starts the indirect cash-flow statement. CFO adjusts net income for non-cash items and operating working-capital changes; investing and financing cash flows reconcile beginning and ending cash. Ending cash feeds the balance sheet. PP&E rolls forward by CapEx less depreciation and disposals; debt by borrowings, PIK and repayments; retained earnings by net income less dividends. Check assets = liabilities + equity. A fourth statement, changes in equity, reconciles share issuance, distributions, earnings and other equity movements. A model must use consistent dates, signs and cash-tax assumptions.

[F1224] Would you rather be a firm that has a P/E ratio of 20 or a interest rate of 6%.

Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
A P/E of 20 implies a 5% accounting earnings yield, which is not directly comparable with a 6% borrowing rate. If deciding whether to fund an acquisition with stock or debt, compare stock earnings dilution at 5% with after-tax debt cost 6%(1-t), then consider risk and capital structure. If comparing investments or firms, growth, cash conversion, claim priority and price are also needed.

[F1225] How to value the price of a taxi cab registration?
Asked by / question source: Morgan Stanley SF
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Value the transferable legal right to operate the taxi, not the vehicle alone. Cross-check recent comparable license transfers, accounting for transfer restrictions and competing transport models. Historical medallion prices may be poor anchors after structural market changes.

[F1226] What are the effects of the 3 financial statements if inventory increased by $10. Assume a 20% tax rate.
Asked by / question source: Morgan Stanley SF
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Buying inventory is not an expense; the cost sits on the balance sheet until the sale. Take $100 of inventory bought for cash and later sold for $150, at a 20% tax rate.

• At purchase: no income-statement effect. Inventory +$100 and Cash −$100. Bought on credit instead, Accounts Payable rises $100 and cash does not move.

• Income Statement, at sale: Revenue +$150 and COGS +$100, so Pre-Tax Income is up $50 and Net Income is up $40.

• Cash Flow Statement: Net Income +$40 and the $100 decrease in inventory is a positive, so cash rises $140 if the sale is collected immediately.

• Balance Sheet: Cash +$140 and Inventory −$100, so assets rise $40; Retained Earnings +$40, and both sides balance.

• Intuition: over the two steps the company recovers its $100 of inventory cost, earns $50 of profit and pays $10 of tax, so cash is up $40.

Do not count the inventory purchase and COGS as two separate expenses, and use AR instead of cash if the customer has not paid.

[F1228] How do you value a private company ?
Asked by / question source: Morgan Stanley SF; Société Générale NY
Also covers: F1533
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:

A private company requires reliable financials and suitable public/deal benchmarks; lack of information increases uncertainty rather than justifying an arbitrary precise value. Use a range with scenario/sensitivity analysis and reconcile results to the business’s cash-generation capacity.

[F1229] Why is an LBO often considered a valuation floor, and how does a dollar held by Apple differ from a dollar held by KKR?
Asked by / question source: Morgan Stanley SF
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
An LBO sometimes provides a lower valuation benchmark because a sponsor needs a target equity return without strategic synergies, but it is not a guaranteed floor. A dollar of unrestricted excess cash is initially worth roughly a dollar to either owner; differences arise from access/taxes and how effectively management can reinvest or return it. Apple’s operating cash is not automatically excess, and KKR-managed fund cash is not identical to KKR’s own corporate cash.

[F1231] Why cant you value a financial institution with EBITDA multiples?
Asked by / question source: Morgan Stanley Singapore
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:

[F1233] How to value a private company given that there is no beta?
Asked by / question source: Morgan Stanley Singapore
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Unlever comparable companies’ equity betas to remove financing risk, use a suitable peer median asset beta, and relever at the target capital structure. A common shortcut, assuming debt beta approximately zero, is beta_U = beta_L/[1+(1-t)D/E], and beta_L = beta_U[1+(1-t)D/E]. Use market-value leverage and a consistent marginal tax assumption. If debt risk is material, incorporate debt beta and a consistent tax-shield model. A private company lacks an observable stock beta, so operating comparables are the starting point; private status alone does not justify an arbitrary adjustment.

[F1234] If i operated a dental clinic and i bought a coffee machine, run me through the impact of this transaction on the 3 financial statements as the year goes by (requires you to think about tax and depreciation? Assume a 20% tax rate.
Asked by / question source: Morgan Stanley Singapore
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Capitalise the machine, then run the year. Take a $1,000 machine, a five-year life and a 20% tax rate.

• At purchase: PP&E +$1,000 and Cash −$1,000, an investing outflow with no effect on profit — buying equipment is not an expense.

• Income Statement, during the year: depreciation of $1,000 / 5 = $200, so Pre-Tax Income falls $200 and Net Income falls $160.

• Cash Flow Statement: Net Income −$160 plus the $200 depreciation add-back, so cash rises $40.

• Balance Sheet: Cash +$40 and Net PP&E $800, so assets fall $160 against Retained Earnings −$160, and both sides balance.

• Intuition: the clinic paid the full $1,000 upfront and recovers $40 a year in tax relief as the machine depreciates.

[F1239] Discuss the e-commerce deal you worked on and the valuation method you used.
Asked by / question source: Morgan Stanley Singapore
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Core methods are public trading comparables, precedent transactions and DCF. An LBO is a sponsor’s return-constrained price analysis; asset-based/liquidation value and sum-of-the-parts are additional approaches. Trading comps reflect current minority market prices; precedents reflect historical deal conditions, control and possible synergies; DCF reflects forecast cash generation and risk. Precedents often exceed trading comps, and LBO prices can be lower than strategic values, but there is no guaranteed ranking or universal valuation floor. Select methods suited to the business, compare their assumptions and present a range rather than averaging incompatible outputs.

[F1240] Company has 100million in revenue, 30% operating margin, D&A of 15 million, no interest and 15% tax rate. It has a EBIT/EV multiple of 10x. What is the P/E Ratio?
Asked by / question source: Morgan Stanley Singapore
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
EBIT = 100*30% = 30 and NI = 30*(1-15%) = 25.5, assuming no non-operating items. If the intended multiple is EV/EBIT = 10x, EV is 300; with no net debt, P/E = 300/25.5 = 11.76x. The literal wording EBIT/EV = 10x would instead imply EV = 3 and P/E = 0.1176x. Clarify the inverted multiple and net debt before answering. D&A is unnecessary to this EBIT-based calculation.

[F1242] If the acquisition is financed entirely with debt, at what interest rate does it become dilutive? [Original case inputs not recorded in this follow-up.]
Asked by / question source: Morgan Stanley Singapore
Answer status: Method / conditional answer — source details needed
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
The source omits inputs needed for a unique conclusion. Accretion/dilution compares pro forma EPS with the buyer’s standalone EPS. Add target earnings and after-tax synergies, subtract after-tax new interest, foregone cash interest, purchase-accounting amortization and relevant ongoing costs; divide by buyer shares plus shares issued. New shares = stock consideration/buyer share price. In a simplified all-stock deal without other adjustments, a buyer with a higher P/E than the target’s purchase P/E is accretive. For debt or cash consideration, compare the target’s earnings yield with the after-tax funding/opportunity cost. EPS accretion does not prove value creation: price paid, risk and economic returns versus cost of capital still matter.

[F1243] How to account for minority interests on a balance sheet?
Asked by / question source: Morgan Stanley Singapore
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
When a parent controls a subsidiary, its statements consolidate 100% of the subsidiary’s operations even if ownership is below 100%; noncontrolling interest represents the outside owners’ claim. Therefore, add the market value of NCI in the EV bridge when EBITDA includes 100% of subsidiary EBITDA. Parent equity value includes only the parent’s economic share. In the income statement, distinguish consolidated net income from net income attributable to the parent; NCI is separately presented within equity. A nonconsolidated equity-method associate generally contributes investment income rather than full EBITDA, so treat its investment value separately and avoid double counting. Debt recoveries must respect entity boundaries and guarantees.

[F1248] If you had a pile of cash how would you invest it?
Asked by / question source: Nomura Global Markets
Answer status: Open-ended answer framework
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:

[F1249] How did you price the options in your trading exercise?
Asked by / question source: Nomura Global Markets
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
An option gives the holder a right, not an obligation. A call payoff is max(S-K,0); a put is max(K-S,0). Value depends on underlying price, strike, maturity, volatility, rates, dividends and exercise/settlement terms. In a one-period arbitrage-free binomial model, q = [(1+r)S0-Sdown]/(Sup-Sdown) and option value = [q*payoff_up+(1-q)*payoff_down]/(1+r). Use risk-neutral probabilities when replication assumptions apply; a stated real-world 50% probability is not automatically q. More volatility generally benefits plain long options. Hedges reduce a specified risk but introduce costs, basis risk and possibly collateral/liquidity requirements; a swap exchanges contracted cash-flow streams.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

[F1250] How I would hedge my position using convertible debt.
Asked by / question source: Nomura Global Markets
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
A common convertible-arbitrage structure is long the convertible and short some underlying shares to hedge its equity delta. That retains credit, volatility, rates, borrow and liquidity exposures. If the question is hedging an existing stock or credit position with a convertible, the correct direction depends on that position and the instrument’s delta/credit exposure. A convertible is not a universal hedge; specify the risk, contract terms and hedge ratio.

[F1253] What is the key rates approach?
Asked by / question source: Nomura Global Markets
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Key-rate duration measures bond/portfolio sensitivity to shifts at specific points on the yield curve, such as 2-, 5- and 10-year rates, holding other key rates fixed under the chosen interpolation method. It helps hedge non-parallel curve moves that one aggregate duration number can hide.

[F1254] How would you use interest-rate swaps to hedge a floating-rate loan versus a fixed-rate government bond?
Asked by / question source: Nomura Global Markets
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
For floating-rate borrowing, receive floating and pay fixed on a swap to offset the loan’s floating interest and approximate fixed-rate funding, subject to basis and credit risk. For a fixed-rate bond asset, pay fixed and receive floating to reduce its fixed-rate duration exposure, matching notional and sensitivity appropriately. Hedge effectiveness depends on resets, curve, maturity, amortization and counterparty/collateral terms.

[F1255] What is a paired swaption ?
Asked by / question source: Nomura Global Markets
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
The source says "paired swaption," which is not sufficiently defined to establish the intended trade. If it meant a payer swaption, the holder has the right, not the obligation, to enter a swap paying fixed and receiving floating; its value generally benefits from higher relevant forward swap rates, other things equal. A receiver swaption gives the reverse right. If two swaptions are paired, specify their payer/receiver directions, strikes, expiries and notionals before explaining the payoff.

[F1256] What is a contingent swap ?
Asked by / question source: Nomura Global Markets
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
A contingent swap becomes effective or settles only if a specified event occurs, often completion of a transaction such as an acquisition. It can hedge funding/rate risk while reducing unwanted exposure if the deal fails. The contingent condition, fees, pricing, termination and settlement terms must be read carefully; it is not simply a standard swap with a free cancellation right.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

[F1257] Can you explain the meaning of CAR, CVaR ?
Asked by / question source: Nomura Global Markets
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
VaR is a loss threshold at a specified confidence level and horizon; it does not describe losses beyond that threshold. Expected shortfall/CVaR measures average loss in the selected tail, subject to modeling conventions. RAROC compares risk-adjusted profit with economic capital; the capital and expected-loss definitions must be specified. CAR often means regulatory capital/risk-weighted assets, but confirm the acronym. Key-rate duration measures sensitivity at individual maturity nodes rather than assuming a parallel yield-curve shift. Combine statistical measures with stress scenarios, liquidity analysis, concentration limits and model-risk review.

[F1265] What does a flat yield curve mean for a fixed income investor?
Asked by / question source: Nomura Global Markets
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
A useful macro answer links growth, inflation, employment and policy to earnings, discount rates, credit and investor positioning. Higher rates generally reduce fixed-rate bond values and increase funding costs; equity effects also depend on why rates rose and on earnings expectations. The Fed’s U.S. goals are maximum employment and stable prices; its inflation objective is measured using PCE, with core PCE often watched for underlying pressure. Fiscal policy changes government spending/taxes, while monetary policy changes financial conditions. An inverted curve can signal expected easing or weak growth but is not a certain recession forecast. Give a base case, a contrary case and indicators that would change your view rather than presenting a forecast as fact.

[F1267] A furniture manufacturer buys ten laptops for $100 each. Walk through the accounting effects. Assume a 20% tax rate. [Financing, useful life and tax assumptions not recorded.]
Asked by / question source: Nomura NY
Answer status: Method / conditional answer — source details needed
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Ten laptops at $100 each is $1,000. Decide first whether it is capitalised or expensed, because many companies expense items below a capitalisation threshold. Take it capitalised over a four-year life, bought for cash, at a 20% tax rate.

• At purchase: PP&E +$1,000 and Cash −$1,000, a $1,000 investing outflow with no income-statement effect.

• Income Statement, each year: depreciation of $1,000 / 4 = $250, so Pre-Tax Income falls $250 and Net Income falls $200.

• Cash Flow Statement: Net Income −$200 plus the $250 add-back, so cash rises $50 a year.

• Balance Sheet: Net PP&E falls $250 a year while cash rises $50, so assets and Retained Earnings both fall $200, and the balance sheet balances.

• Intuition: the $1,000 leaves on day one and $50 of tax relief comes back each year.

If instead the laptops are expensed immediately, Pre-Tax Income falls $1,000, Net Income falls $800 and cash falls $800 in year one, with nothing capitalised.

[F1270] How does a sale affect the three statements?
Asked by / question source: Nomura NY
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Use a transaction-by-transaction three-statement bridge. First identify whether the item affects revenue/expense, an asset/liability, or financing. Record the pre-tax and tax effect on net income. Reconcile net income to CFO using non-cash items and operating working-capital changes, then add investing and financing flows. Update cash, the relevant balance-sheet accounts and retained earnings, and verify assets = liabilities + equity. The numerical result requires amounts, timing, tax treatment and financing terms; an incomplete prompt does not support a unique set of balances. Separate initial recognition, subsequent operations and eventual repayment/disposal.

[F1272] What would happen to a companies stock if the CEO went on TV and started ripping up money?
Asked by / question source: Nomura NY
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
If the CEO destroys company-owned cash, equity value mechanically falls by the cash destroyed, with no direct change in operating EV if operations and risk are unchanged. The market could impose an additional loss because the act signals poor governance, impaired judgment or risk to future cash flows. If it is the CEO’s personal money, there is no direct company cash loss, but reputation and governance expectations may still affect the share price. Magnitude cannot be inferred without the facts.

[F1273] How do you calculate the cost of debt?
Asked by / question source: Nomura NY; UBS NY
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
WACC = E/(D+E)*Ke + D/(D+E)*Kd*(1-t), extending the weights for preferred capital if present. Use market-value, sustainable capital weights. Ke is often estimated with CAPM; Kd is the current marginal borrowing yield for comparable risk and maturity, not necessarily an old coupon. The debt tax adjustment reflects usable interest deductibility. Match currency, inflation and risk to the cash flows. Moderate leverage can lower WACC through tax shields, but greater default risk raises required debt and equity returns; the relationship is not universally decreasing. For a private company, estimate operating risk from public peers and use a defensible target capital structure.

[F1277] If all else equal, company A has a larger PE than company B, which one would you invest in?
Asked by / question source: Nomura NY
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
If everything relevant truly is equal, including positive, consistently measured earnings, future growth, cash conversion, leverage and risk, choose company B: its lower P/E means paying less per dollar of the same earnings stream and receiving a higher earnings yield. That is the answer under the stated premise. In real investing, check that equality actually holds: a low P/E can reflect peak or non-recurring earnings, weaker prospects or greater risk. A zero/negative earnings denominator makes the simple comparison unsuitable. Do not explain away the question by assuming different growth or risk after it explicitly holds those factors equal.

[F1278] Why multiple by (1-t) on ebit and not ebitda?
Asked by / question source: Nomura NY
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
EBIT is after depreciation, which ordinarily reduces taxable operating income, so EBIT*(1-t) captures a depreciation tax shield. EBITDA*(1-t) would ignore that deduction unless you separately add the tax shield. Starting from EBITDA, FCFF = EBITDA*(1-t) + D&A*t - CapEx - change in operating NWC under the simplified tax assumptions. Tax depreciation can differ from book D&A.

[F1282] What would you look at on a 10K/10Q when looking to invest in a company?

[F1283] If a company asked you to advise them on raising debt, what would you look at?
Asked by / question source: Nomura NY
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Credit underwriting asks whether cash flow can pay obligations in downside scenarios and what lenders recover if it cannot. Assess business resilience, leverage, interest coverage, fixed-charge coverage, free cash flow, liquidity and maturity/refinancing risk. Review collateral, guarantees and covenant headroom. Expected credit loss is approximately PD * LGD * exposure, though valuation also includes timing and risk premiums. The “3 Cs” are commonly character, capacity and capital, with collateral and conditions added in a five-C framework. Maintenance covenants are tested periodically; incurrence covenants when specified actions occur. Do not set leverage from EBITDA alone: cyclicality, cash conversion, CapEx and rates can make equal leverage ratios very different risks.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

[F1284] What terminal year value/ratio do people look for when building a DCF?
Asked by / question source: Nomura NY
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
The perpetuity-growth method is TV at year N = FCF_(N+1)/(WACC-g), with WACC greater than sustainable long-term growth g. The exit-multiple method is terminal metric (often EBITDA) times a defensible terminal multiple. Discount TV from its measurement date. Perpetuity growth is tied to long-run economics and reinvestment; exit multiples are grounded in market evidence but can embed cyclical mispricing. Check that growth, margins, reinvestment and returns on capital form a sustainable steady state. A finite-life asset or expiring drug may need a runoff value rather than a perpetual terminal value. Neither method is automatically always higher or more reliable.

[F1285] Why are publicly listed private equity companies difficult for the market to value?
Asked by / question source: Nomura NY
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Listed PE managers combine relatively recurring management-fee earnings with volatile, realization-dependent carried interest, investments on the manager balance sheet and different ownership/share structures. Fund AUM is client capital, not all an asset of the listed manager. Value fee earnings, carry and own investments consistently, considering fundraise cycles, fee-paying AUM, expenses, realization timing and tax/ownership claims.

[F1288] Is Negative NWC always bad?
Asked by / question source: Oak Hill
Also covers: F1289
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Negative operating working capital can be healthy when customers pay before delivery and suppliers are paid later; subscriptions and some retailers fund operations this way. It can also reflect overdue suppliers or distress. Examine cash conversion, deferred revenue, aging schedules and liquidity. For a growing business with sustainably negative operating working capital, growth can release cash; a slowdown can reverse that benefit. Distinguish operating NWC from the broad current-assets-minus-current-liabilities definition.

[F1290] I have two bonds, both with an 8% coupon, one with 6 years to maturity and one with 9. The cost of capital falls to 6%. Which bond's price changes more, and why? Separately, given an indenture, which three covenants would you focus on?
Asked by / question source: Oak Hill
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
On the bonds: the nine-year bond gains more. Both are priced at a yield below their coupon so both move to a premium, but the longer bond has more coupon payments and a more distant principal repayment, so a larger share of its value sits further out and is discounted more heavily. That is duration: with the same coupon and the same yield, longer maturity means higher duration and a bigger percentage price move for a given yield change. Convexity means the gain from a fall in yields is slightly larger than the loss from an equal rise, and that asymmetry is also greater for the longer bond. On the indenture: the three that usually matter most are the limitation on debt incurrence, which governs how much more debt can be layered on and at what level of the structure; the restricted payments covenant, which limits dividends, buybacks and investments that move value away from creditors, including transfers to unrestricted subsidiaries; and the limitation on liens, which stops new secured debt from being placed ahead of you. Change-of-control and asset-sale provisions come next. In every case the definitions and the permitted baskets decide what the covenant is actually worth, so read those rather than the headline, and the right ranking depends on where in the structure you sit.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

[F1291] Explain debt-incurrence covenants, restricted payments and limitations on liens.
Asked by / question source: Oak Hill
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Debt-incurrence covenants restrict additional borrowing unless tests or permitted baskets are satisfied. Restricted-payment covenants limit dividends, repurchases and certain investments. Limitations on liens restrict pledging assets to new secured creditors, protecting existing lenders from subordination. Examine definitions, baskets, grower provisions, permitted debt and exceptions; a headline covenant name does not establish the actual borrowing capacity.

[F1292] How many airplanes fly from Chicago to New York and back per day?
Asked by / question source: Oak Hill
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Build it from airports and aircraft, state the assumptions, and give a range. The city pairs are Chicago's two airports and New York's three, so start with the routes that actually exist rather than one line between two dots. Estimate daily departures per route from the carriers that serve it: a trunk route like O'Hare to LaGuardia or Newark might see 10 to 15 departures a day from each of two or three carriers, so perhaps 25 to 40 one-way departures; thinner pairings such as Midway to JFK add fewer. Sum the routes to perhaps 50 to 80 departures in one direction, then double for the return to get roughly 100 to 160 flights a day between the two cities. Sanity check it two ways: against total daily departures at O'Hare, of which a single major domestic market is a low single-digit percentage, and against seats needed, by multiplying flights by an average 150 seats and a load factor and asking whether that passenger count is plausible for the route. Say clearly what you are counting: scheduled passenger flights only, both directions, all airports in each metro area, and excluding connecting itineraries that merely pass through, which would otherwise be double counted. A defensible range with the method shown beats a single confident number.

[F1297] What is value investing?
Asked by / question source: Oak Hill
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:

[F1298] How do you calculate intrinsic value?
Asked by / question source: Oak Hill
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Choose between an intrinsic cash-flow valuation, market comparables, precedent transactions and, when relevant, asset-based or LBO analysis. Match the numerator to the claimant: EV with pre-interest operating metrics and equity with net income/FCFE. Normalize earnings, align periods and distinguish growth from capital intensity and risk. A private company requires reliable financials and suitable public/deal benchmarks; lack of information increases uncertainty rather than justifying an arbitrary precise value. Use a range with scenario/sensitivity analysis and reconcile results to the business’s cash-generation capacity.

[F1299] What are the disadvantages of the DCF approach?
Asked by / question source: Oak Hill
Answer status: Concept explanation / method
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
Value equals the present value of expected cash flows. For an operating company, forecast FCFF from revenue, margins, taxes, reinvestment and working capital, discount at WACC, and add a consistently estimated terminal value. EV = sum[FCFF_t/(1+WACC)^t] + TV_N/(1+WACC)^N. Bridge to equity by adding excess cash/non-operating assets and subtracting debt, preferred claims and NCI; divide by diluted shares if needed. For a tree or other asset, forecast sale proceeds less maintenance, taxes and reinvestment over its actual economic life. A level end-of-year perpetuity is C/r; a growing one is next-period C/(r-g). Cash flow today is not the same as next-period cash flow.

[F1306] How would you determine the amount of leverage to put on a company in the Consumers industry versus the Mining industry?
Asked by / question source: Oak Hill
Answer status: Prepared model answer
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:

A mature consumer-staples company with diversified recurring demand can often support more debt than a volatile mining company exposed to commodity prices, reserve depletion, large sustaining CapEx and environmental liabilities. Stress mining at a low through-cycle commodity price and consumer businesses for margin, demand and working-capital shocks. Discretionary consumer businesses may also be highly cyclical. ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

[F1307] Compare bonds with different coupons and yields and estimate their durations mentally. [Bond inputs not recorded.]
Asked by / question source: Oak Hill
Answer status: Method / conditional answer — source details needed
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
The source omits inputs needed for a unique conclusion. A bond’s price is the PV of coupons plus principal discounted at the required yield. Price moves inversely to yield. Macaulay duration is the cash-flow-PV-weighted average payment time; modified duration approximates percentage price sensitivity: change in price/price ≈ -Dmod * change in yield. Convexity improves the approximation for larger moves. A zero-coupon bond’s Macaulay duration equals its maturity; modified duration differs by the compounding adjustment. Longer maturity and lower coupon usually increase rate sensitivity. Credit spreads, embedded options and liquidity can move price independently of the risk-free curve.

[F1308] Calculate the duration of a bond issued at par with a specified coupon. [Coupon and maturity not recorded.]
Asked by / question source: PIMCO Product & Strategy
Answer status: Method / conditional answer — source details needed
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
The source omits inputs needed for a unique conclusion. A bond’s price is the PV of coupons plus principal discounted at the required yield. Price moves inversely to yield. Macaulay duration is the cash-flow-PV-weighted average payment time; modified duration approximates percentage price sensitivity: change in price/price ≈ -Dmod * change in yield. Convexity improves the approximation for larger moves. A zero-coupon bond’s Macaulay duration equals its maturity; modified duration differs by the compounding adjustment. Longer maturity and lower coupon usually increase rate sensitivity. Credit spreads, embedded options and liquidity can move price independently of the risk-free curve.

[F1309] Explain the financial crisis to a 7th grader in two minutes.
Asked by / question source: PIMCO Product & Strategy
Answer status: Framework — dated research required
Answer origin: Prepared model answer; not an official answer supplied by the named firms

ANSWER:
